The Complete Book of Taijiquan

《太极拳全书》 — compiled by Shen Jiazhen (沈家桢) et al. · People's Sports Publishing House (1995)
Compilers: Shen Jiazhen (沈家桢) and the editorial team — a single volume gathering the five classic manuals: Chen style (Shen Jiazhen & Gu Liuxin), Yang style (Fu Zhongwen), Wu style (Xu Zhiyi), Wu/Hao style (Hao Shaoru) and Sun style (Sun Jianyun)
Original: People's Sports Publishing House (人民體育出版社), Beijing, 1995
English & figure notes: TaichiNOW Editorial Board

A page-faithful translation of the original edition, rebuilt to the book's own printed page numbers; the posture figures are cropped from the scan and inserted at the positions they occupy in the book. This is the compilation volume that gathers the five classic manuals of the five great Taijiquan lineages (Chen, Yang, Wu, Wu/Hao and Sun) in one book.

《Complete Book of Taijiquan》 Chen-Style Taijiquan Yang-Style Taijiquan Wu-Style Taijiquan Hao-Style Taijiquan Sun-Style Taijiquan Note on the Treasured-Books Revised Edition Our publishing house has been established for more than forty years. In that time we have brought out many books that have been warmly received by our readers. These books have been reprinted again and again, showing their vigorous vitality. Books are humanity's mentors and friends, and sports books are the close companions of sports enthusiasts and sports professionals alike. So that our broad readership may keep these cherished books by their side, our publishing house has carefully selected a batch of excellent titles, and — guided by readers' feedback — revised and changed the content and titles of some of them, and redesigned their bindings, presenting them as treasured editions to our readers. We are certain that these treasured editions will find their way into refined studies everywhere, so that new and long-time readers alike will find them rewarding as soon as they open the covers.

People's Sports Publishing House Publisher's Note Taijiquan has a broad popular foundation in our country. The Yang-, Wu-, Hao- (武) and Sun-style taijiquan that evolved and were derived from the earliest Chen-style taijiquan are already familiar to and mastered by countless taijiquan enthusiasts.

In order to introduce — more systematically and completely to our broad readership — the movement characteristics and practice methods of each style of taijiquan, we have compiled into this Complete Book of Taijiquan the already-published Chen-Style Taijiquan (compiled by Shen Jiazhen and Gu Liuxin), Yang-Style Taijiquan (presented by Fu Zhongwen, recorded by Zhou Yuanlong, and edited by Gu Liuxin), Wu-Style Taijiquan (compiled by Xu Zhiyi), Hao-Style Taijiquan (compiled by Hao Shaoru and edited by Gu Liuxin), and Sun-Style Taijiquan (Revised Edition) (compiled by Sun Jianyun). When editing this book, we unified the table of contents and the pagination, corrected the obvious errors and improprieties, and made no changes to the original texts. In addition, to make the illustrations clear and the reading easy, we have re-drawn the illustrations for Hao-style taijiquan, and replaced the original photographic illustrations of Sun-style taijiquan with newly drawn line illustrations. Chen-style Taijiquan People's Sports Publishing House (Title page)

Chen-style Taijiquan Compiled by Shen Jiazhen and Gu Liuxin People's Sports Publishing House (Colophon)

Chen-style Taijiquan Compiled by Shen Jiazhen and Gu Liuxin Published by People's Sports Publishing House Printed by Beijing No. 1 Printing Works · Distributed by the Xinhua Bookstore, Beijing 787 × 1092 mm · 32mo · 182,000 characters · 10 25/32 printer's sheets First edition, December 1963 · Fourth printing, April 1982 Print run: 43,201–175,200 Unified book number: 7015·1209 · Price: 1.10 yuan Responsible editors: Yan Hai, Wang Jie Cover design: Zhou Menglin, Sun Jinrong Note on the Reprint This book was printed twice, in 1963 and 1964, and was not reprinted thereafter.

The Chen-style Taijiquan introduced in this book is the oldest of the Taijiquan schools. Its forms are divided into the First Route and the Second Route, both being routines transmitted by the late famous boxer Chen Fake. Chapters One, Two and Three of this book were written by Shen Jiazhen; Chapters Four and Five by Gu Liuxin. The movement illustrations were drawn from photographs of Chen Fake taken during his lifetime, and the postures not covered by these were supplemented with photographs of Chen Fake's son, Chen Zhaokui.

During the preparation of the original book, help was received from Zhou Yuanlong, Shao Bozhou, Yang Jingxuan, Chao Zhenmin, Lei Muni and others, and the text was proofread by Chen Zhaokui.

In this reprint only the "Introduction to Chen-style Taijiquan" has been rewritten and the "Preface" omitted; no changes have been made to the content of the original book. Readers are requested to point out any shortcomings, so that they may be improved.

The Essentials of Taijiquan …………………………………………………… 330 · V · Introduction to Chen-style Taijiquan Chen-style Taijiquan was founded by the famous boxer Chen Wangting at the end of the Ming and the beginning of the Qing dynasty. Chen Wangting was a native of Chenjiagou, Wenxian, Henan. From Chen Wangting onward, the Chen family transmitted and practised Taijiquan through the generations, continually refining and distilling the original routines, and gradually forming the First Route and the Second Route of the modern era. The linked movements of these two sets of forms were all carefully arranged; their speed and intensity differ, and their body methods, amount of exercise and difficulty differ too, yet both accord with the principles of gradual progress and of the mutual complement of hard and soft.

The movements of the First Route are comparatively simple — more soft than hard. It rests chiefly on the use of the four cardinal jins — ward-off, roll-back, press and push — and is assisted by the four corner methods of pluck, rend, elbow and shoulder; in the method of applying force it relies mainly on reeling-silk jin, with issuing jin as a supplement; the movements strive for suppleness, taking neutralising jin as the foundation, meeting hardness with softness and neutralising hardness, and in outward form it has the distinguishing qualities of slowness, softness and steadiness. In the beginning one practises with movements deliberately slow, with emphasis on training reeling-silk jin. In movement the body method leads the hand method, and the aim is to achieve the constantly varying effect of moving-apart (centrifugal force) and still-gathering (centripetal force). Because the movements are relatively slow and the frame is set at high, middle or low level, the amount of exercise can be adjusted; it is therefore suited both to those in good health who wish to strengthen their constitution and to the weak and to patients with certain chronic illnesses, for healing and health preservation. The Second Route (Cannon Fist) has more complex movements and demands speed and compactness — more hard than soft. In the use of jin it relies chiefly on pluck, rend, elbow and shoulder, with ward-off, roll-back, press and push as supplements; the movements strive for firmness and hardness and for rapidity, with emphasis on training elastic jin. The routine contains the movements of "darting, springing and leaping; shifting and dodging, flashing and fighting", and has the distinguishing qualities of fast, hard and leaping. In outward appearance its fastness, hardness and leaping seem no different from other styles of boxing, yet in essence it still has its own characteristics: in movement it continually rotates the waist and turns the spine, rotates the wrist and turns the shoulder, and rotates the ankle and turns the knee, forming a whole series of spiral movements in which one part moves and all parts move, threaded through the whole body. Thereby it obtains the unified function of opening with releasing, closing with gathering, and of containing closing within opening and containing opening within closing. Because this route is fast and its explosive power is strong, it is rather better suited to young and able-bodied people, or to those with better physical strength.

· 1 · Through training in the routine one may gradually come to grasp the content and essentials of such techniques as the mutual complement of hard and soft, that is, what is called the skill of "knowing oneself". In order to make use of the methods of adhering, connecting, sticking and following so as to understand jin, Chen-style Taijiquan also created the adversarial practice of push hands, that is, the skill of "knowing the other". Chen-style push hands stresses yielding the self to follow the other, bringing one's own technique into play according to the opponent's external force. When the opponent moves urgently, respond urgently; when the opponent moves slowly, follow slowly. Hence one must alternately practise the form and push hands before one can master the skill of understanding jin and reach a degree of proficiency.

Chen-style Taijiquan is an ancient style of boxing. The other schools of Taijiquan (such as the Yang, Wu, Wu-Hao and Sun styles) all developed and innovated on the basis of Chen-style Taijiquan. Chen-style Taijiquan preserves rather more of the martial characteristic of neutralising softly and issuing hard, and to study and research this school of Taijiquan is of great reference value for the inheritance and innovation of the martial arts.

The First and Second Routes of Taijiquan introduced in this book are the forms fixed in the later years of the late Taijiquan master Chen Fake (a descendant of Chen Wangting, 1887–1957).

· 2 · Chapter One · The Eight Characteristics of Chen-style Taijiquan Taijiquan is an outstanding style of boxing created and gradually developed by our forebears in the course of long life practice. Only after several hundred years of repeated practice and constant summing-up of experience did people gradually come to understand its inner connections and laws of movement. The Taijiquan manuals left behind by our predecessors are the summation of just such practice. They give us valuable clues for the study of Taijiquan and can help us to learn it better. But, being limited by their times, our predecessors also left no little dross in their theory; hence in our practice we should test it against our new understanding, discard its dross, absorb its essence, and gain a firmer grasp of its correct theory, so that this style of boxing may better serve the people's cause of health care. Therefore, in learning Taijiquan one must from the very outset hold firmly to the correct theory found in these Taijiquan manuals, become familiar with where its crux lies, master it thoroughly, and only then develop and deepen it step by step from that foundation.

Throughout the whole process of movement, Taijiquan is threaded from beginning to end with "yin and yang" and "substantial and insubstantial". In Taijiquan movement this shows as the fact that every form possesses the pairs "opening and closing", "round and square", "rolling and releasing", "insubstantial and substantial", "light and heavy", "soft and hard", and "slow and fast", and that its movement contains the unique forms of left and right, up and down, inside and outside, large and small, advance and retreat, and so on — opposites in unity. These are the basic principles that constitute Taijiquan.

· 3 · Taijiquan is not only unique in outward form; it also has its own special requirements in inner work. In practising Taijiquan one must first use intent and not clumsy force; hence Taijiquan is, inwardly, a movement of intent and qi, and outwardly a movement of stirring spirit and qi. That is to say, one must train both intent and qi. This quality of intent-qi movement is where the essence of Taijiquan lies, and it governs the other various characteristics of Taijiquan as well. Moreover, when practising Taijiquan, under the mutual exchange of the extension of the whole body and of reeling silk in the forward and reverse directions, the movement must display both softness and hardness and be rich in elasticity. Its dynamic quality requires that one part moves and all parts move, that it be threaded joint by joint and linked without interruption, completed in a single breath. Its speed requires both slowness and swiftness, the swift and the slow alternating. Its force requires both softness and hardness, hard and soft complementary. Its stance and movement require central correctness without bias, substance within insubstantiality and insubstantiality within substance, and closing contained within opening and opening contained within closing. Only when these conditions are present can Taijiquan fully develop its special function. In physical culture and health care it not only strengthens the organs of movement and the internal organs but also trains and strengthens the directing power of consciousness — that is, the ability to "use intent and not force" — so that one may smoothly direct the qi to be lively throughout the whole body. In this way one trains both qi and intent; intent and qi grow and strengthen each other, and the body is naturally made strong. Likewise in combat it has its own unique function: one may use lightness to overcome heaviness and slowness to overcome swiftness, subdue the natural and then master the natural; and in movement, one part moving means all parts move, "the whole body as one family", attaining the understanding-jin skill of knowing oneself and the other and of knowing the moment and the situation ①.

The theory of Chen-style Taijiquan has points in common with the theory of the other schools of Taijiquan, and points of difference as well. The characteristics of Chen-style Taijiquan are now set out one by one as follows.

  • ① To know the moment is to know time and master time; to know the situation is to know space and master space.

· 4 · Characteristic One · The Movement of Intent and Qi Governed by the Brain The manuals lay down:

(1) "Use the mind to move the qi; see that it is always sunk and steady, and only then can it be gathered and drawn into the bones";

(2) "Use the qi to move the body; see that it is always smooth and compliant, and only then can it move easily as the mind directs";

(3) "The mind is the command, the qi is the banner"; "the qi is best nourished by being kept upright, and then it does no harm";

(4) "The whole body's intent is in the spirit, not in the qi; if it is in the qi, then it stagnates."

From these four provisions it can be seen that Taijiquan is a boxing that uses intent to train intent, and also one that moves qi to train qi. But in practising, one must "use the mind to move the qi"; the mind is the one who gives the order and the qi is the "banner-bearer" that carries out the order; every single movement must use intent and not force, with intent moving first and form moving after, so that one may achieve "when intent arrives, qi arrives", and when qi arrives jin arrives; only then can the movement be steady, and only after long practice can the qi be gathered and drawn into the bones, reaching the deepest skill of "moving the qi". Hence it may be said that Taijiquan is a movement of intent and qi. "Using the mind to move the qi", "using the qi to move the body", and using intent rather than clumsy force, are the first characteristic of Taijiquan.

i. Inner qi and the use of intent As stated above, the qi is directed by the intent, and this qi is not the air of ordinary lung-breathing, but a kind of "inner qi". In the medical theory of our motherland this qi is called "original qi", "upright qi", the qi that passes through the channels, "pre-natal qi", and so on; it is held to be inherited from the mother's womb. In acupuncture and in qigong therapy this view is still followed today. Martial artists, on the other hand, call this qi "central qi", "inner qi", "inner jin" and so on, holding that only when one has practised to the point where this qi appears and one can master it is one's skill considered "at home".

· 5 · In sum, from ancient times down to the present, whether in the medical theory of our motherland or in martial and religious circles, the existence of this qi has been held, and various practical experiences confirm that such a qi truly exists. But modern science has not yet finally established what its substance is, and scholars at home and abroad who study the channel doctrine of our motherland's medicine do not agree on what this qi is, so that one cannot decide whom to follow. For example, some say this qi is simply the nerves, some say it is bioelectricity, some say it is a special secretion within the human body, some say it is a special functional system within the human body, and so on — every man a different view — and it still awaits further exploration. But the physiological phenomena of the human body are holistic: one cannot say that when intent moves, the nerves and bioelectricity do not move. Therefore, in expounding the qi spoken of in the boxing manuals, we provisionally assume it to be a composite of nerves, bioelectricity, the oxygen in the blood and so on, and provisionally assume it to be a function of the human body still awaiting clarification; the aim is first to inherit the theory of our predecessors so that we may further explore it. In practising Taijiquan one seems to be doing "consciousness gymnastics", always emphasising the use of intent, while the movements of the limbs are merely the outward expression of intent. In this "consciousness gymnastics" what is hidden within is the process of the activity of inner qi, and what shows without is the bearing and the stirring display of outer qi; hence inner qi may issue from within to without, and may also be gathered from without to within.

Although in practising Taijiquan one should "use the qi to move the body", in practising one must not merely think about how the qi runs within the body, but must fix the intent upon the movement; otherwise the bearing will become dull and sluggish, and not only will the qi fail to flow smoothly but it will produce the morbid sign of a scattered qi-situation, so that both intent and qi suffer harm. Hence the manuals say, "Intent is in the spirit, not in the qi; if it is in the qi, then it stagnates." For this very reason, in practising one must pay special attention to the outward display of bearing, since the outward bearing is precisely the showing-forth of the inner intent. Inner intent and outer spirit must not be separated for a moment; if the inner intent relaxes even slightly, the outer spirit will scatter. This point must be known in practising.

Chen-style Taijiquan holds that movement should have both softness and hardness, both round and square, both slow and fast, · 6 · opening and closing. We hold this to accord with the physiological laws of the human body. As everyone knows, when the human body moves, the bioelectric potential rises; when the body is still, the potential falls. And the hardness and softness, opening and closing, swiftness and slowness of Taijiquan movement precisely cause the potential to rise and fall accordingly. When the potential rises, the blood circulation quickens, the partial pressure falls, and oxygen and haemoglobin rapidly dissociate, so that one feels qi. Under normal conditions the nerves cannot remain excited at the same level for a long time; hence bioelectricity generally undulates, and the ceaselessly flowing undulations of hard and soft, swift and slow, round and square in Taijiquan movement likewise accord with this law.

In terms of intent and qi too, it accords with the above law. As said above, the outward bearing and the activity of outer qi are the display of intent and qi to the outside and represent the inner intent and qi. The central link in this outer display of spirit and qi is mainly to pour the inner consciousness into the outer movement and to bring the movement to display a concentration of attention that is single-minded, firm, and lively without stagnation. But the intensity of attention, like the activity of the inner nerves, likewise has the quality of rising and falling. Hence in practising one must adapt to this quality before attention can be stabilised. At the same time, only when attention is stabilised will the thoughts not wander. But to maintain attention at an equal intensity for a long time while practising is not easy to do. In fact, even within a moment the degree of fluctuation of attention has its highs and lows. Therefore, in the course of movement, if one adopts a calm, wave-less kind of movement without fluctuation, one not only violates the above physiological law but also destroys the stability of attention. Hence, in order to stabilise attention, Taijiquan adopts a series of provisions (such as the alternation of swift and slow, the mutual containment of opening and closing, the mutual generation of round and square, and the mutual complement of hard and soft), and unifies them within a single movement.

These provisions cause intent-qi movement naturally to produce fluctuation, and cause the outward stirring of spirit and qi and the inward fluctuation of intent and qi to be coordinated, thereby raising the inner intent-qi movement, which in turn promotes the outer movement.

· 7 · Because Taijiquan is a movement of intent and qi, one who has long practised it can, merely by thinking of a certain part of the body, produce activity of qi there. Hence many people spare no time and go through the form morning and evening, constantly correcting the form, precisely in order to achieve this. Once the movements of Taijiquan have been practised into a fixed form, the processes of excitation and inhibition in the cerebral cortex can accurately alternate according to a definite programme; at the same time, the muscles can contract and relax in coordination, and even if one is suddenly stimulated by chance, this coordinated movement will not be impaired. To achieve this shows that a most solid coordinating relation has been established between the activity of the muscles and the internal organs: as soon as intent arrives, qi arrives, and as soon as qi arrives, jin arrives.

ii. The realisation of intent-qi movement It should also be pointed out that in the use of intent and qi, Taijiquan and the static exercises (sitting, standing and lying practice) are the same, both laying stress on training intent and training qi. But Taijiquan trains amid movement (seeking stillness in movement), and so is called a movement of intent and qi; whereas the static exercises have no movement, seeking stillness alone, so the two must not be confused.

Precisely because Taijiquan trains both inner and outer, and seeks stillness amid movement, in order to do the inner intent-qi movement well one must clearly bring out the outer stirring of spirit and qi. As the "Heart Understanding of Practising the Form" says, "The form is like a falcon striking a hare; the spirit is like a cat catching a mouse." And to achieve this skill of inner-outer union and mutual training, one must fulfil the requirements of the seven characteristics set out below in this chapter; that is, only by realising those seven characteristics can this characteristic — that Taijiquan is a movement of intent and qi — be realised. In other words, although the characteristics are divided into eight, they actually dwell together in one unity, with inner connections, and are separated only for convenience of exposition.

Before describing the remaining seven characteristics in detail, let us briefly explain the role of these seven characteristics in carrying out the characteristic of intent-qi movement. Characteristic Two — elastic movement, which is the extension of the limbs and body, and may be said to be, · 8 · the result of elasticity. The soft, yielding elasticity is the inner factor that promotes the stirring of the limbs and body. Without elasticity the movement becomes rigid, and then the outward display of stirring spirit and qi can no longer be formed, and of course it cannot be coordinated with the inner fluctuation of intent and qi.

Characteristic Three — spiral movement, which can strengthen the rising-and-falling fluctuation of movement. If movement goes straight back and forth, without the up-and-down, inside-and-outside turning, it cannot bring about the rising-and-falling fluctuation of spirit, intent-qi and body method. For this, one must combine the wrist-turning and shoulder-turning, ankle-turning and knee-turning, and waist-turning and spine-turning of forward-reverse spiral movement, so as to achieve a Taiji jin that is threaded as one through the spirals and poured into all movements. In this way, when one does not move, so be it; when one moves, the situation of stirring is naturally formed, becoming the movement core for doing intent-qi movement well.

Characteristic Four — adjusting substantial and insubstantial, which is the root of the agile exchange of intent and qi and of the sensation of round liveliness like a pearl, and is the power-source of the stirring. The exchange of substantial and insubstantial in which the upper follows the lower and the lower follows the upper can cause the spirit-qi and the body method to be lively without stagnation, and the stirring of spirit-qi arises therefrom. If upper and lower cannot follow each other and substantial and insubstantial are not adjusted, then inner jin cannot reach central correctness without bias. If inner jin is biased, then inner jin and body method lean to one side, losing the requirement of supporting all eight directions. It is not easy to achieve the stirring of spirit-qi in a posture where the inner jin leans to one side.

Characteristic Five (threading joint by joint) and Characteristic Six (completed in a single breath) are essentially two stages of one characteristic; the former means that within one form the main joints of the whole body are required to be threaded like a dragon, passing through one joint after another in sequence; the latter means that in practising the whole set one form must be linked to the next without interruption, completed in a single breath, so as to enlarge the amount of exercise and achieve the concrete requirement of joint-by-joint stirring. If one cannot thread joint by joint, then broken jin arises, and where jin is broken there can be no stirring to speak of. If one cannot complete it in a single breath, then it is broken and unlinked, and where it is unlinked each form becomes isolated and cannot stir in a single breath. Hence if these two characteristics are not done well, the stirring of spirit-qi cannot be done well, so they are closely interlinked.

· 9 · Characteristic Seven (the mutual complement of hard and soft) and Characteristic Eight (the alternation of swift and slow) are two characteristics that unify the contradictions of two opposites, and are also characteristics that must be possessed technically in order to achieve the stirring of spirit and qi. Without this intertwining-as-one of swift and slow, hard and soft, it is not easy to make the preceding characteristics cooperate closely and to produce rising-and-falling fluctuation. Because these two characteristics require one to achieve "soft yet slow" and "hard yet swift", requiring hardness and swiftness to rise like an advancing wave and softness and slowness to fall back like a receding wave, such mutual intertwining will form a ceaselessly flowing propelling action. This action of the mutual complement of hard and soft and of the alternation of swift and slow can, in physical culture, achieve slow and soft movement of qi and hard and swift movement landing-points, so that qi travels throughout the body without any trace of dullness; and in combat it enables one to "respond urgently when the other moves urgently, and follow slowly when the other moves slowly", so that one can achieve the yielding of "when the other is hard, I am soft" and the sticking of "when the other is soft, I am hard". These two characteristics can drive the inner intent-qi movement and the outer stirring of spirit-qi to the peak of fluctuation.

From this it can be seen that Characteristic One is the characteristic that governs the other seven, but at the same time it can only be realised with the help of the other seven. Their relation is like that of the peony and its green leaves: they complete each other, and also restrain each other and promote each other. This must be known when first learning.

To make the first characteristic easier to grasp, its essentials are summarised as follows:

(1) In practising, the intent must always be concentrated on the movement, using intent to move qi; one must not merely silently think about how the inner qi runs.

(2) In practising, the movement must be smooth and steady, and when jin reaches its end-point it must display its jin category — these are the three measures by which intent and qi are made to stir.

(3) Firmly grasp the outer display of the stirring of spirit and qi, so as to avoid dullness and sluggishness, and in turn promote the inner intent-qi movement. (4) Skilfully use the other seven characteristics, so as to coordinate and raise the intent-qi movement.

· 10 · Characteristic Two · The Elastic Movement of Extended Limbs and Body The manuals lay down:

(1) "Empty the collar and lift the crown; sink the qi to the cinnabar field";

(2) "Hollow the chest and raise the back; sink the shoulders and drop the elbows";

(3) "Loosen the waist and round the crotch; open the hips and bend the knees";

(4) "Gather the spirit and restrain the qi; extend the body and hands".

From the four provisions listed above it can be seen that emptying the collar and lifting the crown and sinking the qi to the cinnabar field serve to extend the trunk; hollowing the chest and raising the back serve to extend the back, using the front of the chest as a pillar; sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows serve to extend the arms; and loosening the waist and rounding the crotch and opening the hips and bending the knees, and enabling the legs to turn roundly and lively, are the result of extending the legs in this particular posture. Hence the stepping of Taijiquan must, in the posture of rounded crotch, loosened waist, opened hips and bent knees, exchange substantial and insubstantial by turning the ankles and rotating the legs. Outwardly this is the display of the reeling-silk jin of the legs; inwardly, in fact, it promotes the extension of the legs. This series of extensions in turn brings about the extension of the whole body; the limbs and body not only produce elasticity, forming ward-off jin, but, because the whole body is extended, the spirit is also naturally raised. Hence, so long as one has the extending posture, one will not easily fall into the fault of straining and drumming up force (clumsy force), and conditions are provided for natural loosening and for the extension of body and hands. Therefore the elastic movement of extended limbs and body becomes the second characteristic of Taijiquan.

i. Extension of the limbs and body As said above, in practising Taijiquan the limbs and body must be extended, so as to strengthen the elasticity of the whole body; only with elasticity can one proceed further to ward-off jin. That is to say, ward-off jin is born of elasticity, and elasticity is born of the extension of the limbs and body. As to how each part of the body is to be extended, it is now set out one by one according to the manuals as follows.

· 11 · (1) Emptying the collar and lifting the crown, and sinking the qi to the cinnabar field — what is meant by "emptily lifting the crown jin" is that the crown jin is emptily lifted upward, and sinking the qi to the cinnabar field is sinking the qi downward into the cinnabar field; taken together, in consciousness there is the intention of pulling apart in opposite directions, and this gives the body the sensation of extension. (2) Hollowing the chest and raising the back — hollowing the chest requires that the chest neither protrude nor cave in, making the chest a pillar for the extension of the back, since in mechanics a compression member is not allowed to be bent. The back relies on this pillar to be extended, and this is the extension of the back. On this point, a beginner must not mistake a protruded chest for raised back; for a hunched back will make the front of the chest cave in, which will make the front of the chest lose its pillar function, so that not only does the back lose its extending elasticity but it is also harmful to health.

(3) Sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows — the main function of sinking the shoulders is to join the arms firmly to the shoulders through sinking down. Only when the arm is joined firmly to the shoulder can the arm take root. At the same time, dropping the elbows brings about extension between the elbows and the shoulders. When the arms perform the spiral reeling-silk movement, it is the dropping of the elbows that serves as its centre. At the same time, dropping the elbows and sitting the wrists can also extend between the elbows and the wrists. Hence sinking the shoulders, dropping the elbows and sitting the wrists constitute the extension of the whole arm.

(4) The rotation of opening the hips and bending the knees — this is the extension of the legs. The legs stand on the ground, so extension is comparatively difficult. Hence the requirement of opening the hips and bending the knees is laid on the legs, requiring that in this particular posture (rounded crotch) the substantial and insubstantial be exchanged by spiral movement, which shows mainly in the rotation of the knee-cap. Thus, when the leg rotates outward, the outer side is extended while the inner side contracts. This rotation of the legs, coordinating with the rotation of the hand, arm and body, becomes the rotation of the whole body, rising step by step, and one may then attain the jin of complete unity — "its root is in the feet, it issues in the legs, it is governed by the waist, and it takes form in the fingers".

Looking over the four provisions listed above, it can be seen that Taijiquan lays a requirement of extension on the trunk, the hands and the feet. Thereby not only is elasticity produced by the extension, becoming the founda- · 12 · tion of Taijiquan's ward-off jin, but also people's spirit is naturally raised, so that one does not fall into the morbid sign of drumming up force and so producing clumsy force ①.

ii. The physiological effect of extension When a muscle is subjected to force it may lengthen to a certain degree, but as soon as the external cause of the lengthening is removed it immediately returns to its original state — this is the elasticity inherent in the muscle itself. Ordinary common exercise is simply the training and raising of this elasticity. Judged by human physiology, this elastic contraction and extension of the muscle can have the following four effects:

(1) It can give the muscle's own ability to contract and extend a good training, and can make smooth the dense network of capillaries within the muscle.

(2) It can strengthen the metabolism of the tissue cells and stimulate all the life processes within the body.

(3) It can strengthen the gas exchange of the muscles and of all other tissues and organs.

(4) It can give the body more oxygen, and at the same time raise the rate at which the various tissues and organs utilise oxygen.

Taijiquan is not a mere movement of the limbs and body. What shows without is the stirring of the bearing, with postures extremely complex and varied; what is hidden within is gathered spirit and restrained qi, "using the mind to move the qi" — all of which has been explained in detail under the first characteristic. Moreover, Taijiquan not only trains both inner and outer, but also performs, throughout the extension of the limbs and body, the spiral forward-reverse reeling-silk movement of twisting back and forth. Thereby not only is the elasticity of the muscle itself

  • ① Extension gives the body and hands a sensation within of being slender and long, whereas the production of ward-off force is due to drumming up force, which gives the body and hands a sensation within of being thick and short. Hence extension of the limbs and body will naturally not fall into the morbid sign of drumming up force and so producing clumsy force.

· 13 · given good training, and the speed of the blood circulation is raised, so that illnesses caused by impeded blood flow can be eliminated. This is one of the important effects produced by Taijiquan's extension of the limbs and body and its raising of the spirit.

Moreover, the elastic movement of Taijiquan also has a marked influence on lowering blood pressure, because in the process of the muscle's contraction and extension there are produced such substances as triphosphoric acid and adenylic acid that dilate the blood vessels. At the same time, in the activity of threading joint by joint the number of capillaries opened within the muscle increases many times over, and this too enlarges the cross-section of the blood-vessel communication, and so can lower blood pressure. Furthermore, because in practising the muscles repeatedly extend and recover, the blood vessels are not easily hardened. Especially with the coordination of the twisting, back-and-forth spiral movement, hardening of the blood vessels can be still further prevented. A person who has long practised Taijiquan for many years will, in practising, feel that the blood vessels in the back and in the four limbs seem to have enlarged, making one feel relaxed and comfortable in movement; whereas after some time without practice one has a sensation of blockage. The production of this phenomenon is precisely due to the increase or decrease in the number of opened capillaries.

iii. The eight gateways of jin and elastic ward-off jin Taijiquan requires the use of intent and not clumsy force, but this does not mean using intent and not using jin, for Taijiquan is constituted of the eight gateways of jin. All eight gateways of jin possess extending elasticity, and so they are called "jin" and not "force". Though the names of the eight gateways differ, in essence they are but one ward-off jin, and the other seven are merely given other names because their direction and function differ. Hence Taijiquan may also be called the boxing of ward-off jin. The content of the eight gateways is now analysed as follows, so as to make the second characteristic easier to grasp.

(1) With the whole in motion, when the centre of the palm reels silk from inside outward, it is called ward-off jin;

(2) With the whole in motion, when the centre of the palm reels silk from outside inward, it is called roll-back jin;

(3) When both hands at the same time ward off the ward-off jin outward crosswise, it is called press jin;

· 14 · (4) The downward ward-off jin in which the centre of the palm circles downward, touching one point without leaving it, is called push jin;

(5) The ward-off jin in which both hands cross and separate to left and right, front and back, is called pluck jin; (6) The jin that rolls the ward-off jin up and stores it, then suddenly shakes and flicks it out within a short distance, is called rend jin;

(7) When the wrist has gone beyond the round-square circle and wards off outward using the ward-off jin of the second line of defence, it is called elbow jin;

(8) When the elbow has gone beyond the round-square circle and wards off outward using the ward-off jin of the body as the third line of defence, it is called shoulder jin.

Summing up what has been said above, in the last analysis the one chiefly trained within is ward-off jin. Ward-off jin is a soft, ceaseless "spring jin". This is the problem that must first be made clear.

iv. Mastering elastic movement (ward-off jin) (1) To train ward-off jin one must first destroy the original stiffness in a person's body. In any movement — for example lifting a heavy object — force must be used, and over the years this makes a person form, from childhood on, the habit of drumming up force to carry or lift weights. Drumming up force is straining, also called clumsy jin, whereas what Taijiquan requires is the spring jin of the whole body extended. Hence in practising Taijiquan there should be two stages: first the stage of eliminating the drummed-up force, then the stage of growing the new spring jin. If the old jin does not go, the new jin is not born; so the boxing discourse says, "Movement is like steel tempered a hundred times; what hardness can it not shatter ①?" That is to say, one must pass through a hundred smeltings and a thousand temperings in which no clumsy force whatever is used, and, in the various postures of extension and loosening, perform the twisting, back-and-forth kneading, before one can reach the point of extreme softness and shatter the person's

  • ① The "Heart Understanding of Practising the Form" is a theoretical document guiding the practice of the form; it is not a rule governing two-person push hands.

· 15 · old stiffness — that is to say, so long as movement is like steel tempered a hundred times, then any stiff jin at all may be shattered without remainder. This is the sum of the experience of former masters of boxing, so this transforming of hardness into softness is an indispensable stage, which the beginner must on no account neglect. The longer this stage lasts the better, because only thereby can one become more thoroughly soft. Otherwise, if one's softness is not thorough, in the future it will be hard for the practitioner to avoid remaining within the shortcoming of having too little softness and too much hardness, and so being unable to reach balance.

(2) Ward-off jin is not a jin inherent in the human body. As said above, of the eight gateways of jin, ward-off jin is the basic one. Ward-off jin is born of elasticity; this elastic jin is not only the elasticity of the muscle itself, but is trained from the joint extension of the bones and ligaments and so on together with the muscles upon the basis of muscular elasticity. Hence it is not a jin inherent in the human body, but a jin that can be produced only after long practice. Its development is from nothing to having, and from having to strength. To train this elastic ward-off jin, one should do one's utmost according to the four provisions of the manual given above. The key essential is still to begin from the use of intent, so that in one's thinking there is the idea of extension. When this has been used for a long time, then together with the concrete extension of the limbs and body, one will not readily go astray.

(3) Gathered spirit and restrained qi are the foundation for strengthening elasticity and raising ward-off jin. When the limbs and body are extended, a person's spirit is raised and concentrated and the qi sinks and is restrained within — this is a naturally occurring phenomenon. Conversely, that is to say, so long as spirit is gathered and qi restrained, one can guide consciousness to have the bearing of extension, causing the limbs and body to extend, and thereby raising elasticity and strengthening ward-off jin. At the instant of gathered spirit and restrained qi, the muscle groups contract more fully, while the opposing muscle groups relax more fully; hence, through long training in relaxation and contraction, the elasticity of each part of the limbs and body is naturally strengthened, and at the same time the constitutional quality of the body is raised.

To make the second characteristic easier to grasp, its essentials are summarised as the following five points:

(1) Taijiquan chiefly trains ward-off jin; ward-off jin is born of elasticity, and elasticity is born · 16 · of the extension of the limbs and body, so one must pay attention to the extension of the limbs and body.

(2) The extension of the trunk and the upper part must be by emptying the collar and lifting the crown, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, and hollowing the chest and raising the back.

(3) The extension of the hands and feet must be by sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows, loosening the waist and rounding the crotch, and the rotation of opening the hips and bending the knees.

(4) In training ward-off jin, first seek softness and yielding so as to remove the old force (clumsy force), and at the same time extend so as to grow the new elastic jin.

(5) Only practising with gathered spirit and restrained qi is the inner factor that strengthens ward-off jin.

Characteristic Three · The Spiral Movement of Reeling Silk The manuals lay down:

(1) "Movement is like drawing silk";

(2) "Movement is like reeling silk";

(3) "However you open out and gather in, never for a moment may you depart from the Taiji";

(4) "The skilled hand, in a single movement, is a single Taiji; when the traces have wholly melted away, it returns to nothingness."

From the four provisions listed above it can be seen that Taijiquan movement must have the form of drawing silk. Drawing silk is drawn out with a revolving motion, for in drawing straight within revolving a spiral form is naturally produced — this is the unity of the opposites curved and straight. As for reeling-silk jin or silk-drawing jin, both mean this. Because in the process of reeling, in extending and contracting the four limbs one likewise produces a spiral appearance, so the boxing discourse says that whether the movement is a large one opening out or a small compact one, one may never depart from this Taiji jin of opposites in unity. When one has practised until proficient, the reeling-silk circles are practised smaller and smaller, reaching the state of there being a circle but no circle seen · 17 · — the state where one knows purely by intent ① — and so the spiral movement of the unity of the opposites of forward and reverse reeling silk becomes the third characteristic of Taijiquan.

i. The essence of movement as reeling silk Taijiquan movement must be like reeling silk, or like drawing silk. Both these figurative comparisons say that the appearance of the movement is like a spiral. At the same time, this spiral must travel along an arc: just as a bullet, after passing through the rifling in the gun-barrel, in moving through space has both a spiral rotation of its own and a parabolic path of movement. The reeling-silk jin of Taijiquan must possess this appearance.

Having explained above the meaning that movement must be like reeling silk, how then should it be carried out in actual movement? It is extremely ordinary and simple: under the requirement of one part moving and all parts moving, the centre of the palm turns from inside outward or from outside inward during the movement ②, making it form the image of the Taiji diagram (as in Figure 1). At the same time, because the centre of the palm turns inward and outward, in the upper limbs this shows as turning the wrist and rotating the shoulder, in the lower limbs as turning the ankle and rotating the leg ③, and in the trunk as turning the waist and rotating the spine. The three combined form a spatial revolving curve whose root is in the feet, which is governed by the waist, and which takes form in the fingers. This is a requirement that Taijiquan must fulfil. Hence the manuals especially point out that in practising, whether the movement opens out broadly or is compact

  • ① The small frame that Mr Yang Shaohou set out in his later years shows only the issuing of jin, not the movement. This is because the movement circles have become so small as to be invisible, leaving only the concrete display of the issuing of jin; it is the proficient skill of compactness in which no circle is seen.
  • ② What is meant by turning from inside outward or outside inward is standardised by the turning of the index finger. As in Figure 1, when the hand goes from point 1 to point 2, the movement of the index finger at this time is a turning from inside outward, and so it is forward reeling; when the hand goes from point 2 to point 3, the movement of the index finger is a turning from outside inward, and so it is reverse reeling.
  • ③ The division of the legs' forward and reverse reeling silk is standardised by the direction of rotation of the knee: when the knee, from the inner side of the patella, turns forward and downward, obliquely reeling outward, or from the outer side of the patella turns backward and upward, obliquely reeling inward, both are forward reeling; when the knee, from the outer side of the patella, turns forward and upward, obliquely reeling inward, or from the inner side of the patella turns backward and downward, obliquely reeling outward, both are reverse reeling.

and for threading joint by joint like the whole body as one family, there is also the coordination of the two pairs of directional reeling silk, large-small and advance-retreat, so as to satisfy the special needs of health and of combat. Hence every form of Taijiquan must, upon the basis of the forward-reverse basic reeling silk, have at least three pairs of directional reeling silk combined together in the movement. So long as one has grasped this law, one may have a definite basis for the movement in drawing arcs, and both learning and correcting the forms will be much easier. In practising, if one feels that some movement has lost its proper position and feel, one may, according to where the reeling silk is not smooth, shift the waist and legs a little, so as to obtain smoothness, and the posture can then be corrected. Hence to have grasped the reeling silk is to have grasped the tool of self-correction. Let us now give examples to illustrate its function.

(1) "Cloud Hands" — this form is the only one among the thirteen postures that contains the large left-right reeling silk of double forward turning to double reverse. In the movement, the basic reeling silk of the two hands is the forward reeling silk in which the centre of the palm turns from inside outward, turning to the reverse reeling silk in which it turns from outside inward; its directional reeling silk is left-right, up-down, and slightly inside-outside. Left-right and up-down are a flat circle; if · 22 · one further makes the drawn circle slightly inside-outside, it can become a three-dimensional circle of a spatial curve, and can attain the function of qi adhering to the back.

(2) "White Crane Spreads Its Wings" — its basic reeling silk is one forward and one reverse, a kind of reeling silk rather common within the forms; its directional reeling silk is left-right, up-down and inside-outside. Because it is one forward and one reverse, in the left hand it is reverse reeling silk turning inward and downward, and in the right hand it is forward reeling silk turning outward and upward; the two together, under the requirement that the two arms be linked ①, become the "right-forward left-reverse separating ward-off circle" of upper-right and lower-left.

The examples above show that although the various forms of Taijiquan are manifold and their turns differ one from another, yet analysed from their basic reeling silk they are extremely simple. All the forms come down to no more than the three combinations "double forward reeling silk", "double reverse reeling silk", and "one forward one reverse reeling silk". If one constantly analyses and ponders one's own accustomed form by this method, and makes a table of it, it can become one's own basis for practice. With such a basis one can distinguish the jin categories clearly, achieve inner-outer union and threading joint by joint, and reach the requirement of correct posture upon the foundation of raised elasticity.

iv. Mastering spiral movement Characteristic Three is the origin of the boxing's name "Taiji", and its function has been as described above. Hence our predecessors, in order to enable later students to practise movement like reeling silk well, made a special treatise in the "Taijiquan Treatise", which is a summation in practice of movement. The first part of it discusses reeling-silk jin. To master Characteristic Three one need only practise according to this part, and use it as the basis for normally checking one's own form, and one can obtain correct posture and movement. We now

  • ① The linking of the two arms means that in movement the two arms seem to be tied to each other by a rope: when one arm moves, the other can also move along with it, keeping the rope essentially taut — that is, the two arms must always contain a tautly drawn ward-off jin.

· 23 · summarise and explain this part as follows.

(1) Grasping Characteristic Three from the spiritual substance. (A) "In every single movement, the whole body must be light and nimble" — if the spirit can be raised, there need be no worry of heaviness and sluggishness; this is the method of seeking lightness. If intent and qi can be agilely exchanged, then intent and qi will not stagnate at any one point; this is the method of seeking nimbleness. The first point in grasping reeling-silk jin is that in the course of movement the whole body must be light and nimble, for only thus can favourable conditions be provided for doing the reeling-silk movement well.

(B) "The movement must be threaded joint by joint" — in movement like reeling silk, one must be light and nimble, and especially must thread through; this too is an important link in movement, which must not be neglected in learning. For its details, see Characteristic Five of this chapter.

(C) "The spirit should stir; the qi should be restrained within" ① — if the mind cannot carry through into the movement but has other thoughts, showing dull intent and sluggish spirit, then the spirit will not easily stir, and at the same time the qi cannot be restrained within so as to follow the mind, with the result that the qi-situation becomes scattered, the jin has no reserve, and the body method is disordered. Hence one must first carry the mind through into the ceaselessly flowing and ever-rising-and-falling movement; then the spirit will of itself stir. Next, one must make the lung-breathing coordinate with the movement. Because the spirit stirs, the qi of itself is restrained and does not become scattered; and when the qi is not scattered, it can, led by the spirit, be stirred together with it.

Looking over the three requirements listed above, one may say that "movement light and nimble and threaded through; spirit-qi stirring and restrained within" is precisely the spiritual substance that must be grasped in mastering reeling-silk jin.

(2) Grasping Characteristic Three from jin categories.

(A) "Let there be no place of defect" — in applying reeling-silk jin, whether forward or reverse, one must always bring the eight gateways of jin onto the back of the spiral's bow — that is, onto the spiral's contact surface — and must on no account be sometimes on the back of the bow and sometimes sunk inside the bow. This is the fault into which reeling silk most readily

  • ① Spirit and qi may be stirred, and may also be restrained within. Hence the boxing discourse says, "If you would have the spirit-qi stir, you must first raise the spirit, so that the spirit does not scatter outward."

· 24 · falls. Once it sinks inside, it not only weakens the ward-off jin but also loses the frictional property in the reeling silk. Hence, if once there is a defect, the jin cannot reach the spiral's contact surface, and the pulling function of the reeling-silk jin is also lost (as in Figure 5).

(B) "Let there be no place of convexity or concavity" — in the path of application of reeling-silk jin, all processes must achieve a gentle curve and form a smooth and compliant posture; at the same time, they must be soft and yielding yet rich in elasticity, and this is one method of eliminating convexity and concavity. Even when issuing jin one must fling it out like a soft leather whip. In this way, because the body and hands are extended, the limbs and body are Figure 5 · Diagram of the defect in reeling silk — a place in the Taiji diagram caves in inward, beside it the label "defect".

Figure 6 · Diagram of the convexities and concavities of silk drawing — the reeling path shows many sharp convex-concave bends and notches.

Looking over the three items listed above, they explain that in the process of reeling silk — that is, in the process of movement — one must on no account produce the faults of defect, convexity-concavity, or break-and-continuation. Of these three faults, even if one commits one, one can no longer develop the function that reeling-silk jin should have. This is a problem that must not be neglected in learning.

To make it easier to grasp, the essentials are now summarised as follows.

(1) Reeling-silk jin is the origin of the naming of Taijiquan; without reeling-silk jin one cannot make the jin rise joint by joint around the limbs and body and reach complete single breath.

(2) One must know that the requirement of "threading through" is not only that the movement must pass through the joints, but also that it must pass through the flesh above and below the whole joint; this is the function of spiral reeling silk.

(3) Taijiquan has one pair of basic reeling silks and five pairs of directional reeling silks, which are the · 26 · the best tool for [learning] Taijiquan.

(4) Movement as reeling silk can be realised only under the conditions of lightness-nimbleness and threading through; at the same time, in respect of spirit-qi there must be stirring and restraining within.

(5) In the application of reeling-silk jin, one must not produce the three faults of defect, convexity-concavity, and break-and-continuation.

Characteristic Four · The Substantial-Insubstantial Movement of an Upright, Centred Body with Upper and Lower Following Each Other The manuals lay down:

(1) "Intent and qi must be exchanged nimbly, and only then is there the delight of round liveliness — this is what is meant by saying that in changing and turning, substantial and insubstantial must be attended to."

(2) "Substantial and insubstantial should be clearly distinguished; each place has its own substantial and insubstantial, and every place always has this one insubstantial and one substantial."

(3) "Standing must be central, correct, at ease and comfortable, supporting all eight directions"; "when upper and lower follow each other, the opponent finds it hard to invade."

(4) "The coccyx is centred and the spirit runs through to the crown"; "upper and lower are one thread."

The four provisions listed above can explain that all the movements of Taijiquan must clearly distinguish substantial and insubstantial. If movement can clearly distinguish substantial and insubstantial in its change-over, then one can endure long without fatigue; this is the most economical kind of motive activity. Hence in practising Taijiquan both hands must have substantial and insubstantial, and both feet must have substantial and insubstantial; and what is especially important is that the left hand and left foot, and the right hand and right foot, must clearly distinguish substantial and insubstantial with upper and lower following each other — that is, when the left hand is substantial the left foot should be insubstantial, and when the right hand is insubstantial the right foot should be substantial. This is the central link in regulating inner jin so as to keep it central and correct. Moreover, in forming the landing-point, within the insubstantial there must be substantial and within the substantial there must be insubstantial, so that in every place there is always this one insubstantial and one substantial, and inner jin everywhere attains central correctness without bias. In the beginning one may use large-insubstantial and large-sub- · 27 · stantial, and afterwards gradually train into small-insubstantial and small-substantial, finally reaching the state where within there is substantial and insubstantial but without no substantial and insubstantial is seen; this is the deepest skill of adjusting substantial and insubstantial.

The core of the nimble exchange of substantial and insubstantial lies in the nimble exchange of intent and qi, and at the same time it must be accomplished under the condition of "the central earth not leaving its place" ① and of central correctness of inner jin. For this, in practising one must at all times adjust substantial and insubstantial by "the coccyx centred", "at ease and comfortable, supporting all eight directions", "emptying the collar and lifting the crown", and "upper and lower are one thread". Hence an upright, centred body and the adjustment of substantial and insubstantial with upper and lower following each other become the fourth characteristic of Taijiquan.

i. Proportions of substantial and insubstantial According to Taijiquan theory, in all movements substantial and insubstantial must be clearly distinguished, so in practising one must see that the movement has, in every place, this one insubstantial and one substantial. In order to adjust substantial and insubstantial well, one must first recognise the correct meaning of substantial and insubstantial. What is called insubstantial is not being wholly without force; what is called substantial is likewise not being wholly weighted down. Taking the two feet, the insubstantial is not that this foot bears no load at all, and the substantial is not that all the load is placed on that one foot (excepting such forms as lifting the leg, standing on one leg, and wrist-locking and seizing), but merely that the insubstantial is somewhat lighter in load than the substantial. The origin of these terms substantial and insubstantial is, mechanically speaking, that the centre of gravity of the body's total load constantly shifts. When the centre of gravity shifts to the right, then the right foot is substantial and the left foot insubstantial; when it shifts to the left, then the left foot is substantial and the right foot insubstantial (as in Figure 8). As said above, the motive power of Taijiquan is itself produced in the exchange of the shifting of the centre of gravity; if there is no shifting — that is, if the centre of gravity sits exactly on the centre-line — then double-weighting ② is formed, the motive power is lost, and the fault of sluggish heaviness arises. At this time, if the two hands are emptily lifted in ward-off, then

  • ① "The central earth not leaving its place" means that the body's centre of gravity does not leave the middle third of the distance between the two legs; see Figure 9 in detail.
  • ② Double-weighting is when the two feet do not distinguish substantial and insubstantial but become double-substantial, and the two hands too do not distinguish substantial and insubstantial but likewise become double-substantial. Hence double-weighting is formed, so that substantial and insubstantial are obstructed and the change-over is not nimble; therefore it is a fault.

· 28 · one can become a skilled adept of double-sinking ①, and can make the movement regain the motive power of change-over.

Substantial and insubstantial are not fixed; they change as the form changes. In beginning to learn, it is fitting to adopt the posture of large-insubstantial and large-substantial, like the ratio two-to-eight (the two-to-eight ratio refers to the proportions of load on the two feet: if the whole body weighs one hundred jin, one foot bears twenty jin and the other eighty jin). As one's skill becomes proficient, one turns to the posture of small-insubstantial and small-substantial, such as when the load on the two feet is distributed in a four-to-six ratio. After passing through this compact skill, because the degree of movement becomes smaller, substantial and insubstantial can be exchanged more nimbly. The inner reason for the nimble exchange is the nimbleness of the exchange of intent and qi, whereby one can avoid stagnating on one side and concentrating on one point: for example, if in some form one should pay attention to the left hand, one can with no effort immediately turn to the left hand ②. In this way one can have the sensation, in practising, of aid on every hand, producing the delight of round liveliness like a pearl rolling on a plate. In terms of posture, under any change-over one may never let "the central earth leave its place"; only without leaving its place can one change to front, back, left and right without obstruction. If the body leans to one side in making the change-over, it must be adjusted before it can become nimble. This Figure 8 · Diagram of the shifting of the centre of gravity — the diagram is labelled: the central coccyx line, the centre-of-gravity line, left foot load 1/2 (insubstantial), right foot load 1/2 (substantial), with e marking the shifting of the centre of gravity.

  • ① Double-sinking is when the two feet, though not yet distinguished into substantial and insubstantial — that is, only slightly insubstantial and substantial — become double-substantial, but the two hands are wholly insubstantial, or only slightly insubstantial and substantial. In this way a leaning-to-insubstantial arises, as in Cross Hands, which is a double-substantial and double-insubstantial of upper and lower following each other — this is double-sinking. At this time, though the two hands and two feet are double-insubstantial and double-substantial, there is still within them a distinction of host and guest, and so it is not a fault.

· 29 · is a gap of lost position, and because an extra procedure is added it makes the movement turn slow and lets slip a good opportunity. In Taijiquan terminology this is called losing the moment. Losing the moment and losing the position are grave faults in Taijiquan; hence the exchange of substantial and insubstantial can attain the requirement of nimble change-over only under the condition of standing centred — this is one of the important keys that must be grasped. ii. The three basic substantial-insubstantial states (1) The substantial and insubstantial of the feet — the division of the feet's substantial and insubstantial is simply that one foot bears somewhat more and the other somewhat less. According to mechanical principles, if the centre of gravity of the body's weight is located in the middle third of the distance between the two legs, then both feet can have their footing, and this is called half-light half-heavy ① (as in Figure 9). If the centre of gravity goes beyond the range of the middle third, then the insubstantial foot, being too insubstantial, will produce the phenomenon of floating and swinging Figure 9 · Half-light half-heavy　　Figure 10 · Leaning-light leaning-heavy (2) One should be "sinking", not "heavy" — what is called "heavy" means the phenomenon of sluggishness produced by over-filling. What is called "sinking" means that although it is a sinking down, one can still "of itself soar into emptiness"; that is to say, sinking is produced within upper and lower following each other: if the foot sinks down and is substantial, while the hand lifts up in ward-off and is insubstantial, then one can make substantial-within-insubstantial. Hence "sinking" is not a fault, whereas "heavy" is a fault (except for half-light half-heavy). Therefore in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "sinking", not "heavy".

(3) One should be "light", not "floating" — "light" is to make the movement manifest nimble lightness with footing within the square-and-circle; whereas "floating" is going out of the square-and-circle, making the heel float up and drift without footing — that is, being insubstantial to excess. Hence floating is a morbid sign. Therefore in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "light", not "floating".

(4) The three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial — in practising the form one should learn and achieve the three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial: "double light①", "double sinking", and "half-light half-heavy". Among these three

  • ① Under the movement of qi in which the intent is empty-and-nimble without delusion and clear brightness resides in the person, one drums and surges the top jin; above, the two arms are linked, and below, the two legs follow; substantial and insubstantial differ only by a minute amount, yet they can naturally and nimbly convert — this is double light, and therefore it is not a fault.

· 34 · faultless substantial-and-insubstantial, the skills of "double light" and "double sinking" are comparatively fine and hard to do; if not done well, there is the possibility of drifting into "double floating①" (hands insubstantial and feet also insubstantial) and "double heavy" (hands substantial and feet also substantial), and to this one must give full attention. In particular, the skilled hand of "double light" and "double sinking" and the faulty hand of "double floating" and "double heavy" differ by only a hair's breadth in the shifting of hands and feet; hence one should all the more guard against the possibility that this hair's-breadth difference becomes a thousand-li error. (5) The separating hand is an important measure for remedying leaning-heavy and leaning-floating② — in practising alone

  • ① Double floating is when the two hands are insubstantial, and the two feet, because of excessive great insubstantiality and great substantiality, are such that in the process of movement not only does that insubstantial foot float up, but even that over-substantial foot, when changing, is dragged so that one stands unsteadily and floats up, so that the whole body drifts without footing — this becomes double floating, and is therefore a fault.

Therefore the dividing of substantial and insubstantial with upper and lower following each other is precisely proposed in order that leaning-heavy and leaning-floating may not occur.

· 35 · practice one can achieve the requirement of changing substantial and insubstantial without going out of the corner — that is, one will not go out of the square-circle and produce leaning-heavy and leaning-floating substantial-and-insubstantial. But when pushing hands with a person, two sides are already involved, and one absolutely cannot, by subjective wish, one-sidedly think that one can refrain from going out of the corner and thereby refrain from going out of the corner. If the opponent uses the separating hand of pluck and rend to seize hard and strike hard, then one will sometimes unavoidably go out of the corner. Therefore one cannot but use the separating hand to remedy this out-of-the-corner substantial-and-insubstantial, so as to make it return again within the square-circle and attain the substantial-and-insubstantial of half-light half-heavy. For example: the right hand goes out of the corner and the left hand strikes out; if the person meets the left hand, then the right hand can again return within the four cardinal directions of the square-circle. This is the technique of remedying one's own substantial-and-insubstantial going out of the corner. (As in Figure 12.)

(6) To do substantial and insubstantial well, do not forget the separating hand — for example, when pushing hands, if the opponent is one who greatly opens and greatly spreads and leans and tilts, and often thinks to use the out-of-corner technique to control others, then at this time, if one does not dare or is not accustomed to use the separating hand to deal with his separating hand, but still thinks to use the four cardinal directions to deal with his four corners, and with him to stick, adhere, and draw circles, · 36 · pushing ceaselessly, then such a movement goes against the rule of corner hand dealing with corner hand, and will make one unconsciously produce the substantial-and-insubstantial of leaning-heavy and leaning-floating; one may say this is a defect produced by being habituated to using the four cardinal directions. Therefore the boxing treatise says: "Pluck, rend, elbow, shoulder are all the more marvellous; in doing them one need not spend mental effort" — this precisely explains the importance of the corner hand. If one forgets the grasp of the corner hand, then the leaning-heavy and leaning-floating of substantial and insubstantial cannot be corrected, and moreover one will be impelled further to go out of the corner. This is the defect produced by being habituated to the four cardinal directions and forgetting the four corners, becoming a "one-legged" person.

In order conveniently to grasp the fourth characteristic, its main points are summarized as follows.

(1) Clearly distinguish the three main substantial-and-insubstantial: namely the substantial-and-insubstantial of the feet, the substantial-and-insubstantial of the hands, and the substantial-and-insubstantial of one hand and one foot.

(2) Pay attention to adjusting the substantial-and-insubstantial of hand and foot in the left hand and left foot, and the right hand and right foot — this is the main key to "when upper and lower follow each other, one is hard to invade".

(3) According to the principles of light, heavy, floating, and sinking, constantly examine the defects in one's own division of substantial and insubstantial.

(4) One must achieve the three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial of double light, double sinking, and half-light half-heavy; this requires constant attention and long training before it can be formed.

(5) When pushing hands, do not forget the principle of "corner hand dealing with corner hand". The four-cardinal hand and the four-corner hand must convert into each other, and both must be practised.
