Fifth Characteristic: The Joined-Segment Continuous Movement of Waist and Spine Leading, with Inner and Outer Mutually Fitting

Fifth Characteristic: The Joined-Segment Continuous Movement of Waist and Spine Leading, with Inner and Outer Mutually Fitting

The boxing manual lays down:

(1) "The waist and spine are the first rulers; when one moves, nothing does not move";

(2) "The whole body, segment by segment, is strung together, not allowing the slightest interruption";

· 37 · (3) "If one wishes the whole body to be one family, one must first have the whole body free of defects";

(4) "Move the qi like a nine-bend pearl, so that there is no subtle place it does not reach".

From the above four provisions one can see that, in order to attain "when one moves, all move", one must take the waist and spine as the centre, because the waist is the central axis of the left-right parallel turning, and the spine is the foundation of the up-down bending. Since the movements of Taijiquan require that when one moves all move, then on the movement path one cannot merely turn horizontally left and right, nor can one exclusively do bending movements up and down, forward and back; rather one must unite waist and spine so that the path of movement forms a spatial curve that is at once left-right and also up-down, forward-back, thereby establishing the foundation of "when one moves, all move". That is to say, only through taking waist and spine as the centre can one cause the nine main movement joints of the whole body② to be strung together in sequence. Moreover, one must achieve whole-body freedom from defects, strung together like a nine-bend round pearl; only thus can one's skill advance to the stage of the whole body as one family. Therefore the joined-segment continuous movement with waist and spine leading and inner and outer mutually fitting becomes the fifth characteristic of Taijiquan.

I. The Essence of Joined-Segment Continuity

In order to make clear the essence of joined-segment continuity, let us take the lower half of the body as an example for explanation. When the jin starts from the heel, passes through the ankle joint, circles around the calf and rises to the knee joint, then from the knee joint rotates and rises, circling the thigh to the hip joint, and one can do this without the slightest interruption — this is called the joined-segment continuity of the lower half of the body. This shows that the so-called continuity is not only moving at the joints, but should make the whole leg circle and rise in motion. If one does not pass through the large and small legs, but moves only through the joints of ankle, knee, hip, and so on, then that belongs to a movement leaping from one segment to another, and this is a kind of "zero-break jin". Therefore only the jin that rises through the large and small legs is the true "continuous jin"③.

  • ① The nine main joints refer to: neck, spine, waist, hip, knee, ankle, shoulder, elbow, and wrist.
  • ② "Zero-break jin" is only joint movement, whereas "continuous jin" is muscle and joint moving together.

· 38 · Once the continuous jin is made clear, one can find the point of application of force. If the leg is front-bowed and back-collapsed without left-right rotation, then no matter how one tries it is impossible to string joints and muscles together; at this time one can only manifest the joint's contraction and release, which has no direct relation to the lengthening of the muscle. If the arm straightens and retracts directly, the situation is likewise. Therefore this requirement of continuity cannot be attained except by using the reeling-silk spiral-style rising.

II. The Relation of "When One Moves, All Move" to Waist and Spine

The movements of Taijiquan first require that the nine main external joints can move in sequence and in continuity, for only thus can the internal organs be caused to produce a "massaging" action. When practising the form one must absolutely not have a few joints moving while other joints do not move. In order to make all the body's joints move in sequence and in full, one must find on the human body its central link and use it to lead the various joints to move in sequence; only thus will the movement become comparatively simple. Otherwise, one would have to use mental effort to attend to nine joints moving segment by segment together, which would cause one to attend to this and lose that, bustling without rest, and not only would one fail to attain the goal of continuous all-movement, but one would also lose the requirement of seeking stillness within movement.

图 L0F13
Diagram of "when moving then separating, when still then joining": (a) elevation, (b) plan; the diagram marks separating, joining, and the arm

We know that the two organs, waist and spine, occupy the middle of the human body; they naturally · 39 · possess the function of a central axis. Therefore, if one can make waist and spine cooperate with the spiral movement of the third characteristic, one can attain the requirement of joined-segment continuity; hence in Taijiquan the waist and spine are called the first rulers. Because of this central axis, the two hands can use the unity of centrifugal and centripetal force to achieve "when moving then separating, when still then joining" (as in Figure 13).

Book page 34

III. Joined-Segment Continuity and Strengthening the Joints

III. Joined-Segment Continuity and Strengthening the Joints

When Taijiquan has been practised to the point of joined-segment continuity, one can then attain the skill of the whole body as one family. Having formed this skill, one need only simply move very slightly, and one can make all parts of the body, inner and outer, move in coordination. This movement of continuity through the various joints can strengthen the joints and prevent them from degenerating. According to the laws of human physiology, regular joint activity helps preserve the normal structure of the cartilage tissue on the joint surfaces; if one does not often move, the cartilage tissue will undergo the degenerative action of fibrous change. If one does not move for a long time, its accessory organs will further harden, and thus a stiff state of immobile joints is formed. The cause of these pathological changes lies in the decline of the secretion of the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint surfaces.

From this one can see that the requirement of joined-segment continuity in Taijiquan plays an important role in strengthening joint function. In general, in practising Taijiquan one first seeks extension, and extended movement also enlarges the range of the human skeleton's activity. Therefore, when practising Taijiquan, a series of sounds often comes from the joints, making one feel relaxed; this shows that the joints have been exercised. Not only can this preserve the normal function of the joints, but it can also make the function of the bones steadily increase and accelerate the blood supply to the joints and their surroundings; hence even in old age one may step as briskly as a youth.

IV. The Adjustment of Joint Mobility

Although Taijiquan requires joined-segment continuity, with one movement moving all, nevertheless the mobility of its movements · 40 · is of varying size. The influence of a person's daily movements on the joints is uneven: among the nine joints, the one that turns most easily and most often is the wrist joint, and the one that turns least and least often is the spine. Yet the requirement of joined-segment continuity in Taijiquan is exactly contrary to this: it requires that the wrist joint move as little as possible, while the spine is required to lengthen and to move rather more — that is, the mobility of straightening and bending must be made greater. When the mobility of the wrist joint is reduced, one is forced to enlarge the body method to help attain the requirement of joined-segment continuity, and is forced to take waist and spine as ruler; otherwise one cannot turn smoothly and freely. If the mobility of the wrist joint is not reduced, then at one turn of the wrist a movement can easily turn and slip past without relation to the spine, and of course the waist moves little. Therefore the famous masters of Taijiquan often say: "In practising Taijiquan one should practise on the body, not on the hands." As for the wrist joint, one must reduce its mobility, forcing every movement to use the body method and to come out from the waist and spine.

The author had a friend who had practised Taijiquan for years, but paid attention only to hand technique, and his movement did not reach the body; in movement one saw only the arms moving, while the body was like a wooden stick, advancing and retreating with the stepping. Later, on another's advice, he used two pairs of thin boards to clamp his two wrists (four pieces in all), bored two holes in each end of the boards, and tied the boards with rubber bands, allowing the wrist only a small degree of bending. After practising thus for no long time, he transferred the former movement of the hands onto the body; once it reached the body, then when one moved all moved, and the requirement of joined-segment continuity also made comparatively good progress, the temper also gradually surged, and the body and limbs produced the flavour of round livingness like a pearl. This is the result of reducing the mobility of the wrist joint in order to raise the body method.

In movement one must use the waist and spine as the motor, with the waist and spine as the centre; only thus can one practise well the skill of joined-segment continuity. And in order to make waist and spine the ruler, not attending to this and losing that and not dispersing one's thought, one can only use the centrifugal force possessing an angle of inclination to initiate the movement (Figure 15); only then can one naturally carry the jin onto the waist and spine. Therefore when practising the frame one must certainly cultivate this habit of movement, so that in movement one does not disperse one's mental attention; not only can one achieve the movement of waist-and-spine leading, but one (3) Do well "softness moves the qi, firmness lands the point" — after the whole-body lengthening has met the requirement, one can further, at the landing point of each opening and closing, in conjunction with the outward manifestation of spirit and qi, form the square point, manifesting the jin categories of the four cardinal and four corner directions; this is the practice of the square within Taijiquan's "square and round generating each other". At the square point one must manifest extremely firm firmness (that is, one must make the body and limbs taut to the extreme and long), and after the firmness has passed, one requires that throughout the entire process of movement one manifest extremely soft moving of qi. The whole round of the frame should be carried out under such a condition of firmness and softness mutually aiding. Therefore when practising the form one should firmly remember the six-word essential: "softness moves the qi, firmness lands the point".

(4) The application of firm and soft and "vigorous spirit and bearing" — the application of firm and soft must be combined with the application of intent, spirit-and-qi, and breathing; that is, on the basis of "vigorous spirit and bearing"

· 55 · one coordinates the use of deep and long exhalation to make the body and limbs sink and lengthen, thereby strengthening elasticity and becoming elastic firmness (as in issuing jin); on the basis of quiet intent and gathered qi, one makes the muscles of the limbs loosen along with it, thereby forming a lively and unclogged softness, and from softness changing in ten thousand ways. Both of these are physiologically a kind of natural phenomenon.

In short, the firmness of Taijiquan is not the firmness of bulging effort, and the softness of Taijiquan is not an elasticity-less softness; rather, "vigorous spirit and bearing" manifested outwardly becomes firmness, and quiet intent and gathered qi concealed inwardly becomes softness. When intent moves, spirit and qi follow; as spirit and qi conceal and manifest, so firm and soft transform. Therefore in practising one round of the frame, spirit and qi should conceal and manifest suddenly, intent should unceasingly direct, and spirit and qi should also unceasingly conceal, manifest, and drum-and-surge; only thus can the muscles unceasingly transform firm and soft. This is an important path for grasping and practising the transformation of firm and soft.

In order conveniently to grasp the seventh characteristic, its essentials are summarized as follows.

(1) In the initial period one must transform away the original rigid jin, and the softer the better; the longer this period the better too, generally requiring one or two years.

(2) After the whole body has been practised to pliancy, one can then proceed to concretely practise the lengthening of the whole body, in order to practise firm jin.

(3) Moving the qi uses softness, the landing point uses firmness — this is Taijiquan's dividing line between firm and soft.

(4) Intent combined with the sudden concealment and manifestation of spirit and qi and with breathing is Taijiquan's rule for the transformation of firm and soft.

(5) Firmness and softness alike attaining a high level is the standard for the title of Taijiquan marvellous hand①.

  • ① According to Chen Xin's "General Discussion and Elucidation": "Pure yin without yang is the soft hand, pure yang without yin is the hard hand; one yin and nine yang is the root-headed stick, two yin and eight yang is the scattered hand; three yin and seven yang still feels hard, four yin and six yang is akin to a good hand; only five yin together with five yang, yin and yang without bias, is called the marvellous hand; the marvellous hand in one movement is one Taiji, and when the traces are fully transformed it returns to nothingness." This is the Chen style's standard for the softness-firmness degree of Taijiquan. Because Chenjiagou lies in the Yellow River's slope, where many practise hard-style boxing, and hence people fear that they will be tempered by their environment into gradually tending to hardness, there are the names hard hand, scattered hand, good hand, marvellous hand, to serve as the standard limiting practitioners from tending to hardness.

Eighth Characteristic: The Movement of Alternating Fast and Slow, from Slow to Fast and from Fast to Slow

Eighth Characteristic: The Movement of Alternating Fast and Slow, from Slow to Fast and from Fast to Slow

The boxing manual lays down①:

(1) "When the opponent moves urgently then respond urgently, when he moves slowly then follow slowly";

(2) "When he does not move, I do not move; when he moves slightly, I move first";

(3) "When first learning one should be slow, but slow must not become idiotic; after practice one becomes fast, but fast must not become chaotic";

(4) "The form resists the five peaks, the posture presses the three summits; from slowness enter swiftness, from shallow enter deep".

From the above four provisions one can see that when first practising the Taijiquan routine (one round of the frame), the movements should be as slow as possible, and the time may be drawn out. Only when the movements are slowed is there opportunity to make corrections, and only thus can one examine the places that are not smooth. But slowness must not go so far that the face shows idiocy; this is the limit of slowness. Later, as one's proficiency increases, one may gradually speed up, shortening the time needed to walk one round of the frame. But in turning from slow to fast there must likewise be a limit, namely that although fast, the movements must still be steady, still be able to manifest the categories of jin, and must not give rise to floating and drifting or chaotic phenomena. This refers to the length of time needed to practise one round of the frame. On this premise of being able both to be slow and to be fast, when applying it to each boxing form one must unify this pair of opposites, fast and slow, into

  • ① In the boxing manual, the meaning of fast and slow has two contents:

The first meaning refers to the length of time needed to practise one round of the frame. If A takes twelve minutes to practise one round of the frame and B takes fifteen minutes, then we say "A is fast and B is slow".

The second meaning refers to the speed of movement within each boxing form. It is slow at the conversion, gradually quickens after passing the conversion, is fastest when carried to the landing point, and after issuing returns again to slowness.

Among the four lines of principle quoted here, the first two refer to the second meaning, and the latter two to the first meaning. This is a question that must be distinguished clearly when learning.

· 57 · a single boxing form: that is, at the conversion it must be slow, after passing the conversion it gradually quickens, it is fastest when carried to the landing point, and afterward slows again, and so on in a cycle. (As in Figure 17.) Therefore every boxing form of Taijiquan must undergo the training of being able both to be slow and to be fast; only thus can one, in pushing hands, "when he moves slightly, I move first" and "when he moves urgently then respond urgently, when he moves slowly then follow slowly", creating conditions favourable to oneself, and can attain the unity of alternating fast and slow.

Therefore the movement of alternating fast and slow, from slow to fast and from fast to slow, becomes the eighth characteristic of Taijiquan.

I. The Development Sequence of Fast and Slow

At the initial stage of learning Taijiquan, one must absolutely not be fast, and must strive for slowness with all one's might, the slower the better. Because slowness allows one to carefully ponder the correctness of the postures, proceeding from coarse to fine, and there is ample time to examine the ins and outs of every movement; thus the postures are easily corrected, and at the conversion one can examine whether it is smooth. But slowness is not to be slow without limit; generally after one or two years of learning, imitating, checking, and correcting, it will do. On this point one must have a correct notion when first learning. This is the period of seeking only correctness of posture, not distinctness of jin categories.

The slowness of this period must further have a condition, namely that the slowness must be sought on the premise of raising the spirit and not letting the spirit scatter. If in the movements one is so slow that in spirit and qi one manifests dullness and rigidity, and in action manifests sluggishness and immobility, then this is contrary to the requirement of Taijiquan's intent-and-qi movement. Therefore slowness must be sought under the drumming-and-surging of spirit and qi and the nimble conversion of intent and qi; this is Taijiquan's standard for slowness. For this reason, when first learning one must absolutely not contract this habit of sluggish intent and dull spirit, causing difficulties for later improvement.

Later, as one's proficiency increases, one may gradually quicken the speed; but fast must not be chaotic — this is the period of training the categories of jin. Finally, after one's skill has become refined, the boxing forms may develop from extension to compactness, so that the speed of movement gradually slows again, while at the conversion · 58 · its angular velocity is even faster. This is the three-layer skill of first slow, then fast, then again slow, and is also the three stages of the development of fast and slow.

II. The Time and Conditions for Turning from Slow to Fast

At what time and under what conditions is it most suitable to turn from slow to fast? To answer this question, one must first clarify the two standards for turning from slow to fast.

(1) Movement steady — within the whole round of the frame, even if one moves somewhat faster than before, one still must not change the original steadiness of the movement; this is correct speeding up. If one cannot, and floating and drifting appear, then it shows the movement has been speeded up too much, and one should at once slow down somewhat. Under the guidance of this standard, one can gradually speed up as proficiency increases.

(2) Being able to manifest the categories of jin — Taijiquan is composed of the eight gates and five steps. In moving jin one should fully manifest one of the eight jins (such as the four cardinal's ward-off, roll-back, press, push, or the four corners' pluck, rend, elbow, shoulder). If the movement is too fast, it slips past in a single turn, and it is not easy to manifest the required category of jin. Therefore if one feels it is very hard for one to manifest the category of jin again, it shows the movement has already been speeded up too much, and one should slow down somewhat. This is also a standard for turning from slow to fast①.

The above two points are the two standards for turning from slow to fast. With these two standards, one can be guided correctly to grasp the time and conditions for turning from slow to fast, making the speed of movement turn from slow to fast just to the right degree. The fast referred to here does not mean changing all the movements of Taijiquan into fast movements, but rather that in the opening and closing of every boxing form, at the conversions and foldings and pilings, one must manifest, in a manner of relaxed-yet-not-relaxed and about-to-extend-yet-not-extended, the lingering attach-

  • ① However much one speeds up, in order to manifest steadiness and the categories of jin, the first route's thirteen-posture frame is at fastest no more than eight or nine minutes. This was the speed at which teacher Yang Chengfu publicly performed Taijiquan at the annual meeting of the Nanjing Physical Education Research Society in 1914.

· 59 · ment and vermicular soft slow movement. Therefore the so-called fastness is manifested only in the process of turning from round to square. (As in Figure 17.) This accelerated movement is the foundation from which the eight categories of jin arise; without this angular acceleration, one cannot manifest the categories of jin of the four cardinal and four corner directions, nor can one suit the requirement of "when he moves urgently then respond urgently". The issuing jin of Taijiquan is realized precisely by using this accelerating process: under the condition of closing concealed within opening and with the inner jin curved-stored, when one reaches near the target object, one suddenly shakes and issues like a bowstring released from its catch, sending the inner jin out from within a short distance. Martial artists call this "inch jin"①.

III. Alternating Fast and Slow, and Evenness-and-Clearness, and the Categories of Jin

III. Alternating Fast and Slow, and Evenness-and-Clearness, and the Categories of Jin

From the above theory one can know that any isolated slow movement or isolated fast movement does not conform to the requirement of Taiji yin and yang aiding each other. Secondly, as regards man's attention,

  • ① "Inch jin": any storing and issuing of jin within a distance of one chi is called inch jin.

· 60 · in terms of stability, from the psychological and physiological basis one can see that it is impossible to make attention engage in long-term attention of equal intensity without destroying its stability. To make attention stable and the intent not scatter, one must make the intensity of attention high and low. Now Taijiquan is an intent-and-qi movement, and it requires pouring intent into the movement; therefore, in order not to let the intent scatter, the movement must alternate fast and slow, and only thus can it suit the rising-and-falling characteristic of intent and qi, impelling attention to become stable and spirit and qi to drum-and-surge. In fact, the alternation of fast and slow in movement is also a natural instinct of mankind; it is both necessary for health and indispensable for combat. Therefore, taking a single boxing form, one requires the attainment of alternation of fast and slow (as in Figure 17). Yet taking one round of the frame, this alternation of fast and slow of each boxing form further requires an even range of variation. That is to say, from the beginning of the movement to its end, when slowness is needed it is all equally slow, and when fastness is needed it is all equally fast; in Taijiquan terminology this is to achieve "evenness-and-clarity". If one can attain this requirement, then one's breathing will certainly be regulated very "evenly and clearly", and there will be no phenomenon of gradually becoming urgent. This skill of making both movement and breathing attain "evenness-and-clarity" is a concrete manifestation of being well cultivated in Taijiquan, and is the true skill obtained from long practice. Therefore when first turning from slow to fast, one must not fear urgency of breathing and so not dare to do the speeding-up movement — that would be to give up eating for fear of choking. In short, Taijiquan should be like the waves of the great Long River, surging endlessly and yet with even clarity, rising and falling in movement.

Taijiquan is composed of the eight gates and five steps. When first learning, in order to transform away the original rigid clumsy force of the body and limbs, one may temporarily not manifest the categories of jin, and may be only round without square. The reason why it is permitted in this period not to manifest the categories of jin is that one has not practised enough, one's skill is not deep, and the habit is not yet formed; it is because if at this time one were required to manifest the categories of jin, one would easily produce the fault of straining and bulging effort, and would no longer be able to produce the elastic jin of lengthening the body and limbs.

After practising for one or two years the skill of seeking softness and destroying rigidity, and when one feels the rigid jin has been wholly removed, one may then manifest the categories of jin when walking the frame. Manifesting the categories of jin is the practising · 61 · This is indispensable to Taijiquan and is also what the eight jins require — namely that the accelerating force, on reaching the landing point, must manifest:

(1) Outward there is ward-off jin, inward there is roll-back jin, double closing there is press jin;

(2) Downward there is push jin, double separating there is pluck jin, issuing out there is rend jin;

(3) When the wrist has gone out of the square-and-circle there is elbow jin, and when the elbow and arm again go out of the square-and-circle there is shoulder jin.

Only movement like this can be called a Taijiquan composed of the eight gates and five steps. For this reason, after practising the form for a certain period, when walking the frame one should fully do well this movement of alternating fast and slow. By long practice of alternating fast and slow, one can make the eight-gate jin go from nothing to having, and from having to strong, becoming eight gates and five steps in name and reality.

IV. The Grasping of Alternating Fast and Slow

(1) When first learning, strive for slowness with all one's might — when first learning, in order conveniently to check and correct every movement, one must be slow, and must progressively pass through this period of seeking slowness; one must not be impatient, lest one create difficulties for later improvement.

(2) One must seek slowness under the conditions of raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi — when first learning, one cannot but be slow in order to check and correct the postures. But as said above, slowness must have a limit; that is to say, one must not be so slow as to seem to move and seem to stop, with fixed eyes and dull spirit, as if there one were thinking of something else. This kind of slowness is close to the standing skill of standing the frame, and is not what is needed for moving. Therefore slowness must be sought on the premise of raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi; only thus will one not produce the faults of idiocy and scattering of spirit.

(3) One must seek fastness under the conditions of steady movement and being able to manifest the categories of jin — seeking fastness, like seeking slowness, is likewise not going toward fastness without limit; it likewise must have a limit: although fast, the movement must still be steady. Steady fastness is the fastness required by Taijiquan; unsteadiness is a morbid sign. At the same time, one must seek fastness under the condition of being able to manifest the categories of jin, because manifesting the jin limits the fastness. Such fastness is beneficial and harmless · 62 · fastness — it will not float and drift without sinking, nor be indistinct in the categories of jin, nor lose the function of square and round generating each other.

(4) Slow at the conversion, quicker when turning toward the square point — the above three points explain the measure of fast and slow one should grasp in walking one round of the frame; now let us speak further of the principle of fast and slow for each boxing form. Taijiquan lays down that at the conversions and foldings and pilings one should be slow, and after passing the conversion one uses accelerating jin to move toward fastness, and carries on thus in a cycle. At the same time, within one round of the frame, this transformation of alternating fast and slow further requires attaining "evenness-and-clarity". This is the foundation for training the eight categories of jin, making them go from nothing to having and from having to strong.

In order conveniently to grasp the eighth characteristic, its essentials are summarized as follows.

(1) When first learning one must be slow, in order to have opportunity to check and correct.

(2) Seeking slowness must take raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi as its premise.

(3) As proficiency increases, one should gradually shorten the time needed to walk one round of the frame. But seeking fastness must take steady movement and being able to manifest the categories of jin as its premise.

(4) The principle of alternating fast and slow is: slow at the conversions and foldings and pilings, and after passing the conversion gradually quicken, and after passing the square point slow again. At the same time, at the conversion moving the qi must be slow, and at the landing point at the end must be fast.

(5) Within the whole round of the frame, the range of variation of alternating fast and slow is required to achieve evenness-and-clarity.

Conclusion

The eight characteristics of Taijiquan are selected and refined from the Taijiquan manuals, again and again. The precious form-practising experience left by our predecessors has long since become the principles for practising Taijiquan at present, and is also the standard that people unanimously follow in practising Taijiquan.

It should further be pointed out that although the characteristics are divided into eight, their essence is one; therefore when practising the frame or pushing hands, one must not treat these characteristics in isolation, and must in every movement gradually come to conform to these characteristics. Because every boxing form or movement must use concentrated consciousness to direct the whole course of the movement (characteristic · 63 · one), making the body and limbs elastic on the premise of raised spirit (characteristic two), and, amid nimble transformation of substantial and insubstantial (characteristic four) and forward-reverse spiral reeling silk (characteristic three), bringing about the union of inner and outer, attaining the joined-segment continuity of "when one moves, nothing does not move" (characteristic five) and the accomplishment in one breath of unbroken connection (characteristic six), manifesting the quality of firmness and softness mutually aiding (characteristic seven) and the speed of having both slow and fast (characteristic eight) — these are the special features that Taijiquan should possess.

From the above analysis one can see that these characteristics are mutually dependent, mutually constraining, mutually promoting, and mutually transforming. Therefore, if one treats them in isolation and attempts to carry out only one characteristic while abandoning the others, then one not only harms the latter but also affects the former. Hence these characteristics are not peculiar to one particular movement, and still less is it that a certain movement has only a certain one characteristic; rather, they are characteristics that every boxing form constituting the entire Taijiquan routine should possess.

In the Taijiquan popular today, whatever the style, and regardless of whether the postures are extended or compact, and regardless of whether the frame has a few more or a few fewer boxing forms, one need only observe carefully: these Taijiquan frames, though differing in outward appearance, all possess these common characteristics more or less within. The only difference is that some manifest them clearly on the outside, while others conceal them within by way of hidden jin. This also explains why Taijiquan, popular for several hundred years, has not been assimilated by other martial arts and can still stand alone as a style of its own — it is these common characteristics that have served as the mainstay. Therefore when learning Taijiquan one must not treat it lightly.

But when first learning, to wish to grasp these eight characteristics all at once is impossible. When first learning, one need only recognize these characteristics, know that they are the summary of experience left by predecessors, and understand that they are the basic elements constituting Taijiquan; then it is not difficult, following the predecessors' experience and proceeding steadily along the direction they have already pointed out, to obtain the efficacy that Taijiquan should have.

A Few Notes on the Illustrations

1. The action-breakdown diagrams in the illustrations of the first route were drawn from photographs of the postures of fellow student Chen Zhaokui. The action-breakdown diagrams in the illustrations of the second route (Cannon Fist) were drawn from photographs of the postures of teacher Chen Fake; in addition, according to the needs of the action breakdown, some diagrams were added, drawn according to fellow student Chen Zhaokui's build.

2. To make it convenient for readers to check the directions of the boxing forms, the directions of the postures in the photographs are agreed as follows: facing the reader equals facing south, the back to the reader equals facing north, the reader's right of the facing figure equals east, and the reader's left of the facing figure equals west. After the reader has practised proficiently, he may choose any direction according to the shape of the ground, and need not necessarily begin the preparatory form standing facing south.

3. All arrows in the diagrams, whether drawn with a solid or a broken line, indicate the direction of the action of the hand or foot, and the arrows in all the diagrams indicate the direction of action passing from this diagram to the next. Where a movement is relatively simple and can be explained by the text, its direction of action is no longer shown in the diagram, and one may refer to the text and the following diagram to understand it; moreover, for a boxing form identical with some earlier form, where the action-breakdown diagrams are abbreviated from several to one or two, one may refer to the breakdown diagrams of the same earlier boxing form, and no longer show its direction of action in the abbreviated one or two diagrams.

4. Arrows drawn with a solid line indicate the direction of action of the right hand or right foot, and arrows drawn with a broken line indicate the direction of action of the left hand or left foot.

5. Because the movement of the feet in Taijiquan is also fairly fine, in order to show the feet and the ground, shadows are drawn beside the feet to distinguish them. (See the diagram below.)

· 67 · (Continuation of point 5 of the notes on the illustrations — the method of showing the shadow of the foot on the ground)

a. A shadow joined as one body beside the foot indicates that the whole foot is on the ground.

b. Where there is no shadow beside the foot, it indicates that the whole foot is off the ground.

c. Where the shadow beside the foot is joined only at the heel, it indicates that the heel is on the ground.

d. Where the shadow beside the foot is joined only at the toe, it indicates that the toe is on the ground.

Chen-Style Taijiquan, First Route
First Form: Preparatory Form

Stand with the body upright and centred, with the two feet a little wider apart than the shoulders, the two toes turned slightly outward, the two arms hanging naturally down, and the eyes looking level ahead. (Figure 1)

Essential points:

· 68 · The preparatory form is the preparation in consciousness and in posture before beginning the movement; it requires: solidifying the spirit within and showing ease without; hollowing the crown and holding up the top jin — that is, the head must be upright and the crown must be hollowly held up, holding the top jin as if suspended; the lips lightly closed, the teeth lightly together, the chin slightly drawn in; sinking the shoulders — that is, the two shoulders slightly rolled forward and relaxed and sunk; containing the chest and drawing up the back — that is, the chest contained without being concave inward or convex outward, and the spine and back having the intention of pulling and lengthening upward and downward; the crotch must be open and have a feeling of round emptiness; the two knees slightly bent, standing without being stiffly straight, with the knee joints keeping a margin; the whole body relaxed, the breathing natural, and the intent stored in the cinnabar field.

The above essential points must be attended to at every moment, not only when doing the preparatory form but also when doing any movement in the entire set. Moreover, as said above, although each aspect has its own requirement, they also each influence one another. For example: because the shoulders are slightly rolled forward and relaxed and sunk, it is easy to achieve containing the chest and drawing up the back, solidifying the spirit within, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, and hollowing the crown and holding up the top jin; because the knees are slightly bent, the crotch is easily opened and rounded (the crotch is the perineal part between the two excretory openings; opening the crotch means feeling that there is qi lifted up and that the skin of this part does not sag).

Action one: The body slightly squats, the two elbows slightly bent, the two palms facing down (the two hands having the intent of closing strength), and the eyes looking level ahead. · 74 · When the circle turns to the upper ward-off, the hand is insubstantial, and the foot beneath that hand becomes substantial; the reverse is also true. This too is the key to seeking the centre-correctness of inner jin (but the case of lifting one leg and standing alone is excepted: because one foot stands, in order to keep centre-correctness and balance the centre of gravity, the single standing foot is substantial, and the hand above the substantial foot must still be substantial). This is shown most clearly in Figures 10 and 11. 4. Lazily Tucking the Robe is one of the basic postures of Chen-style Taijiquan; it is formed by the left hand's small inner reverse reeling and the right hand's large outer forward reeling. It requires that there be no hollows, no defects, and no breaks in the inner jin; the small inner reverse reeling is especially difficult, and only much attention and practice will meet the requirement. In this posture one must above all take note that within the closing (when the circle is contracted) there is opening, and within the opening (when the circle is released) there is closing jin; the secret lies in adding more of the inner-and-outer reeling within the process of closing and opening, which makes this requirement easy to attain; only when this requirement is met can one "draw along the coming and going so that the qi clings to the back."

5. The two arms' ward-off turns into a closing jin: because the qi clings to the spine and the two upper arms strike one another, the ward-off jin is not lost, and there arises the wondrous use of "opening hidden within closing"; likewise, because the two upper arms strike one another, when the two arms separate and become an opening jin, there is inwardly nonetheless a closing jin, and there arises the wondrous use of "closing hidden within opening."

Fourth Form: Six Seals and Four Closings

· 75 · Movement One: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg becomes solid; at the same time the two hands, each in its own place, first wind the arm and draw a small circle (to initiate the movement): the right hand winds its arm with a large forward reeling and wards off to before the abdomen, while the left hand with a small reverse reeling wards off to before the chest, and the two hands form a closing jin; the body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts right, the left hand with the side of the thumb presses close to the right ribs and rolls inward, until the palm faces left, while the right hand reels reverse and turns the palm to face downward (Figure 15A, Figure 15B). The body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts right, and the right leg becomes solid; at the same time, the right hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and the left palm makes a small reverse reeling, the two hands holding their jin together and pressing out in an arc up and to the right (Figure 16).

2. The posture Six Seals and Four Closings means six parts sealing and four parts closing. Its function resembles the "Vajra shaking force" in Hua Tuo's Five Animal Frolics. When the two hands press down, one must purse the lips and slowly breathe out one deep, long breath; this greatly helps to regulate the respiratory system.

The right single-leg-standing set posture: head upright and body straight, the two hands closing their jin before the left knee.

Key points: 1. In action one (Figure 39), the two palms must, with the two upper arms linked, close their jin facing one another front and back. The body turns right, and as the two hands reel half a circle to the right with the left reverse and the right forward, the two palms face downward and at the same time the right leg gradually drops; after the half circle, the two hands begin to raise, and the two palms again face one another front and back; the left foot is lifted, the body stands up, and it becomes the right single-leg-standing posture, the two palms · 86 · and again the hearts of both palms slant toward the front and down, closing their jin. In double reverse reeling one must take note of the little fingers of the two hands.

2. This posture is the meaning of drawing back the lute for the first time: it requires using the elastic jin after the right leg drops, together with the slight reeling-silk jin of the two hands (left reverse, right forward), to make the body turn and rise into the single-leg-standing posture.

3. This posture is a single-leg-standing posture of closing jin; to attain stability in it is harder than attaining stability by an opening jin. The key lies in lifting the top jin, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, reeling the two hands reverse, and fixing the intent on the little fingers of the two hands — thus it is easy to attain stability.

Tenth Form: Forward Treading Brush Step

Action one: Next, the left foot begins to descend; at the same time the two hands fall to the right side with the left reeling forward and the right reeling reverse downward (the inner jin must not be lost; continue from the preceding posture). (Figure 42) The left foot's reeling jin descends forward (east), the toes slanting toward the left front, and the body turns left. At the same time the left hand reels forward, winds its arm to before the chest, the palm facing the right front; the right palm reels reverse to above the left forearm, the palm facing the left front; the two arms cross. The body continues to turn left. (Figures 43–44)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the right foot strides one step across to the right front (southeast) diagonal; at the same time the two palms reel reverse and separate, extending to left and right, the two palms both facing outward and the fingers pointing up. (Figure 45 and the front view of Figure 45)

Twelfth Form: Herding Again

The movements, directions, and key points are all the same as the Ninth Form, "First Herding". (Figures 39–41)

The movements, directions, and key points are all the same as the Tenth Form, "Forward Treading Brush Step". (Figures 42–45)

Fourteenth Form: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the right leg is lifted; as the body turns and the centre of gravity shifts left, the right palm changes into a fist and reels forward to before the chest; the left palm reels reverse and closes on the upper side of the right arm, crossing with the right arm, the palm facing the right shoulder. (Figure 49) The two hands reel forward and sink, and the crossing point of the two arms moves forward; at the same time the right foot stamps on the ground with a stomp as the qi sinks. (Figure 50)

Action two: The left foot steps toward the left front (northeast) diagonal, and the centre of gravity gradually shifts left; at the same time the crossing point of the two arms continues to move forward, and thereupon the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right forward, reel to the left · 89 · up and to the right and down, separating in arcs, the right palm facing down and the left palm facing outward. (Figures 51–52)

图 L1F50
The posture in which the two hands reel forward and sink, the crossing point of the two arms moves forward, and the right foot stamps on the ground with a stomp as the qi sinks.
图 L1F51

Action three: The body turns slightly right, and the whole body's qi sinks downward. At the same time the right fist reels forward, goes to the right and up past before the chest, and is drawn back to the right side of the ribs; the left hand goes from reverse reeling to forward reeling and moves to before the chest. (Figure 53)

Action four: The body turns slightly left; at the same time the two hands reel forward and close before the chest, the left palm and the right fist both facing up, the right fist placed on the left palm (seemingly stopping yet not stopping, the body continuing to sink to store jin). The centre of gravity shifts rapidly left, forming a left bow stance, the right leg slightly bent and not straightened · 90 · straight. At the same time the right fist is issued swiftly toward the right front (east, slightly south), its fist-heart turning to face down; the left hand is also swiftly drawn back to the left side of the ribs. (Figure 54 — From Figure 49 onward the foot descends in the direction of the front view of Figure 45; in fact the direction of the left foot's stepping in the movement is the northeast diagonal; Figures 49–54 show their front faces)

Action three is the same as action three of the Second Form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar". (Continues with Figures 7–8)

Key points: 1. Turning from the opening jin and issuing jin of the preceding posture, Cover-Hand Forearm Punch, into the closing jin of this posture, the right hand must draw in slightly and then give a small ward-off forward in the direction of the issuing jin, to tease the broken jin back into connection, so that the inner jin is unbroken and threads through into the closing jin of the double closing that follows.

2. In this posture each half-circle movement that opens as wide as possible changes into a contracting movement that closes into an extremely small half circle; it is required to feel full throughout the body, with majestic momentum.

3. This posture differs from the first two Vajra Pounds the Mortar in that: the first time manifests the ward-off jin of the five paired directions in Taijiquan; the second is the opening jin that follows on from the Single Whip, turning · 93 · into a closing jin; the third mainly teases back into connection the broken jin after the issuing jin of the previous posture. It is the close of the fifth posture of the thirteen Taiji postures.

Sixteenth Form: Drape-Body Punch

Action one: The two hands reel reverse and extend to left and right, the five fingers hanging down and the palms facing inward. (Figure 60) The two hands continue to raise and turn to forward reeling, and when they are level with the shoulder the palms turn to face front and up. (Figure 61) The whole weight shifts onto the left leg, the right foot is lifted and thrust out with its heel along the ground to the right, and thereupon the centre of gravity shifts right, forming a horse stance; at the same time the two hands continue to raise slightly, and as the right foot steps to the right they reel forward toward the chest and cross, closing together, the left palm outside. (Figures 62–63)

· 94 · Action two: The two hands change into fists; the right fist, before the face, reels reverse from inward to the right and opens, thereupon turning from right to forward with a forward reeling and closing, circling one full circle, the fist-heart facing inward; the left hand reels reverse to the left and opens, thereupon turning to forward reeling and closing slightly as the right hand closes, the fist-heart facing right; when the right hand has circled half a circle to the right, the centre of gravity shifts slightly right and the body turns slightly right; when the right hand has circled one full circle, the centre of gravity shifts back and the body turns straight. (Figure 64)

图 L1F66
The set posture in which the centre of gravity shifts right and the right leg forms a bow, the right fist arcs down to the right with a forward reeling to beside the right leg, and the left fist reels forward from left to right passing before the face, closing its jin together with the right fist.

· 95 · Key points: 1. This posture turns from the closing jin of the preceding posture, Vajra Pounds the Mortar, into a double reverse opening jin; after opening it changes to double forward reeling, the two palms turning to face outward in a closing jin of the two hands, and thereupon the two hands reel forward and cross, closing together; during these openings and closings one must take note of the substantial and insubstantial of the two hands and of the two feet, and especially of the substantial and insubstantial between hand and foot. On this point see the fourth characteristic.

2. Actions two and three (Figures 64–66) are movements after the two palms change into fists; they must be made continuous as one, and performed under the requirement that the qi cling to the spine and the waist be the axis; the key lies in specially enlarging the inner-and-outer reeling silk and in letting the earlier reeling silk lead the later reeling silk; only thus can the movements in the three figures be joined into one, and the inner jin be not lost, changing over without any hollows or protrusions. On this point see the fifth characteristic.

3. Throughout all the processes of this posture's opening-and-closing and closing-and-opening, it is rich in soft jin; it is the soft jin of the four corners, serving as an auxiliary within the four cardinal frame.

Seventeenth Form: Back-Bending Shoulder

Action one: The body turns left by 90 degrees. At the same time the right hand reels reverse and raises in an arc, the fist-heart facing left; the left hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and descends in a left arc to the side of the left waist, the fist-heart facing back. (Figure 67)

图 L1F68
Back-Bending Shoulder, action two: the posture in which the right arm is bent before the top of the head, the face of the left fist presses close to the left waist, the back near the right shoulder leans to the right rear, and the crotch opening sinks further.

The set posture in which the right fist raises in a right arc and turns again to forward reeling until the fist-heart faces left, and the left fist changes to forward reeling, bends its elbow with the forearm across, and descends past before the chest to be placed before the abdomen with the fist-heart facing up.

Action two: The body turns slightly left. At the same time the left fist changes into a palm and extends with a reverse reeling toward the right front, the palm facing the right rear; the right fist reels forward, bends its elbow, and descends to be placed before the chest above the left arm, the fist-heart facing inward. (Figure 71) The centre of gravity shifts slightly right. At the same time the left hand reels forward and sinks, the palm facing the right rear; the right fist reels forward and gathers in beneath the chest, closing its jin together with the left palm, drawing the spine taut. (Figure 72) The body turns slightly left, and as the kua jin sinks, the right fist winds its arm with a reverse reeling and suddenly "releases the catch" from the spine, issuing jin toward the right front with the ulnar side near the wrist; the left hand reels forward and is drawn back at the same speed as the right fist's issuing, to be placed at the side of the left waist. (Figure 73)

图 L1F72
The posture in which the left hand reels forward and sinks, the right fist reels forward and gathers in beneath the chest, closing its jin together with the left palm, and the spine is drawn taut.
图 L1F73
The set posture in which the body turns slightly left, the right fist winds its arm with a reverse reeling and "releases the catch" from the spine, issuing jin toward the right front with the ulnar side near the wrist, and the left hand reels forward and is drawn back to be placed at the side of the left waist.

Key points: 1. Chen-style Taijiquan applies reeling-silk jin not only in the two hands; in fact the two legs also simultaneously ap- · 98 · ply it. Because this posture has a long stride and a wide crotch opening, it is the clearest example of the legs manifesting reeling-silk jin. Leg reeling silk is: when the hand on one leg reels forward, that leg likewise generally reels forward with the knee turning out; conversely, the knee turns in with a reverse reeling (for the principle of leg reeling silk see the second key point of the Twenty-first Form, "Punch Beneath the Elbow"). From the posture in this figure, the two legs seem not to have moved at all, and one sees only the two arms changing movement; in fact the legs too are reeling silk.

2. Taiji jin is the inner jin that arises from the heel, is issued from the leg, is governed by the waist and spine, and takes form in the fingers; reeling silk is a fairly long path of movement through which this inner jin passes. In the whole body there are two such paths, namely from the left heel to the right fingers and from the right heel to the left fingers, and they cross each other on the spine, one after the other.

3. To thread all the joints of the whole body through like a single line, one must complete it by the spiral of reeling silk. Reeling silk is governed by the waist and spine, leads the two arms, and has its foundation in the two legs; if the legs have no reeling silk, one cannot attain the realm of the whole body as one family. On this point one should take note.

4. The reason this posture is called "emerging from water" is that this kind of issuing jin is like "a thing about to be raised being given a downward check" — that is, at the end of the downward half circle there is an upward jin, and so it is also named the shaking jin of emerging from water.

5. The issuing jin of this posture belongs to the rend jin among the four-corner hand; the reason it is not called a "strike" or a "blow" is that rend jin is a short-distance strike, and so some also call it "inch jin".

Nineteenth Form: Double Push Hands

Action one: The centre of gravity shifts slightly right, and the body turns slightly right. At the same time the right elbow bends slightly, the right fist gathers slightly, the fist-heart facing inward; the left palm extends forward to the inner side of the right wrist, and thereupon the two hands ward off outward slightly (to draw on the movement that follows). Essential points:

1. At the beginning of this posture, attention should be paid to the size of the forward and reverse silk-reeling. In order that the movement gain posture and gain jin, when the right palm passes below the left elbow it should tighten the diameter of its circle; this is also the time when the large and small forward and reverse reeling begins to form. Before the double opening one must inhale, and on changing to the double opening one must exhale, exhaling all the way until the two hands have opened to their fixed point; this too is what brings this movement to a state of spirits-and- · 110 · one of the methods.

2. In the double closing (figure 98), it is required that the closing harbour an opening; the key is that before the double closing the qi must adhere to the back, and when the two palms cross and close the palms must turn outward and down, for thus the closing can harbour opening jin; if one has not attained parting within the closing, the jin will be balled up and stuck on the body, losing its elasticity and becoming the defect of collapsing.

3. In this posture, when the body squats down squarely upright, the kua opening must be broad. Thus the qi of the perineum will naturally rise from the coccyx, which is very beneficial. But when squatting, the height of the kua opening must not be lower than the knee, lest a sagging crotch form; if there is a sagging crotch it will make the outer sides of the two feet float emptily, and thereby cause sluggishness in the transformation of empty and full, so at the same time one should also avoid the defect of double weighting in the legs.

Twenty-Fifth Form: White Crane Spreads Its Wings

Action one: The body turns slightly left; the right foot steps up beside the left, touching its toes beside the left toes. At the same time, the right palm turns its arm forward-reeling and draws an arc leftward past before the abdomen, the palm facing up; the left palm reels reverse, passes before the face, and bending its elbow to the right joins above the right arm. (Figure 100, the front view of attached figure 100) The right foot steps out on the slant to the right front (southeast). What follows is the same as action two of the seventh form, "White Crane Spreads Its Wings". (Continuing to figures 31–32)

Thirtieth Form: Single Whip

The action and the essential points are both the same as the fifth form, "Single Whip". (Figures 21–25, then continuing to figure 113)

Thirty-First Form: Wave Hands

Action one: The body turns left, the right knee slightly extended and not straightened. At the same time, the right hooked hand becomes a palm and reels forward, moving in an arc leftward up to before the right forehead, the palm facing left; the left palm reels forward from inside to outside-left, extended slightly, the arm not straightened, the palm facing down. (Figure 114) The body turns slightly right and the left foot draws half a step toward the right, touching with its toes, the right leg becoming full. At the same time, the right palm changes from forward reeling to reverse reeling and opens out to the right, its palm changing from facing down to facing right; the left palm, from the left, goes down and reels forward rightward past before the abdomen to the right of the body, the palm slanting to the upper right. (Figure 115) The body turns slightly left, and the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left. At the same time, the right hand falls in an arc, the palm facing down; the left hand changes from forward reeling to reverse reeling, turns its arm and turns the palm to face outward, and draws an arc upward. (Figure 116)

Forty-First Form: Heel Kick

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts slightly left; at the same time, the two palms' centres turn over to face forward, and the crossed circle contracts, whereupon the two palms reel reverse and open out to left and right past before the abdomen (the mind dwelling on the two little fingers); the body turns back to square as the two hands separate, and the crotch opening sinks further. (Figure 162) The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, the right foot is drawn back and touches with its toes beside the left foot; at the same time, the two palms become fists and reel forward, going down from left and right to hold jin together before the abdomen, the two forearms crossing with the left arm on top, both fists' centres facing inward-down. (Figure 163, the front view of attached figure 163) The body continues to turn slightly left (the whole body's ward-off jin not lost), the two arms shrink the crossed circle (to store jin), and the right foot is lifted. (Figure 164, the front view of attached figure 146)

Action two: The two fists reel forward and issue jin to left and right; at the same time the right foot hooks up its toes and kicks out to the right side with the heel, issuing jin. (Figure 165)

Essential points:

1. The difference between this posture and the thirty-fifth form, "Heel Kick", is that the former form kicks the left foot while this one kicks the right foot. In doing this Heel Kick, one must first prepare a full storing of jin before kicking, and then issue, so as to attain the requirement of "storing and then issuing".

图 L1F162
Action one of Heel Kick: the posture in which the body turns slightly left with the centre of gravity shifting slightly left, and the two palms' centres turn over to face forward and the crossed circle contracts, whereupon the two palms reel reverse and open out to left and right past before the abdomen (the mind dwelling on the two little fingers), the body turning back to square as the two hands separate and the crotch opening sinking further.
图 L1F163

Forty-Second Form: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch

Action one: The right foot lifts its knee and is drawn back, the left leg standing alone; at the same time, the right fist reels forward and falls before the crotch, and the left fist reels forward and drops slightly downward. (Figure 166) With the left heel as pivot, the body turns right (east). At the same time, the right arm turns outward and reels forward inward, going up from before the crotch, and following the body's turn rolls down in an arc to the right side beside the right leg, the right arm hanging down with the fist's centre facing up; the left fist turns its arm and reels reverse from inner-low to outer-high, raising the left forearm upright with the fist's centre facing inward. (Figure 167)

图 L1F164
Continuing from figure 163: the earlier part of action two of Heel Kick, the posture (rear view) in which the body continues to turn slightly left, the two arms shrink the crossed circle to store jin, and the right foot is lifted.
图 L1F164附图
The front view of the same movement as figure 164.
图 L1F165
Action two of Heel Kick: the posture in which the two fists reel forward and issue jin to left and right, while the right foot hooks up its toes and kicks out to the right side with the heel, issuing jin.

Action two: The two fists become palms and meet before the chest, both reeling forward and dropping, the right hand slightly lower than the left, the right leg still lifted. (Figure 168) The two palms rise from left and right, leading the body up (like the double leading jin of two hands shooting a basketball), the right toes lifting up. (Figures 169–170; after the body is led up in the two figures, it should still face the same direction as figure 168, and the two · 140 · figures show its front and side) the right foot presses the ground flat with the palm of the foot and extends, the body turns slightly right, the left foot steps forward-left (northeast), both legs bend at the knees and squat; at the same time, the right palm becomes a fist and reels reverse to before the left abdomen, and the left palm reels reverse and draws in to ward-off before the chest, the left palm placed crossed above the right elbow. (Figure 171)

Essential points:

The movements of this form are like dancing while holding a long spear, the two arms forming a closing jin. First the left palm, like holding the spear shaft, leads up to the upper left, and the right palm, at the right and to the upper left, holds across like holding the spear pole, carrying the right leg up; at this moment the skin on the left side of the waist is tight and the right side is relaxed — this is a special movement that uses the waist to give a feeling of comfort.

· 153 ·

Essential points:

1. Wild Horse Parts Its Mane is a great spreading body method that makes the qi reach the four tips, like a wild horse galloping without restraint. The sole requirement of this form is that the skin and muscle on both sides of the chain of vertebrae from below the chin down to the spine must have the meaning of a double opening-and-separating jin, as a horse parts its mane; for in this part of the body "lengthening is easy but separating is hard", and the movement is so slight that it is difficult to separate it, so one must practise repeatedly to left and right.

2. This form most easily shows the great forward and reverse reeling-silk jin. Under the requirement of standing upright, centred, at ease, and supporting the eight directions, all its movements must relatively show the Taiji six reeling-silk jins; the two hands turn with this one up and that one down, this one down and that one up, this one inside and that one outside, this one outside and that one inside, this one forward-reeling and that one reverse-reeling, this one reverse-reeling and that one forward-reeling, opening containing closing and closing containing opening. Hence it can well serve as one example representing the Taiji six reeling-silk jins.

3. Taiji demands that all movements be governed by the waist and spine, so that the qi adheres to the back of the spine is the core of the movement. But the back of the spine (such as the seven vertebrae of the neck region) is the hardest part to separate and knead; therefore this fist form was included in the set precisely to meet this requirement.

· 166 · the body turns right (west); at the same time the two palms become fists, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward; the right fist passes before the chest and goes right and down, while the left fist turns its arm, bends its elbow and, together with the other, issues energy from the left upward; the right fist is at hip height with its centre facing up, and the left fist is slightly higher than the head, with its centre facing right. (Figure 231)

Key points:

1. This posture passes from a tight closing to a great opening; at this time the momentum is required to sink. While turning left the two hips must be linked together — this is opening hidden within closing; afterwards it opens again — this is closing hidden within opening.

2. Because the left palm slaps crosswise against the outer side of the right foot's face, it is called Crosswise Lotus Swing . After the slap, the left fist lifts up and the right fist turns down, both issuing energy at the same time; the coordination of this energy-issue is what brings stability after the turn of the body.

3. In performing Crosswise Lotus Swing one often feels comfortable and the back becomes warm — this is the phenomenon of causing the chi to pervade the whole body.

Action one: The left foot springs up slightly to the left, and the right foot falls to where the left foot had been, stamping the ground with a shock; the body turns right, the left foot steps diagonally forward-left (southwest), and the centre of gravity gradually shifts left. As the right foot falls and stamps, the left hand turns its arm and reels forward to the right of the chest; the right fist reels forward from the right upward and falls to the left, resting on the left forearm; as the left foot steps out, the left fist squats down; at the same time, the two palms turn their arms and reel reverse, the right palm opening out to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, the right palm's centre facing obliquely upper right and the left palm's centre facing obliquely lower left, forming Bestride the Tiger. (Figure 247)

Key points: 1. The only form in this set that retreats continuously is Repulse the Monkey, and the only one in which, after stepping forward, one immediately steps back one step is Step Back and Bestride the Tiger. The preceding form follows the requirement of energy and steps forward, while this form likewise follows the giving of energy and steps back. This is a method of practising one advance to one retreat.

· 174 · 2. In the preceding form the two wrists roll from below inward and forward, and there is naturally a Ward-off energy issuing; in this form, after turning back through one circle, one gives a sudden shake, an energy like slipping off a handcuff, and then the two separate and open, while at the same time the breath and the blocking energy must sink down.

Form Eighty: Turn the Body and Double Sweep the Lotus Action one: Using the right heel as an axis, the body turns 180 degrees back to the right, and the left foot is lifted and swings back to the right with the turn of the body. At the same time, the right palm, with the turning of the body, also revolves horizontally through 180 degrees, reeling reverse and lying crosswise at the upper right, the palm's centre facing right; the left palm reels forward and sweeps horizontally back to the right until it is before the right elbow, the palm's centre facing right. (Figures 248–249)

Key points:

In Taijiquan movements, whenever a circle is to be enlarged, it must first be made smaller; this is to strengthen the "ward-off" energy , so that under the condition of "qi clinging to the spine" the internal power is threaded through and reaches the root of the palm. When the two hands perform the inside-outside, left-right double backward reeling and open up before the chest, the combining energy arises — right in front, left behind; finally, like the character ∞, the two circles meet before the chest to guard the heart; at the same time the circles are gradually made smaller, forming stored power like a drawn bow, to strengthen the ward-off energy.
