After the above, with the two fists guarding the chest, the two fists open into palms and perform silk-reeling — right forward, left backward — uniting before the chest. At this moment the right hand is above and the left hand below, with the right palm · 189 · Key points: When the left [fist] has turned to the left crotch and the left arm is again plucked, in order neither to lose nor to resist, one should adapt to the essential force of the pluck and, following the direction of the opponent's essential force, strike out to the left with energy. This is a direct and straightforward technique for seeking release. Therefore in this posture the left fist counter-strikes as the main action, but the root of the strike lies in the right fist, which rotates with forward twining at the upper right, and through it the internal energy is threaded and poured into the left arm.

Fifteenth Posture Chan-shou (Chopping Hand) (chest southeast, turning north) Movement: This posture supposes that in the strike of the preceding posture "P'ieh-shen Ch'ui" no release was obtained; then once more, following the direction of the essential force, step up with the right foot; the right hand, with forward twining, turns up from the right rear and over with the body, and joins above the left hand; at the same instant that the plucked left hand is suddenly lifted, the edge of the right palm chops down like a knife, forming the double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, accompanied by a sinking stamp of the right foot. This is stepping up with the right foot so as to place both hands within one's own square-and-round circle; it is a technique of striking free in which two hands and one foot act simultaneously. At this moment the chest has turned to the north. (Figure 20)

图 L2F20
Fifteenth Posture, Chan-shou: stepping up with the right foot, the right hand turns up with forward twining and then the edge of the right palm chops down, the left hand simultaneously lifting, forming a double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, the chest turning to the north.

Key points: This is the method of releasing the plucked left hand a second time. The method most commonly used in plucking energy is the downward-pressing pluck, which forces the opponent to find it hard to follow, so that the plucked person cannot but tend toward a kneeling posture; hence he cannot but adopt a hand-leading-the-body step-up, so as to hasten the method of release in which the "right chop," the "left lift," and the "foot stamp" are all three applied together. Therefore, under the requirement that the right hand's energy be unbroken, one uses a small forward-twining rotation to step up with the right foot, bringing the plucked left hand within one's own square-and-round circle; this is the basic method of using lightness to overcome heaviness. Before stepping up and after stepping up, as well as · 190 · When chopping down, the tail gate (coccyx) must in every case be centered and upright; on no account may the downward strike cause the tail gate to topple forward.

Sixteenth Posture Fan-hua Wu-hsiu (Turning the Flower, Dancing the Sleeve) (chest north turning south, then turning northeast) Movement: Suppose the second release has still not succeeded, that is, beneath the lifting-up and chopping-down the opponent's plucking hand still cannot be chopped away; then one must, by a turning-over movement of the body, release further — that is, following the opponent's upward-resisting chop energy, suddenly leap up; the left hand, with reverse twining, lifts up and circles over the top of the head, and the body turns over. This is a great turning of the body from below upward. The inertial force of the turn is led by the left hand. At this moment the right hand also uses reverse twining from below upward to assist, and with double-opening energy the body leaps up and turns over. At the same time the left foot lifts, and brings the right foot to leap up along with it. This movement includes using the energy of both arms and the shoulder-leaning to release the plucked hand. (Fig. 21; this figure is the instant of leaping up and turning the face) Then, in the continuing top-to-bottom rotation, when the left hand on the left side passes from reverse twining to forward twining and moves downward, the left foot simultaneously lands with a foot stamp. This is an action performed by the left hand and left foot at the same time. When the left foot lands and the right foot steps forward to the right, the right palm must simultaneously pass from reverse twining at the rear-upper position to forward twining, and chop down forward with the edge of the palm (at the chop the energy is the same as the chopping energy of splitting the frame). At the same time, the left hand forms a fist and, with forward twining, strikes out to the left rear as the guest. At this moment the left foot is solid. (Fig. 22; this figure is the posture at the moment of rotating the body, landing, and giving one chop)

图 L2F21
Sixteenth Posture, Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, the leap-up and turn of the face: the body leaps up, the left hand lifts and circles over the top of the head turning over, the right hand assists, the right foot leaps up along with the left foot.
图 L2F22
Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, landing with one chop: the left foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, the right foot steps forward, the edge of the right palm chops forward and down, the left fist strikes out with forward twining to the left rear.

· 191 · Key points: The characteristic of the preceding posture's chopping-hand release method is that both parties' arms are at the front, and the distances from the point of application of force to both parties are equal; whereas the body-turn of this posture "Fan-hua Wu-hsiu" employs the rotating action of the body method and the lumbar spine, causing the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast (near to oneself, far from the opponent). That is to say, the release point is made far from the opponent and near to oneself. This relationship of one near and one far forms a change in the magnitude of the torque. After turning the body, of the two feet the left foot lands first with a foot stamp and the right foot lands slightly later; in this way the inertial force of the rotation of the waist axis is strengthened, and consequently the downward-chopping energy of the right hand is also strengthened — this is where the key to yet another method of seeking release lies. This kind of release uses the downward chop of the edge of the right palm to take over the rotational inertia of the right hand's forward-twining turn-over. At the same time, the downward chop must be loosened and elastic, for only thus can the next posture be prompted to leap up nimbly. This kind of release is also another example of using lightness to overcome heaviness, and is the concrete expression of one technique serving two purposes, that is to say, a dual use in which release conceals a strike and the strike conceals a release. Therefore this posture consists mainly in one hand releasing while the other hand chops down following the rotation.

Seventeenth Posture Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan (Covering-Hand Forearm Punch) (chest northeast, turning east) Movement: This is a posture whose main purpose is the practice of storing energy and of issuing energy; within the frame of the Second Routine, it is mostly used to link things up whenever it follows a special posture. This is the first Covering-Hand Forearm Punch of the Second Routine. It borrows the elastic energy of the chop of the preceding posture: both hands, with double forward twining, leap the body up, and the front-rear positions of the left and right legs are exchanged; then the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot steps forward with a lifting (ch'ien/jian) movement and becomes empty. At the same time, with double reverse twining the whole body's energy is bent and stored, and the ring-circle of both arms is made smaller to strengthen the stored energy. At this moment the left hand is above and the right hand below, the right foot is empty and the left foot is solid. (Figure 23) Then, the latter half of the section is the issuance of energy. Before issuing, the right hand first makes a small reverse-twining circle and places it at the waist, the center of the fist facing upward; at the same time the left hand relatively does reverse twining, the center of the fist facing downward — this is the left storing of energy. When the right hand is at the right waist, the right hand sinks its energy, and amid that steadiness still uses reverse twining to sud- · 192 · With the momentum of the issuance, the energy is sent forward. At this moment the center of the fist faces downward. At the same time, the left hand relatively turns to reverse twining, releasing the fist backward to draw it back, and places it at the left waist. The center of the fist faces downward. When storing energy, the right foot is solid; when issuing energy, the left foot is solid. (Figure 24)

图 L2F23
Seventeenth Posture, Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, storing energy: the right foot solid and the left foot empty, the left hand above and the right hand below, with double reverse twining bending and storing the energy.
图 L2F24
Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, issuing energy: the right fist is sent forward, the center of the fist facing downward, the left hand releases energy backward and draws back to the left waist; at the issuance the left foot is solid.

Key points: This posture is the one most frequently used (six times) in the second frame, and its key point lies in strengthening the practice of the energy of "storing energy like drawing a bow." It is led by containing the chest and pulling up the back, causing both arms to possess a joining energy shaped like the character 6. When practicing the issuance of energy, there must be the issuance energy of lifting a thing up and then bringing it down. Therefore the first half-section must be like drawing a bow to strengthen elasticity, and the second half-section must further have the twining energy of releasing an arrow deep into the target. This is the concrete expression of making the movement issue far and long. For this reason, before issuing energy there must be a sinking small circle, so that the drawn-out stored energy and the issued energy become one; one may not simply use a straight-line storing-and-issuing energy that has no drawing along with it.

Eighteenth Posture Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou (Flying Step, Twisted Phoenix Elbow) (chest east turning north, then turning south) Movement: After the issuance of energy of the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," both fists make a small reverse twining in their original position, joining energy front and rear; when the right fist with reverse twining goes forward and the left fist with reverse twining goes backward to open, the right foot is accordingly lifted, and leaps forward with a flying step, landing as solid. At the same time, with · 193 · With the right foot serving as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot and comes to the east side of the right foot, causing the body to spin in the air through 270°. (Figure 25) This supposes that in the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," after the right hand has issued its energy, it is plucked by the opponent, and it is a posture adopted when there is no time to draw it back. The opponent is applying energy along the direction of the issuance, so one cannot but follow quickly, to adapt to the person, using a flying step to comply with and transform the energy. In the course of complying with the flying step, one naturally turns the body to the left, using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand; this is similar to the various "Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle" postures of the First Routine.

图 L2F25
Eighteenth Posture, Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou, the body spin: with the right foot as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot, the body spins in the air through 270°, the left fist with reverse twining trailing behind.
图 L2F26
After the great 270° turn, the wide horse stance: both hands draw apart to form one great ring, the body sinks into a horse stance, the left foot on the left, both fists separated front and rear.

It is likewise a leaping step, but the hand method is different. (Figure 26) After the great 270° body-turn, suppose the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the great turn still cannot release the plucked right hand; then after the turn, both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, causing both arms to form a transverse ring, and the right elbow energy strikes forward. This is the final application of one technique to two uses: it is release and also advance-and-attack. After the turn, the right foot is solid; at the issuance of elbow energy, the left foot is solid. The Niu-luan Chou finally formed is as in Fig. 27.

图 L2F27
Niu-luan Chou, the fixed posture: both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, both arms form a transverse ring, the right elbow strikes forward; after the turn the right foot is solid, and at the issuance of elbow energy the left foot is solid.

· 194 · Key points: This is the final method of using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand. Because of the rotation of the body, it can also cause the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast favorable to oneself, so as to achieve overcoming heaviness with lightness; it is a posture and strike that releases without seeking to be released. At the same time, what distinguishes this posture from the preceding several is that the left palm is pressed at the right elbow, and the back and elbow are joined to strike the opponent transversely. This is a special posture that presses down the opponent's plucking forearm, fixing the opponent's plucking point so that he cannot change it, and throws the person out sideways. Therefore it is likewise one technique with two uses. Its key point lies in being able, after flying out with the step, still to land with the body established upright and centered. Most especially, one must note that after issuing, both arms must still be bent and stored with reserve, rather than extending the hands fully straight. Therefore one must use the flying step to come out in order to suit the essential energy. This is the method of final release in a whole series of release movements; that is, it is an example of the Second Frame's practice of plucking and of releasing from the pluck. Although this posture strikes forward with elbow energy, its root is still in the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the right side. For this reason, its essential requirement is that only on the basis of establishing the body upright and centered can the unity of using elbow and leaning together be obtained.

图 L2F29

图 L2F30
Nineteenth Posture, Yün-shou, the third movement: the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left, the center of gravity shifts left, the left foot becomes solid and the right foot becomes empty, both hands with left reverse and right forward twining, the left palm passing before the face and the right palm before the abdomen, moving and turning to the left.

Nineteenth Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands / Cloud Hands) (the first three, chest south) Movement: Both hands move simultaneously to the left, then simultaneously to the right, and then move to the left again, forming Key points: In this posture one must, under a smooth and gentle curved movement, perform the silk-twining transformations of left forward and right reverse, and right forward and left reverse, and must lift and lower the legs under the condition of not moving the step, fully expressing the requirement of the division of solid and empty in which hands and feet follow one another above and below; this is also the basic requirement of this posture. The Second Frame, having passed through the preceding several leaping and strenuous fist postures, can here adjust its breathing movement a little. Therefore in this figure-∞ movement of the hands, the speed of movement may be slow or fast; this is the place where the Second Frame is naturally divided into sections.

Twentieth Posture Kao T'an Ma (High Pat on Horse) (chest west) Movement: After performing the first three Moving Hands, with the left heel as the axis the body turns right, and the right heel leaves the ground; at the same time both hands, the right with reverse twining and the left with forward twining, move and turn to the right, the right palm passing before the face and the left palm passing before the abdomen; when the left palm has moved and turned to the right of the body, the center of the hand faces upward. (Figure 31) Then the right foot is lifted, and the body continues to turn right; at the same time the right palm, with forward twining, passes beneath the left palm · 196 · draws in from the side, the center of the palm facing upward, and the left hand with reverse twining pushes forward past the upper side of the right palm, the center of the palm facing outward and downward. (Figure 32)

图 L2F31
Twentieth Posture, Kao T'an Ma, the Moving Hands before it: both hands with right reverse and left forward twining move and turn to the right, and when the left palm has moved to the right of the body the center of the hand faces upward.
图 L2F32
Twentieth Posture, Kao T'an Ma, the fixed posture: the right palm draws in from the side, the center of the palm facing upward, and the left hand with reverse twining pushes forward past the upper side of the right palm, the center of the palm facing outward and downward.
图 L2F33
Twenty-first Posture, Yün-shou (the last three), the exchange: both hands with right reverse and left forward twining, the right hand turning toward the right front and the left hand turning toward the front of the chest, the whole body with the left foot as the turning axis rotating 90°, the right foot landing with a foot stamp and becoming solid.
图 L2F34
Yün-shou (the last three), the left sideways step: the left foot opens one step sideways to the left, touching the ground first with the heel, and the center of gravity shifts to the left leg.

Twenty-first Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands) (the last three) Movement: After performing Kao T'an Ma, then both hands, with right reverse and left forward twining, turn the right hand toward the right front, while the left hand turns toward the front of the chest. At the same time as this exchange of the two hands, the whole body, with the left foot as the turning axis, rotates 90°. At the same time, the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot opens one step sideways to the left, touching the ground first with the heel. (Figure 33) The center of gravity shifts to the left leg. The left foot · 197 · Steady the foot; the right foot steps half a step to the left, touching the ground first with the toe. At the same time, the two hands turn: the left hand with reverse (ni) coiling and the right hand with forward (shun) coiling; the left palm passes in front of the face and the right palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the left. (Figure 34) Then the right foot stamps firmly, and the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left; at the same time, the two hands turn: the right hand with reverse coiling and the left hand with forward coiling; the right palm passes in front of the face and the left palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the right. (Figure 35)

Key points: In the second routine (form) there are the first three and the last three "moving hands" (yün shou); the first three face the chest south, the last three face the chest north. Their basic requirements and functions are the same, so they will not be repeated. Therefore this form's key points no longer discuss the moving-hands action itself, but only the turn from doing the high pat-on-horse (kao t'an ma) after raising the leg to the front, into the turn toward the back. This action requires turning the body around within a gentle curve, with unbroken silk-reeling and continuous inner strength; therefore one must make a good small circle of the left hand drawn back in front of the chest in reverse coiling. Through this reverse coiling one shifts the torso, and the torso and the silk-reeling can be changed over suspended in the air. In this way not only is the inner strength kept unbroken, but it can also be threaded through into the next action. Hence this form is also a rather difficult action for practising the threading-through of section after section.

In order to make the turn-around easier, after Chen Fa-ke came to Peking, and to popularize Chen-style taijiquan, he added two boxing forms — cloud hands (yün shou) and high pat-on-horse — into this turn. Thus there was no longer the requirement of threading through while turning sharply in the air, and it became easier to do.

Twenty-second Form: High Pat on Horse (chest north turning northwest) Action: After the right turn-palm of the previous form, when the body turns left again, the two hands first both turn forward (shun) and close together, so that the two hands cross in front of the chest and pass each other; then both turn reverse (ni) and open.

图 L2F35
Hands moving with left reverse and right forward coiling, body turning and left foot opening half a step sideways

up. When closing, the left foot is full. (Figure 37) When opening, the right foot is full (Figure 38). This is a boxing form linking to the next, and its jin is the same as "white crane spreads its wings" in the first routine; only the hands are more evenly levelled in height, and the two legs straddle wider, so as to manifest a rounded crotch.

Key points: This is a boxing form that closes from double forward (shun) coiling and then opens from double reverse (ni) coiling; it requires that in the process of turning open after closing there be no corners, ridges or hollows, so that the silk-reeling jin is carried onto the back of the bow. At the same time, it requires that in the enlarged and expanded posture one strengthen the elastic training with section-after-section threading, so as to raise the taut (beng) jin. When closing, pay attention to the two thumbs, chiefly the left-hand fingers; when opening, pay attention to the two little fingers, chiefly the right-hand fingers.

图 L2F37

Twenty-third Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part one (chest northwest turning west) Action: From the opening jin of the previous form to the closing jin of this form, it is a closing by double reverse coiling. At this time, the right hand reverse-coils to the right of the chest, palm facing outward left; the left hand reverse-coils to the front of the chest, palm facing outward right; the two hands close into one closing jin in front of the chest. At this time the left foot is full, the right foot empty. Then the two hands forward-coil and press out (peng) to the front; at the same time the right foot becomes full, and when the two hands press out and come down with double forward coiling, the left foot retreats one step and the centre of gravity immediately shifts left, sitting on the left leg as full. When the two hands sink down (t'a), the whole body forms a posture of storing jin. (Figure 38) Then the two hands again turn to double reverse "covering-hand forearm punch (yen shou kung ch'ui)," and afterwards do the third "white snake spits out its tongue"; this makes it much easier to do). When practising the forward stride of the opposite step, at first it feels a little awkward, so one must practise a great deal. At the same time, this boxing form is a short-distance storing and issuing, so one must hollow the chest and raise the back, with the spinal column leading, so as to achieve section-after-section threading and the issuing of jin from the spine. This is the representative action of the whole set for issuing jin from the spine. If the curved issuing is manifested only by the two arms, it does not meet the requirement. It would be even better if one could take it out for special practice.

图 L2F46
Right hand in front forward-coiling and storing to the front of the chest with palm facing left, left hand reverse-coiling to the left flank, centre of gravity shifted back with right foot full and left toe touching ground
图 L2F47

Twenty-sixth Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part two (chest east) Twenty-seventh Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part three (chest east) Action: The stored jin of the previous "white snake spits out its tongue" was completed by the closing posture of "riding the qilin backwards" splitting and turning and then one more closing jin. But the stored jin of this "white snake spits out its tongue" is stored after the issuing jin of the "white snake spits out its tongue." This is the point of difference between the two "white snake spits out its tongue." At the start, the right hand in front forward-coils and stores to the front of the chest, palm facing left. At the same time, the left hand, on the left, reverse-coils and turns to the left flank. When storing, the two arms hold the jin together, the centre of gravity shifts back, the right foot is full, and the left toe touches the ground as empty. (Figure 46) Then the right palm, in front, chiefly forward-coiling a small circle, strikes out with the taut (beng) jin of the fingers. At the same time, the left palm behind, with reverse coiling, coordinates with the right palm and issues together. At this time the left foot steps forward half a step and lands full, the right foot immediately follows up, grinding the ground with a sound, completing the second "white snake spits out its tongue." (Figure 47) This form also, according to the practitioner's need, may be done several extra times, the same number of times as the "linked pearl cannon."

Key points: Same as the first white snake spits out its tongue.

Thirtieth Form: Turning Over the Flower at the Bottom of the Sea (chest east turning west) Action: This is a special boxing form. After the previous form's right hand has issued the pressing-out (peng) jin forward, it immediately closes with the left hand behind in a double forward coiling that crosses. After closing, with the double opening jin of right forward and left reverse, the body is turned right 180°. At this time the centre of gravity shifts onto the left foot, forming an independent posture. In the course of turning to the west, the left and right hands become fists; the right fist strikes with the back of the fist downward and backward, the fist-heart facing forward. The left fist strikes upward and backward, the fist-heart facing right. (Fig. 48. From Fig. 48 onward to the last figure, because formerly when photographing Teacher Chen Fa-ke all the photographs of the action were taken from the reverse side, in all the following figures, facing the reader is north, back to the reader is south, the left side as one faces the reader is east, and the right side as one faces the reader is west. This will not be repeated hereafter.)

Key points: This boxing form chiefly exercises the elbow joint. The left fist striking backward and upward and the right fist striking backward and downward — striking up and down — is a rarely seen issuing backward, so its key point lies in requiring that the balance of the body be maintained when issuing up and down and backward.

图 L2F48

Thirty-first Form: Covering-Hand Forearm Punch (chest west) Action: In the previous form the right leg is raised, and the two fists strike backward to the sides, one above and one below backward, the right fist, after slightly lifting up with forward coiling, sinks down again with forward coiling, the back of the fist facing down, and the right foot simultaneously stamps the ground. At the same time, the left fist, coordinating with the right fist, after slightly sinking with reverse coiling, is immediately raised; the whole body's centre of gravity is all on the one stamp of the right leg. When the right fist forward-coils until the fist-heart faces up again, and after adding a sinking jin, then it changes to reverse coiling and sends the jin out. The issuing hand must still keep some leeway, and must not be fully extended. At the same time, the left fist, raised with reverse coiling, turns once into forward coiling and issues backward as the guest (secondary), so as to maintain a double issuing with host and guest. (Figure 49)

Key points: Same as the seventeenth form, "covering-hand forearm punch."

Thirty-second Form: Turn the Body, Six Harmonies (chest west, from north turning south) Action: From the opening of the previous form "covering-hand forearm punch," the right hand which had issued in front is gathered with forward coiling before the left shoulder; at the same time, the left hand reverse-coils and extends before the chest. At the same time the centre of gravity shifts right, and the body turns right. (Figure 50) Then, next, the two fists separate to left and right. (Figure 51) Then · 214 · open; because it is a relaxed chopping power, when doing the next fist-form one uses the elasticity of the downward chop to lead the body up, as if gathering the power from all four sides into a single point and lifting with it. And by the time the right foot lands with a stomp and the left foot stretches out in a step, there is again in the mind the intention of spreading the power out. This is the spirit this fist-form should have.

Book page 198

Form 41. Taming the Tiger (chest turning from east to southeast)

Form 41. Taming the Tiger (chest turning from east to southeast)

Movement: after the issuing of power of the right fist in the preceding form, the right fist is drawn back with a ni twist, while the left hand, twisting ni, becomes a fist and is released open toward the left-front. As the right fist twists ni to the rear, the right foot behind shifts a further half step to the rear-right and becomes solid; and when the right fist, twisting ni, has made one large circle to the right-outside and then a small circle, so that it reaches the left forehead corner, the fist-form of Taming the Tiger is completed. At the same time, the drawn-back left fist makes a small circle to the left-inside, and when it turns to the left waist side, it props at the left waist. Now the right foot is solid and the left foot empty. (Figure 69)

Key points: When this form rotates one large circle left and right, front and rear, up and down (a great storing of power), the body must sink ever lower as it turns, and at the same time the large circle must also turn ever smaller—this is the clearest example of forming a downward spiral of the body. What distinguishes this form from ordinary fist-forms is that it forms its stored movement in an open posture; for the lower the body turns, the greater the elasticity of the power stored in the legs. This stored power can prepare the elastic force for the light and nimble springing up of the next form. This is the lowest fist-form in the Second Routine, and also the clearest fist-form of the silk-reeling of the legs coordinated with the silk-reeling of the hands.

Form 42. Wiping the Brows Red (chest turning from southeast to north, then to south)

Movement: the preceding fist-form is a great body-storing method; in doing this form, then, it is on the basis of the preceding Key points: According to the requirements of motor skill, the simpler the fist posture, the harder it is to fulfill the requirement that one movement moves everything. In this posture only the single right hand circles, with the right foot coordinating in up-and-down division of empty and solid to carry out the movement; such a movement is comparatively simple, and therefore it is a basic exercise for training the silk-reeling energy to achieve joint-by-joint continuity. To achieve "one movement moves everything," the key still lies in the leading of the waist-spine and the loosening-open of the arm's energy, circling like a whip — this is where the crux of doing this posture well lies.

This is precisely the second segment of the second routine of the form, and it may be repeated several times as needed. Because before "stirring the water," a whole series of fairly intense movements has been performed in succession, so here one may obtain a certain rest and recovery.

· 217 · Forty-fourth Posture: Left Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times (chest facing south, turning north)

图 L2F75
After turning the body, the left fist opens and meets upward to the right, the left hand circles to the left with reverse-twisting, and the right hand after a small forward-twist rests at the right waist
图 L2F76
Left hand circles to stir the water in front of the body, left foot lifts as empty
图 L2F77
Left hand circles upward, left foot lands as solid

Movement: Continuing from the previous posture, turn the body around and change to the left hand "stirring the water" and circling. Its method is basically the same as the right hand's "stirring the water" movement; the difference is that when the left and right hands alternate and the body turns, the internal energy must be kept unbroken. In the previous posture, when the right hand has circled down and turned left, the left fist propping at the left waist opens and reverse-twists upward to the right to meet it, forming a joining with the left slightly lower and the right slightly higher. At this moment the right foot lifts as empty; as soon as they cross, both hands immediately become double reverse-twisting, and led by the waist-spine and drawn by the right hand, the body turns and carries a turn of 180° to the right. At the same time, the right foot lands as solid and serves as the pivot of the rotation. Following this, the left foot also immediately arcs around with the body and is placed to the west side of the right foot, completing the process of turning the body. At the same time, the left hand circles to the left side from reverse-twisting to forward-twisting, while the right hand, after a small forward-twist, is placed at the right side of the waist. (Figure 75) This is the starting point after "Left Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times" has turned the body. Thereafter, just as with "Right Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times," when the left hand circles downward, the left foot must lift as empty. (Figure 76) When the left hand circles upward, the left foot again drops as solid. (Figure 77), completing one "stirring the water." Then do two more "stirring the water" movements. (Fig. 78, 77, then again 78, 77, 78)

Key points: The requirements of this posture itself are the same as those of "Right Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times," but special attention must be paid to the fact that at the moment of turning the body and changing hands, one must not only turn with a gentle curve, but at the same time must also keep the movement threaded through as one breath, allowing no interruption and no hollows or bumps to occur. The crux lies in that when the left hand opens and joins with the right hand, forming a mutual linkage of the two arms, one can, upon separating again for one turn, pass the energy from the right hand over to the left hand.

Although the key points and movement of this posture are the same as the previous posture, in order to give the left hand the same degree of nimbleness as the right hand, this posture may be done several or a dozen times; in this posture the position of the right foot does not change, so doing it several times in place does no harm to the structure of the entire form.

Forty-fifth Posture: Left Kick with One (Single) Leg (chest facing north)

图 L2F78
Left hand forward-twists and arcs from inside outward, left hand propping the waist opening and closing, left foot shifting between empty and solid
图 L2F79
Both hands gather and close in front of the abdomen, opposed to the body's center, both feet standing
图 L2F80
Left arm forward-twists and arcs outward, right hand opens and circles in opposition, left foot lifts — the initiating pose of the kick

Movement: After the above "stirring the water," when the left arm forward-twists and arcs from inside to outside, the right hand propping the waist opens and takes the opportunity to join in a circling that is at once opposed and at once divided; when turning after passing one circle and then turning downward, it becomes a double closing energy. At this moment palm faces palm, both hands opposed and slightly narrower than the shoulders, placed in front of the abdomen. When the right hand joins in and finally closes, the left foot goes from solid to empty. (Figure 79) With the two hands ceaselessly circling, continue to tighten into a single closing with a double forward-twist, making both palms become fists crossing before the chest. At this moment the left hand is outside and the right hand inside; at the same time, raise the left leg. (Figure 80) After reaching the end point of the crossing, issue the energy with both hands and the left foot together, each with full force to left and right. This is kicking out the left foot with energy while standing on the right foot alone. At this moment the left hand is host and the right hand is guest. (Figure 81)

Key points: The elastic energy of this posture is a double opening energy produced within the double closing, because when the two hands are in a double closing, the elbows and upper arms have a double opening energy. At the same time, when the two feet bend slightly and close doubly, the rounding of the crotch gives the legs a double opening energy as well. This shows that both arms and legs have a linked outward-bracing energy; this is the crux of being able to issue energy crisply. When the two hands and the left foot split and issue to the left and right sides together, because of the stabilizing effect of the two hands' splitting, the torso obtains a certain stability at the moment of issuing. This kind of energy issuance is a good method for training the joint ligaments and strengthening their elasticity.

Forty-sixth Posture: Right Kick with One (Single) Leg (chest facing north, turning south)

Movement: After the previous posture "Left Kick with One Leg," the two hands close to the left with reverse-twisting, drawing the torso to turn left; at the same time the left foot lands with a stamping of the foot, and the right leg is raised, forming standing on the left leg alone, with the two hands closing their energy on both sides of the right knee. (Figure 82) Then issue the energy with both hands and the right foot together, each with full force to left and right — this is kicking out the right foot with energy while standing on the left foot alone. At this moment the right hand is host and the left hand is guest. (Figure 83)

Forty-ninth Posture: Sweeping-Leg (turning the waist and smashing, chest facing east, turning north, then turning south and again turning north)

Movement: After the energy issuance of "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch," the right hand in front draws back with reverse-twisting and then makes a circle forward, while the left hand behind circles forward and then backward with reverse-twisting. (Figure 86) When the right hand again draws back with reverse-twisting from the front to before the right waist, the right foot stamps the ground with a stamping of the foot; at this moment the left fist raises forward-upward with reverse-twisting. (Figure 87) Immediately after the stamping of the foot, the right toe turns outward and steps out a small half-step to the right rear, forming a rotational momentum, carrying the body to turn toward the right rear · 222 · about 280°; the right leg squats down, and the left foot follows by extending the leg and arcing around to sweep-turn 280°, sweeping to the northwest of the right foot. (Figure 88)

Key points: This posture is for practicing the ankle-striking energy when the foot sweeps horizontally. In order to rotate the left leg stably and sweep one full circle horizontally, one must make the intent and energy manifest as though the right foot had taken root in the ground. Second, in order to strengthen the leg's horizontal sweeping energy, one must use the right foot's stepping a small half-step to the right rear with the toe turned out, to drive the rotation of the torso and form a rotational momentum. Third, one must coordinate upper and lower consistently, so that the torso can rotate nimbly yet steadily; this applies mainly to the first half-circle of the movement, where the change of posture goes from high to low, while in the latter circle of the movement the internal energy must again go from low to high and then land. This is also a comparatively difficult movement, a movement of leg-leading-body, which can lengthen and strengthen the leg muscles. In order to strengthen the leg's horizontal sweeping energy, it may be singled out for specialized free-hand practice, and one may also do two 360° sweeping-legs.

Fiftieth Posture: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch (chest facing north, turning east)

Movement: After the previous posture has turned through 280°, both hands cross and close before the chest ; then the two palms change and separately arc upward and spread out to the left and right sides; at the same time, the right foot lifts off the ground, and the left foot immediately pushes off the ground and springs up. Then the right foot lands to the southwest, and the left foot follows to land to the northeast. Both hands from above close before the chest with double reverse-twisting, then open with forward-twisting and close with reverse-twisting; then the right fist strikes out, and the left fist is drawn in beneath the left ribs. (Figure 90) What differs between this posture and the previous seventeenth posture is only the leaping-step movement; once both feet have landed, it is the same as the other "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch" postures.

· 225 · —the swings gradually grow smaller, reducing step by step to a single circle; finally, as soon as the intention is aroused, the shaking energy can be issued in the same way. This is the deepest skill in issuing shaking energy.

Fifty-second Form — Right Thrust (chest facing east)

Movement: Because the movement begins with the right leg in front, it is called "Right Thrust". In this form the right leg is in front first, and finally changes to the left leg in front; the two fists first travel from the left rib side to the right rib side, and after describing two large circles they shake out the energy. In these two respects this form is exactly the opposite of the previous form, so its movement path is symmetrical to that form. (Figs. 95, 96, 97)

Key points: Same as "Left Thrust".

Fifty-third Form — Reverse Throw-Down (chest facing east, turning northeast)

Movement: After the previous form has issued the double shaking energy, suppose the right hand is plucked (this kind of plucking energy often makes the one plucked kneel down); in order to achieve sticking, adhering, connecting and following, so that there is no opposing resistance, the right hand follows downward with reverse twining, bringing the right hand together with the left hand. As they join, the left hand is placed beneath the plucking hand, and the right hand presses down, making a preliminary release. At this moment the right hand is full downward, the right foot steps up as empty, standing alongside the left foot with the toes touching the ground, so that the two hands are close to the upper and lower parts of one's own body; this is "release within joining", another example of overcoming weight with lightness. (Figure 98)

图 L2F96

图 L2F97
Right leg in front bow stance, both fists shaken forward

· 226 · Fifty-fourth Form — Turning the Flower at the Seabed (chest facing east)

Movement: If in the previous form the reverse insertion cannot achieve "release within joining", then sink further and suddenly turn, lengthening the body, and change into opening the hands above and below. This is done with the energy adhering to the spine, the body led up by the crown energy, as a second release; it is the method of "release within opening" after "release within joining". Simultaneously with this "opening release", the right hand twines with forward twining to the upper right and then turns to the lower right, the left hand twines with reverse twining to the lower left and then turns to the upper left; the whole body lengthens, the left foot stands alone, the right foot is lifted (as preparation for a kick); the left fist releases energy upward to the left, with the fist centre facing right; the right fist releases energy downward to the right waist side, with the fist centre facing forward. Its movement is the same as the previous "Turning the Flower at the Seabed" forms, except that this form turns the body only slightly, whereas the previous forms turned the body through a larger range. (Figure 99)

图 L2F98

图 L2F100

图 L2F103

Key points: Taijiquan often uses downward plucking energy, so that the opponent cannot easily use connecting and following to gain release; for this reason the right hand twines with reverse twining downward, the right foot steps forward, and the left hand is placed beneath the plucking hand. Because the right foot steps up in "Reverse Insertion", one's own two hands are brought close to one's own centre of the circle, thereby increasing the moment applied to the opponent while reducing one's own moment; one large and one small — this is again a model of overcoming weight with lightness, and can make one · 230 · —preparation for storing energy. (Figure 105)

After the left step has been taken in the previous form, the second right step is taken in succession; this is the final step of the ren-shaped upward step. The two fists, like a windmill, twine over one another inside and outside in front of the chest through one large circle. In the previous movement, when the right fist twines forward, upward and inward with forward twining, the right foot is drawn back half a step with the toes touching the ground. Then the right fist sinks its energy downward in front of the chest in coordination with the left fist moving upward, so as to release the plucked right hand a second time. At the same time the right foot shakes downward in a stamp, and taking advantage of the momentum darts forward along the ground. Simultaneously the right fist, arm held horizontally, moves forward and issues energy horizontally outward. (Figure 106)

Key points: If the warding-off issuing energy of the previous form is still not enough to release the plucked right hand, then to avoid opposing resistance one must use connecting and following and, dragging along, step up in succession. Therefore the main content of practice in this form is to step forward two paces in succession without any break in energy occurring, and to have at all times the opportunity to release and to strike. To attain this requirement, the key point is that the two arms are linked together so that the two fists turn over up and down in the course of advancing, shaking the spine to shake off the plucking of the right hand.

图 L2F105
Body turned sideways, both fists twining, energy stored and ready to issue
图 L2F106
Bow stance, arm horizontal warding off forward, right fist issuing energy to the right front

Because the first "Seizing the Two Arms" still cannot obtain release, one must follow the required energy and, in the course of pushing the opponent backward, issue energy outward horizontally, releasing and striking at once. This is the unified action of pushing and releasing. Therefore, whether it steps with the left foot or the right foot, it must · 231 · —turning the spine and advancing. This is the key to whether, when warding-off energy is issued, the stored energy of the spine can be released like a bowstring slipping its catch.

Fifty-eighth Form — Linked Pearls Cannon (chest facing west)

Movement (one): After the right hand has issued warding-off energy in the previous form, the left fist stored at the left rear strikes and shakes out like a bowstring slipping its catch, while the right fist twines forward, drawn back to rest at the right rib side. When the strike is issued the left leg is full. (Figure 107)

Movement (two): Movement (one) is the shaking energy of the left fist; movement (two) is the shaking energy of the right fist. The two are basically the same; the difference is the shaking of the spine. When the left fist is drawn back with forward twining to rest in front of the chest, the right fist is sent out like linked pearls. When the right fist is sent out the right leg is empty. (Figure 108)

Movement (three): Same as movement one. (Figure 109)

Key points: "Thrust Punch" is shaking energy issued by both fists together; this form is shaking energy issued by each fist separately. Its key point lies in loosening the limbs, then suddenly shaking outward; it is a short-range hard energy. After issuing, the arm must still be bent and stored; the degree of bending and storing is determined by the ability to issue again.

Form 65: Forward Phoenix Elbow (chest toward north)
