Movement three: the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the right hand circles downward and outward to the left before the abdomen and closes into a fist at the right of the abdomen, the palm toward the chest, the right arm in the manner of embracing a tiger; the left hand pushes slowly forward as an upright palm (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the left hand level with the eyes; facing the northwest diagonal. Movement four: the right fist, its centre turned down, moves downward and opens into a palm past the side of the right leg; the left hand accordingly falls with its palm turned down; when the two hands have descended to the same level, the two hands part to left and right at the same time and arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth, the two palms turned slightly forward. At the same time as the two hands part left and right, the left foot follows forward to beside the right heel, touching the ground with the toe, and the two legs are still full-right and empty-left. The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms.

Thirty-fourth posture — Single whip (Figure 91)
Thirty-fifth posture — Raise the hand and lift the posture (Figures 92–93)
Thirty-sixth posture — High pat the horse (Figure 94)

Three postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "Single whip"; movements two and three are "Raise the hand and lift the posture"; movement four is "High pat the horse".

Movement one: the right toe turns inward about 90 degrees and settles; the right leg sits full, and at the same time the body turns left; the left foot steps out to the left, touching first with the heel; then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat with the toe pointing toward the left corner, and the two legs still become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the left hand rises and the right hand falls, both becoming upright palms; when the two hands come level with the mouth they part to left and right, the left hand level with the eyes and the right hand level with the mouth; facing a diagonal slightly east of south. (Figure 91)

Movement two: the right foot lifts, passes along the inner side of the left foot, and steps forward, touching first with the heel;

then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat with the toe pointing ahead, the left leg bends slightly, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the body turns slightly right. The two hands follow the movement: the right hand moves from the right downward and scoops to the left to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing forward; the left hand rises, the palm turned up, with the intent of lifting upward, level with the crown. As the right leg bows forward, the right hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the right hand level with the chest; facing due south. (Figure 92)

(Figure 108 甲) Then the left toe turns slightly outward and settles, the whole weight shifts onto the left leg, the right leg lifts and the right toe kicks forward, level with the knee, the left leg bending slightly; at the same time the two hands part left and right, the right high and the left slightly lower, the right hand level with the shoulder, the right arm in line with the right leg, and the right hand having the intent of slapping the top of the right foot; facing due east. (Figure 108 乙)

Movement three: the right leg falls; the right foot passes behind the left heel and settles flat on the left side behind the left heel, the two legs full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands draw in before the chest, the right hand level with the mouth and the left hand level with the chest. (Figure 109 甲) Then the left foot steps back one pace, the toe pointing toward the left-front diagonal, the left leg slightly bent, still empty-left and full-right; at the same time the two hands shift back with the retreating step. The weight shifts back, sitting the left leg full, and the right toe tilts up, so that the legs become full-left and empty-right; at the same time the two hands move from the front downward, drawing back in an arc before the chest. Then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the legs still become full-right and empty-left; at the same time the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the right hand level with the eyes and the left hand level with the chest; facing due east. (Figure 109 乙)

As the body shifts forward and the right foot follows, the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 142)

# Illustrated explanation of Wu-style taijiquan push-hands Taijiquan push-hands was originally called "hitting hands". Of what Wu Yuxiang and Li Yishe handed down, there is only the one kind — moving-step push-hands. Why adopt only moving-step push-hands and not fixed-step? The reason is that moving-step push-hands can be applied with agility and has no defect of stiffness; it trains both the stepping method and the body method, and at the same time allows practice of "stick, connect, adhere, follow". Moreover, in the course of the movement one is constantly able to keep a centred and stable posture, and can still issue energy while in motion. Once practised to familiarity, one can reach what the ancients called "walking, stopping, sitting, lying" — all of them states of practising the form.

The stepping method of Wu-style push-hands is three and a half steps forward, three and a half steps back. On the first and second steps forward, the advancing foot is placed on the outside of the opponent's front foot; on the third step forward, one foot is placed between the opponent's steps; on the fourth step the rear foot moves up beside the front foot with the toe touching the ground lightly, which is called a half-step. Whether placed on the outside of the opponent or between his steps, one should keep slightly close to the opponent's front foot. On one straight line I advance and he retreats, and he # Appendix — Classical treatises on the art

Book page 646

Treatise on taijiquan

Treatise on taijiquan

Wang Zongyue of Shanyou Taiji is born of wuji and is the mother of yin and yang. In movement it divides; in stillness it joins. Neither excess nor deficiency: follow the bend and yield to the extension. When the other is hard and I am soft, this is called "walking away"; when I am yielding and the other is against his own advantage, this is called "sticking". If the movement is urgent, respond urgently; if the movement is slow, follow slowly. Though the transformations are myriad, the principle is one throughout. From familiarity with the postures one gradually awakens to understanding energy (dong jin); from understanding energy one ascends step by step to the divine illumination. Yet without long application one cannot break through to sudden comprehension. Empty the collar and lift the crown of the head; sink the breath to the dantian. Neither lean nor incline; now hidden, now revealed. If the left is heavy, the left becomes empty; if the right is heavy, the right vanishes. Look up and it grows higher; look down and it grows deeper. Advance and it grows longer; retreat and it grows more pressing. Not even a feather can be added, nor an insect alight. The other does not know me; I alone know the other. That the hero meets no enemy wherever he turns comes about from this alone. There are very many side doors to this art; though the postures differ, they amount to no more than the strong cheating the weak and the slow giving way to the quick. Strength beating weakness and a slow hand yielding to a quick hand are all natural endowments of the inborn body, not something that comes from learning. Consider the saying "four ounces deflect a thousand catties" — plainly it is not victory by strength. Observe the form of the aged defeating a crowd — of what use is speed? Stand like a balance beam; move like a wheel. Lean to one side and you follow; be double-weighted and you stagnate. One constantly sees men of several years' pure practice unable to transform, and it is invariably because they let themselves be controlled by the other — they have not awakened to the fault of double-weighting. To avoid this fault one must know yin and yang. Sticking is walking away, and walking away is sticking; yin does not leave yang, nor yang leave yin. Only when yin and yang aid each other is there understanding of energy. After understanding energy, the more one practises the finer it becomes; silently recognizing and pondering, one gradually arrives at doing as the heart desires. The root of it is to give up the self and follow the other; many mistake this and give up the near to seek the far.

As the saying goes, "a difference of a hair's breadth is an error of a thousand li" — the student cannot but examine this carefully. This is the treatise.

The thirteen postures (also called the long form, also called the thirteen postures)

Wang Zongyue of Shanyou The long form: it is like the great Yangtze and the great sea, rolling on without cease.

The thirteen postures: ward-off, roll-back, press, push, pluck, split, elbow, shoulder, advance, retreat, look left, gaze right, and central equilibrium. Ward-off, roll-back, press and push are the four cardinal directions, kan, li, zhen and dui. Pluck, split, elbow and shoulder are the four diagonal corners, qian, kun, gen and xun. These are the eight trigrams. Advancing, retreating, looking left, gazing right and central equilibrium are metal, wood, water, fire and earth. These are the five elements. Taken together, they are called the thirteen postures.

Book page 647

Song of practising the thirteen postures (author unknown)

Song of practising the thirteen postures (author unknown)

Do not slight the thirteen postures in all; Their life and intent have their source in the waist's gap. In changing fullness and emptiness, take care; Let breath go through the body, not dulled in the least. Touched in stillness, moving yet still as before; To change with the enemy is the wonder. In every posture keep the mind weighing intent; What is gained comes without felt expenditure of effort. Moment by moment keep the mind at the waist; Within the belly, loose and still, the breath rises. The tailbone centred, spirit threading the crown;

The whole body light and nimble, each part suspended. Attend closely and seek it out in yourself; Bend and extend, open and close, follow what is free. Crossing the threshold needs guiding by word of mouth; Ceaseless application, and the method settles of itself. If you ask what the standard of body and use is: Intent and breath are the lord, bone and flesh the minister. Push the question of intent to its end — where does it lie? Long life, lengthened years, an unwithering spring. Sing, O sing — a hundred and forty lines; Every word is true, its meaning beyond doubt.

If one does not seek it out along this path, one wastes one's labour and will only lament too late!

Song of pushing hands　Revised by Wang Zongyue

Song of pushing hands　Revised by Wang Zongyue

Ward-off, roll-back, press and push — take them seriously; When upper and lower follow one another, the opponent finds no way in. Let him come at me with all his giant strength — A pull of four ounces deflects a thousand catties. Draw him in, let him fall into emptiness, issue as he closes; Stick, connect, adhere, follow — never lose the crown of the head.

Body method　Wu Yuxiang

Body method　Wu Yuxiang

Sink the chest, raise the back, wrap the crotch, protect the ribs, lift the crown, suspend the crotch, soar and shift, flash and battle.

Essential words on pushing hands　Wu Yuxiang

Explanation: Use the mind to move the breath; one must be sunk and steady, and only then can it gather and enter the bones — this is what is meant by "the source of the command of intent lies in the gap of the waist." The intent and breath must be exchanged with agility, and only then is there the delight of roundness and liveliness — this is what is meant by "in changing and turning, fullness and emptiness must be heeded." Stand with the body centred and upright, at ease and comfortable, bracing in all eight directions; move the breath like a nine-bend pearl, so that no subtlety is unreached — this is what is meant by "the breath goes through the whole body without the least dullness."

In issuing power one must be sunk, steady, loose and still, concentrating on a single direction — this is what is meant by "touched in stillness, moving yet still as before." In going and returning there must be folding; in advancing and retreating there must be turning — this is what is meant by "to change with the enemy is the wonder." Seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue — this is what is meant by "in every posture keep the mind weighing intent; moment by moment keep the mind at the waist." If the spirit can be raised, then there is no fear of slowness and heaviness — this is what is meant by "within the belly, loose and still, the breath rises." With an insubstantial crown lifting the power, the breath sunk to the elixir field, neither leaning nor inclining — this is what is meant by "the tailbone centred, spirit threading the crown; the whole body light and nimble, the crown suspended." Move the body with the breath, and one must be smooth and compliant, and only then can one be agile and follow the mind — this is what is meant by "bend and extend, open and close, follow what is free." The mind is the command, the breath the banner, the spirit the commander-in-chief, the body the servant — this is what is meant by "intent and breath are the lord, bone and flesh the minister." Explanation: Though the body moves, the mind values stillness; the breath must gather, the spirit should be at ease. The mind is the command, the breath the banner, the spirit the commander-in-chief, the body the servant; moment by moment keep the mind on it, and only then is anything attained. First in the mind, afterwards in the body. When it is in the body, one no longer knows that the hands dance and the feet stamp. This is what is meant by "completing it in one breath," "giving up the self and following others," "drawing him in to fall into emptiness," "four ounces deflecting a thousand catties." Know that when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved; when one thing is still, nothing is unstilled. Regard movement as stillness, regard stillness as movement; inwardly solidify the spirit, outwardly show ease and comfort. One must follow others, not proceed from oneself; following others one lives, proceeding from oneself one stagnates. He who prizes breath has no power; he who nourishes breath is purely firm. When the other does not move, I do not move; when the other moves slightly, I move first. Leaning on others with oneself, one must know oneself, and only then can one turn and follow and follow and meet; sticking to others with oneself, one must know others, and only then can one be neither behind nor before. If the spirit can be raised, there is no fear of slowness and heaviness; if sticking and leaning can follow with agility, only then is the wonder of falling into emptiness seen. In going and returning, yin and yang must be distinguished; in advancing and retreating, there must be turning and closing. The opportunity is issued from oneself; the force is borrowed from others. In issuing power, upper and lower must follow one another, and then one goes forward invincible; in standing, the body must be centred and upright, not inclining, and then it can brace in all eight directions. Still as a mountain, moving as a river. Step as if on the brink of an abyss, move power as if drawing silk, store power as if drawing a bow, issue power as if loosing an arrow. Move the breath like a nine-bend pearl, so that no subtlety is unreached; move power like steel tempered a hundred times, and what hardness will it not shatter. In form like a falcon seizing a hare, in spirit like a cat catching a mouse. Seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue. Gathering is issuing, continuous without break. Utterly soft, and only then can one be utterly firm; able to stick and lean, and only then can one be agile. Nourish the breath by what is straight and it does no harm; store the power by what is curved and it has surplus. Gradually one comes to respond to things as they come — this too is "knowing to stop, and so attaining."

Again it is said:

First in the mind, afterwards in the body; belly loose, breath gathered into the bones, spirit at ease, body still, moment by moment keeping the mind. Remember always: when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved; when one thing is still, nothing is unstilled. Regard stillness as movement, regard movement as stillness. In moving, pulling to and fro, the breath clings to the back, gathered into the spine — be still. Inwardly solidify the spirit, outwardly show ease and comfort. Step as a cat walks, move power as if drawing silk. The whole body's intent lies in storing spirit, not in breath; if in breath, then it stagnates. He who has breath has no power; he who has no breath is purely firm. The breath is like a cartwheel, the waist like the axle.

Again it is said:

When the other does not move, I do not move; when the other moves slightly, I move first. As if loose yet not loose, about to unfold yet not — unfold. The power breaks but the intent does not break.

Again it is said:

In every movement, the hand alone first applies force, and then immediately loosens. One must still thread it through, and this is nothing other than beginning, sustaining, turning and closing. First the intent moves, then the power moves; the transition must be strung on a single thread. The breath should be stirred and agitated, the spirit should be gathered inward. Do not allow any place of defect, do not allow any place of concavity or convexity, do not allow any place of break or interruption. Its root is in the feet, it issues from the legs, it is governed by the waist, it takes form in the fingers. From feet to legs to waist, it must always be one complete breath. Advancing and retreating, only then does one gain the opportunity and the position; where one does not gain opportunity and position, the body becomes scattered, and one must come to lean and tilt — the fault must be sought in the waist and legs, and it is so above and below, before and behind, left and right. All of this is intent, not outward form: where there is above there is below, where there is front there is back, where there is left there is right. If the intent wishes to go up, then lodge the intent below; if a thing is about to be lifted, and you add a breaking force to it, then its root breaks of itself, and it is destroyed swiftly, beyond doubt. Fullness and emptiness should be clearly distinguished: each place has its own fullness and emptiness, and every place is always this one fullness and emptiness; the whole body is threaded joint by joint — do not let there be the least interruption.

Book page 651

Releasing in pushing hands

Releasing in pushing hands

Ward-off péng (upper level tone) · yè (entering tone) · yī (rising tone) · ké (entering tone) · hū (rising tone) · kēng · hē · hā.

Five-word formula　Li Yiyu
One: the mind is still

If the mind is not still, then it is not focused; as soon as one raises a hand, front, back, left and right have no fixed direction at all — hence the mind must be still. At first the movements cannot come from oneself; one must calm the mind and personally recognise it, following what the other does, yielding and extending with him, neither losing nor resisting, not extending and contracting on one's own. If he has force, I too have force, and my force is first; if he has no force, I — also have no force, and my intent is still first. One must keep the mind on it moment by moment: wherever one is touched, the mind must be applied there; one must seek the news within "neither losing nor resisting." Working on in this way, in a year or half a year one can apply it in the body. This is entirely intent, not the use of force; in time, others are controlled by me, and I am not controlled by others.

Two: the body is agile

If the body is stagnant, then one cannot advance and retreat freely; hence the body must be agile. In raising a hand one must not have a stupid look. When the other's force has just touched my skin and hair, my intent has already entered his bones; both hands brace, and one breath runs through. When the left is heavy, the left empties and the right has already gone; when the right is heavy, the right empties and the left has already gone. The breath is like a cartwheel: the whole body must follow along. Where it does not follow, the body becomes scattered and cannot get force — the fault must be sought in the waist and legs. First use the mind to command the body, following others and not oneself. Afterwards the body can follow the mind, and even proceeding from oneself is still following others. Proceeding from oneself one stagnates; following others one lives. If one can follow others, then in the hands there is measure. Weigh the size of his force, and there is no error of a fraction; gauge the length of his advance, and there is no difference of a hair. Advancing and retreating, everywhere exactly fitting — the longer the work, the finer the skill.

Three: the breath gathers

If the breath's momentum is scattered and loose, then there is no containment, and the body easily scatters; one must cause the breath to gather into the spine. The breathing is numinous and unobstructed, and the whole body has no gap. Inhaling is closing and storing; exhaling is opening and issuing. For inhaling naturally lifts one up, and can also lift the other up; exhaling naturally sinks one down, and can also send the other out. This is moving the breath by intent, not driving the breath by force.

Four: the power is whole

The power of the whole body is trained into one family, distinguishing clearly fullness and emptiness. In issuing power there must be a root: the power rises from the heel, is governed at the waist, takes form in the fingers, and issues from the spine and back. One must also raise up the whole of one's spirit: at the moment when the other's power is about to issue but has not yet issued, my power has already joined his power — exactly neither behind nor before, like skin catching fire, like a spring gushing out. Advancing and retreating, there is not the least scattering; seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue, and only then can one succeed at once with the hand. This is what is meant by "borrowing force to strike the man, four ounces deflecting a thousand catties."

Five: the spirit gathers

When the above four are all present, they all return to the gathering of the spirit. When the spirit gathers, then one breath forges and casts, refining the breath and returning it to the spirit, and the breath's momentum soars and shifts. The spirit is poured in; opening and closing have order; fullness and emptiness are clear. When the left is empty, the right is full; when the right is empty, the left is full. Emptiness is not being utterly without force — the breath's momentum must have soaring and shifting; fullness is not being utterly locked up — the spirit must be valued and poured in. The crux lies entirely in the transforming within the chest and waist, not outside. Force is borrowed from others; breath issues from the spine. How can breath issue from the spine? The breath sinks downward, gathering from both shoulders into the spine and pouring into the waist — this is the breath going from above to below, and it is called closing. From the waist it takes form in the spine, spreads to both arms, and is applied in the fingers — this is the breath going from below to above, and it is called opening. Closing is gathering; opening is issuing. If one can understand opening and closing, then one knows yin and yang. Arriving at this stage, one day's work is one day's refinement of skill, until gradually one follows what the mind desires, and nothing fails to accord with one's intent.

Book page 652

Secret formula for releasing　Li Yiyu

Secret formula for releasing　Li Yiyu

Lift, draw, loosen, release Lift up his body, borrowing his force. Within it is the word "numinous." Draw him to the front of the body, and the power only then stores. Within it is the word "gather." Loosen my power and do not let it bend. Within it is the word "still." In releasing, the waist and feet must recognise the exact point. Within it is the word "whole."

Book page 653

Essential words on practising the form and pushing hands　Li Yiyu

Essential words on practising the form and pushing hands　Li Yiyu

The men of old said: "One can draw in and let fall into emptiness, and can deflect a thousand catties with four ounces; one cannot draw in and let fall into emptiness, and cannot deflect a thousand catties with four ounces." The words are very comprehensive, and the beginner has no way to grasp them. I add a few phrases to explain them, so that those who have the will in this art may find the way in, and so advance daily with achievement. If one wishes to draw in and let fall into emptiness, and to deflect a thousand catties with four ounces, one must first know oneself and know others. If one wishes to know oneself and know others, one must first give up up the self and follow others. If one wishes to give up the self and follow others, one must first gain the opportunity and the position. If one wishes to gain opportunity and position, one must first make the whole body one family. If one wishes to make the whole body one family, one must first have no defect in the whole body. If one wishes to have no defect in the whole body, one must first have the spirit and breath stirred and agitated. If one wishes the spirit and breath stirred and agitated, one must first raise up the spirit, so that the spirit cannot scatter outward. If one wishes the spirit not to scatter outward, one must first have the spirit and breath gather and enter the bones. If one wishes the spirit and breath to gather and enter the bones, one must first have strength in the front section of both thighs. Both shoulders loosen, the breath sinks downward, the power rises from the heel, changes in the legs, is contained in the chest, moves in both shoulders, and is governed in the waist. Above, the two arms are linked; below, the two legs follow. The power is exchanged from within: gathering is closing, releasing is opening. When still, all is still; stillness is closing, and within closing is lodged opening. When moving, all moves; movement is opening, and within opening is lodged closing. Touched, one then turns and revolves freely, and nowhere fails to get force. Only then can one draw in and let fall into emptiness, and deflect a thousand catties with four ounces. In ordinary practice of the form, this is the work of knowing oneself: at each movement, first ask whether one's whole body accords with these several items; if it accords but slightly not, then change at once — hence in practising the form one should be slow and not fast. Pushing hands is the work of knowing others; movement and stillness are indeed knowing others, but it is still asking oneself. If one has arranged oneself well, then when another touches me, I do not move him a hair's breadth, but take advantage of his momentum to enter, join and fix his power, and he falls out of himself. If one has a place where one cannot get force, then it is double-weighting not yet transformed, and one must seek it in the opening and closing of yin and yang. This is what is meant by "know yourself and know others, and in a hundred battles you will win a hundred victories."

Note: The above classical treatises on boxing are selected and transcribed from the definitive edition of the Taijiquan Manual that Li Yiyu copied out and presented to Hao Weizhen in 1881; the text has not been altered by later hands.

Four-word secret formula　(author to be verified)

Fu (spread): Fu means moving the breath in one's own body and spreading it over the other's power, so that he cannot move.

Gai (cover): Gai means using the breath to cover the place from which the other comes.

Dui (match): Dui means using the breath to match the place from which the other comes, fixing the aim and then going out.

Tun (swallow): Tun means using the breath to swallow him wholly and enter into transformation.

These four words are without form and without sound; only after understanding power, when one has refined to the most exquisite stage, can one know them — completely it is spoken of in terms of breath. If one can nourish one's breath by what is straight and without harm, only then can one apply it to the four limbs, and the four limbs will speak without words.

Textual note: Li Fuyin, grandson of Li Yiyu, compiled the Lianrang Hall edition of the Taijiquan Manual in 1935 and took the "Four-word secret formula" to be a work of Wu Yuxiang, basing this on the Brief Account of My Late Grandfather, the Honourable Lianquan, written by Wu Laixu, grandson of Wu Yuxiang. Laixu said of his grandfather that "receiving the art, his insights came entirely from the four-word formula," and so Fuyin took the "Four-word secret formula" to be Wu Yuxiang's work. Considering that this formula's boxing theory is lofty and subtle, with a level above Li Yiyu's "Secret formula for releasing"; that Li Yiyu's Taijiquan Manual, written out for Hao He in 1881, fully records Wu Yuxiang's boxing treatises; that Wu Yuxiang died in 1880; and that Wu and Li stood as teacher and student and lived in the same village — if this formula were Wu Yuxiang's work, there is no way it would not have been included. Hence this formula is probably not Wu Yuxiang's work, and may have been composed by a disciple of Wu or of Li. Li Yiyu died in 1892, so it is also possible that he wrote this formula. It is singled out here for further examination.

(Appendix note by Gu Liuxin)

Book page 655

Preface

Preface

Guided by the Party's policy of "letting a hundred flowers bloom, a hundred schools of thought contend," the editor drew on the posthumous work of her late father, Mr. Sun Lutang — The Study of Taijiquan (《太极拳学》) — and on the way he practiced in his later years, and compiled Sun-Style Taijiquan (《孙式太极拳》), published in 1957. To meet the needs of the broad masses in their physical training, the editor has now revised the 1957 edition. The movement descriptions have been amended and expanded, the movement photographs have been retaken, and the applications of certain principal movements have been added, while the original structure has been retained in the main. Although the editor received instruction from her late father in person from early childhood, she is conscious that her own skill falls short of depth and purity; still, for the convenience of those who love Sun-style Taijiquan and wish to practise it, she has done her best.

Confined as it is by the editor's level, the book will inevitably contain errors; readers are earnestly asked to point them out.

— The Editor

Brief Introduction to Sun-Style Taijiquan

Brief Introduction to Sun-Style Taijiquan

The founder of Sun-style taiji (太极, tàijí) quan was Sun Fuquan (孙福全, Sūn Fúquán), courtesy name Lutang (禄堂, Lùtáng), late sobriquet Hanzhai (涵斋, Hánzhāi), a native of Wanxian in Hebei. From childhood he was passionately fond of martial arts. He studied Xingyi Quan (形意拳, Xíngyì Quán) under Li Kuiyuan (李魁垣, Lǐ Kuíyuán), and then studied under Li's own teacher Guo Yunshen (郭云深, Guō Yúnshēn), from whom he received the true transmission. He also studied Baguazhang (八卦拳, Bāguàzhāng) under Cheng Tinghua (程廷华, Chéng Tínghuá). After several years of study and polishing his skill ran deep. He later studied taijiquan under Hao Weizhen (郝为真, Hǎo Wéizhēn). Sun Lutang (孙禄堂, Sūn Lùtáng) devoted his whole life to the study of martial arts; he was proficient in Xingyi, Baguazhang and taijiquan, and gathering the essential meaning of the three schools into one, he created Sun-style taijiquan.

The characteristics of Sun-style taijiquan are: advance and retreat follow one another; when stepping forward one must follow, when stepping back one must withdraw. The movements are extended, rounded and lively, nimble and natural. In practice the two feet are clearly distinguished as empty and full (虚实, xūshí). The whole set, once begun, is like drifting clouds and flowing water, continuous and unbroken. At every turn of the body "opening" and "closing" (开合, kāihé) join, and so it is also called kaihe huobu taijiquan (开合活步太极拳, kāihé huóbù tàijíquán). It is suitable for people of any age and any constitution to practise.

General Explanation of Taijiquan

Taijiquan is one of the martial arts peculiar to our country. It is an exercise of "cultivating both within and without" (inwardly it governs calming the mind and nurturing the nature, outwardly it governs training the body); it takes suppleness and curvature as its substance and firmness and straightness as its function. Without suppleness and curvature one cannot neutralize; without firmness and straightness one cannot apply. In substance and function it is the fighting method of "using softness to overcome hardness, drawing aside four ounces to deflect a thousand catties." In practising this quan one should sink the qi to the dantian (丹田, dāntián), neither lean nor incline, so that inner and outer join; one must on no account use clumsy strength. One should move the strength by the intent (意, yì) — where the intent arrives, the strength arrives.

As to the method of practising taijiquan, my late father often said: Mr. Hao Weizhen spoke of three levels of mental state in practising taijiquan. At the first stage of practice it is as though the body were in water, both feet treading the ground, and the movements meet the resistance of the water. At the second level it is as though the body were in water with both feet floating up, like a swimmer drifting in the water, able to move freely. At the third level the body is light and nimble, the two feet as if walking on the surface of the water — treading on the brink of the abyss, on thin ice — with the spirit and qi gathered inward, not daring to let there be the slightest scattering or disorder. Then the quan is accomplished.

The postures and movements of taijiquan all have definite essential points, and each has its own meaning. The essentials are introduced in summary below:

Head: The head should push up, but one must not use strength. The chin is naturally drawn in, the top of the head upright, the spirit concentrated. The whole body is relaxed and open; in lifting, pressing, extending and contracting one always uses intent and does not use clumsy strength, and the mind is naturally empty and numinous. This is what is called "empty and numinous, suspending the head-top" (虚灵顶劲, xūlíng dǐngjìn).

Mouth: The mouth should be loosely closed, the tongue touching the upper palate, breathing through the nose.

Chest: The chest should be contained and must not be thrust out. When the chest is contained the qi sinks to the dantian. When the chest is thrust out the qi surges into the chest region, the upper is heavy and the lower light, and the heels float — a thing taboo to the martial practitioner. When the chest is contained the qi clings to the back, and strength issues from the spine — this is true strength. The above is what is called "containing the chest and raising the back" (含胸拔背, hánxiōng bábèi).

Shoulders: Both shoulders must be relaxed and hanging down. One must especially avoid hunching the shoulders, otherwise the qi surges upward.

Book page 658

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

Elbows: The two elbows should hang loosely downward, the two arms naturally bent. This is the meaning of "seeking the straight within the curved, storing and then issuing."

Hands: The five fingers are spread, the wrist sunk (塌腕, tāwàn), the tiger's mouth slightly rounded, the palm slightly drawn in, as though grasping and holding a ball.

Waist: The waist must be sunk (塌, tā). For the waist is the pivot of the whole body's movements and the source of strength. A person's turning, advancing and retreating, and the changes of empty and full all depend on the waist strength running through them.

Legs: The two legs are bent, and one must clearly distinguish empty and full — that is, the body's centre of gravity is placed on one leg. If the centre of gravity moves onto the right leg, then the right leg is full and the left leg is empty. Conversely, the left leg is full and the right leg is empty. Distinguishing empty and full is the essential meaning of taijiquan; moving thus, the turning is light and nimble. Otherwise the stepping is heavy and sluggish, and one is easily led about by others.

Breathing: What is called "sinking the qi to the dantian" (three inches below the navel) means deep and long abdominal breathing. But one must on no account use strength to press the qi downward; one must simply let the breathing be entirely natural (呼吸, hūxī).

Intent and strength: One of the characteristics of taijiquan is that it uses intent and does not use strength. For taijiquan requires the use of living strength; the whole body must be relaxed and open, not allowing the least bit of clumsy strength to linger between sinews, bones, blood and vessels. It requires being extremely soft and yet extremely firm and hard, extremely heavy and yet extremely nimble. Where the intent arrives the strength arrives, applied with ease. If clumsy strength is used, then it is sluggish and not nimble. If the strength floats on the outside, it does not accord with the requirements of taijiquan. What is meant by using intent and not using strength, and how does living strength arise of itself? It is because where the intent goes the qi arrives; thus the qi and blood flow and pour, day by day infusing and circulating through the channels and network vessels of the whole body, never for a moment stagnating. With long practice true inner strength (内劲, nèijìn) is then produced.

Movement and stillness: The quiet sitting of qigong is seeking movement within stillness; boxing art is seeking stillness within movement. In practising the quan the mind must be still and the spirit concentrated; only then can the movements be rounded and lively.

The above has discussed the essentials of movement separately. But the student must certainly note that taijiquan is an exercise of the whole body, and what is trained lies in the spirit. The spirit is the commander, the body is the servant; if the spirit can be raised, then the movements are naturally light and nimble. Only when mind and intent are in harmony with the movements of the form can inner and outer join as one. In practice one must take care that above and below follow one another, and that all parts of the body are complete and unified. If there is one place where the movement is not whole, the spirit and qi will be scattered and disordered. Furthermore, in practising the quan one should move the strength by the intent, linked without interruption, "like the long Yangtze River, rolling on without cease." "In movement, like drawing silk" —

Book page 659

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

— such is the meaning.

To make it easy for the reader to remember, these essential points are now put into a mnemonic verse as follows:

Taijiquan is originally an inner-school boxing (内家拳, nèijiāquán);
do not use clumsy strength — intent comes first.
Empty and numinous, suspending the head-top (顶头, dǐngtóu), the spirit concentrated;
draw the chin back and it is then natural.
Containing the chest, one can naturally raise the back;
on no account form "hunchback shoulders."
In practice sink the shoulders and drop the elbows;
with shoulders hunched and elbows suspended it is not the quan.
Sinking the waist (塌腰, tāyāo) can raise the strength of the whole body;
if the waist is not sunk, nimbleness is difficult.
The two legs bent distinguish empty and full;
here lies the essential meaning of taiji.
Breathing (呼吸, hūxī) sinks down to the dantian point;
let it be purely natural, do not force it.
Above and below follow one another and become one body;
the movements, continuous and unbroken, are forever linked.
Seek stillness within movement, movement within stillness;
in practice the spirit and qi must be complete in every part.
Be sure to remember these points and not forget them;
with lasting practice the benefit will show of itself.

Part One. Two: Explanation of the Movements

Part One. Two: Explanation of the Movements
First Posture: Beginning Posture (起式, Qǐ Shì)
  • ① The body stands upright, both hands hang down, both shoulders relax; the tips of the two feet are separated by about 90°; the eyes look straight ahead, the mind is quiet, and one pauses briefly. (图 1)

The eyes look straight ahead, the mind is quiet, and one pauses briefly. (图 1)

图 1
practitioner standing upright facing front, arms hanging naturally at the sides, feet apart, weight evenly on both legs.
图 2
practitioner standing with the body turned slightly to the left, right toes raised and pivoting on the right heel, feet at roughly 45° to one another.
图 3
practitioner standing with both arms raised forward to about shoulder height, palms facing each other as if holding a ball, legs unchanged.
图 4
the whole body sinks into a crouch, both hands come down in front of the abdomen, the left heel is lifted.
图 7

图 10

图 6
the right foot has followed up to the inner side of the left ankle, the toe touching the ground, both hands holding a ball in front of the chest.
图 9
the right hand having drawn a half-circle to the right and backward, the forearm is upright and the left hand supports the right wrist.

The right wrist pushes forward together with it, both arms slightly bent; at the same time the right foot steps forward, the heel touching the ground first and gradually settling; the left foot thereupon follows behind the right foot, about 10 cm apart, the toe touching the ground; the eyes look at the right hand, and one pauses briefly. (图 9、10)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the movement must run through in a single continuous flow and must not be interrupted. Application (用法, yòngfǎ): Lazy Tucking the Robe is composed of warding off, rolling back, pressing and pushing (掤捋挤按, péng lǚ jǐ àn). ① Ward-off (掤, péng): when the opponent strikes with the hand, one presses his wrist down with the front hand and draws it backward, The rear hand quickly seeks out his elbow. If the opponent's attacking hand comes high, then both hands lift his arm from below and drive it backward and downward, or one may also drive it level toward the side and rear.

图 11
practitioner standing, both hands held in front of the chest at about shoulder height, forearms curved, palms facing each other.
图 12
practitioner standing, both hands held forward in front of the chest, palms facing each other, feet apart with the weight settled.
  • ③ Ward-off (掤, péng), that is, propping (not dead propping with brute resistance). When the opponent rushes at one with both hands, one sticks both arms upward to his hands, sits the waist back and withdraws the left step, turns the waist slightly to the right, pats to the right with the left hand and hangs to the right with the right hand; at this moment the opponent's force has already been neutralized, and one issues at the appropriate instant. The subtlety of the ward-off method lies in "sticking": neither letting go nor resisting, the two arms like springs, so that what the opponent touches seems both present and absent. Ward-off may be done with both hands or with one; if one wards off the opponent's two hands with a single hand, one gains the more advantageous position.
  • ④ Push (按, àn): if the opponent attacks toward one, one lightly presses down both of his arms with both hands and immediately pushes out forward. Push may be done with one hand or both, with opening energy or closing energy as the situation determines, but one must stick to the opponent's arms so that he cannot turn and move freely.
图 13
practitioner in a wider stance with the arms opened out to the sides at shoulder height, both palms turned outward.
图 14
both hands opened left and right in front of the chest until they face the two shoulders, fingertips pointing up, the practitioner standing with one foot before the other.
图 15
both hands brought together in front of the chest, about a face-width apart, both knees bent, the tip of the left foot touching the ground.
图 16
both hands raised level to the left and right, the arms in a level-raise position, the two palms facing outward, standing with the feet apart.

[The left foot] buckles inward to the left by about 90°, and the body turns to the left along with it; at the same time, with the two palms facing each other and the fingertips pointing upward, [the hands] separate to left and right (as if holding a balloon whose air expands outward, opening until the tiger's mouths of the two hands face the two shoulders), the two hands about 10 cm apart, and one pauses slightly. (图 11)

Fourth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

Following on from the previous posture, with the two palms facing each other the hands slowly close inward; when they have come to about a face-width apart, one pauses slightly; at the same time both legs bend, the right foot is on the ground, the left heel lifts with the toe touching the ground; the eyes look at the space between the two hands. (图 12)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the whole body must relax; there must not be the slightest forced strength.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): Opening and Closing the Hands — if the opponent suddenly embraces one's two arms from behind with both hands, one immediately props against his two arms with the elbows, quickly presses downward, and following the momentum turns the body to the left or turns the body to the right.

Fifth Posture: Single Whip (单鞭, Dān Biān)

Following on from the previous posture, the two hands rotate inward and, as if driving a long pole, slowly separate to left and right, the two arms reaching a level-raise position, the two palms facing outward, the palm upright, at the height of the eyes; at the same time the left foot steps sideways to the left, the leg slightly bent; the right leg slightly straightened; the eyes look at the right hand, and one pauses briefly. (图 13)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the upper body must be straight, the two shoulders must be relaxed, the breathing must be natural, and one must not use clumsy strength to press qi (气) down into the dantian (丹田, dāntián).

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): ① Single Whip deals with opponents on both the left and right sides. Although the two hands separate at the same time, one must be empty and the other full (虚实, xūshí); which is full and which is empty depends on how near or far the opponent's attacking force is. If the left hand ...a solid strike. The centre of gravity must fall on the left leg, while one keeps watch to the right; at the same time the right foot may be raised to kick an opponent on the right.

Twelfth Posture: Advance the Step, Deflect, Bar and Punch (进步搬拦捶, Jìn Bù Bān Lán Chuí)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand rotates inward and brushes downward and to the left to in front of the ribs, palm facing down; the right hand rotates outward and upward, extends forward past beneath the left hand, palm facing up; at the same time the left foot steps forward, the tip of the foot turned slightly outward. Fifty-Fourth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

Fifty-Fifth Posture: Diagonal Single Whip (斜单鞭, Xié Dān Biān)

Following the preceding posture, the left foot steps out to the left front, and the two hands separate level. (Fig. 113)

Fifty-Sixth Posture: Parting the Wild Horse's Mane (野马分鬃, Yě Mǎ Fēn Zōng)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left foot draws in beside the right foot, the whole sole on the ground; at the same time the left hand sweeps downward in an arc to the front of the abdomen; the eyes look at the right hand. (Fig. 114)
  • ② The left hand goes upward past the chest and then sweeps in an arc to the left to the left side of the body; at the same time the left foot steps out to the left, the tip of the foot turned slightly outward; the eyes look at the left hand. (Fig. 115)
  • ③ The right hand sweeps downward in an arc to the front of the abdomen, then upward past the face and in an arc to the right to the right side of the body; at the same time the right foot draws in beside the left foot (the tip of the foot touching the ground, the two feet about 10 cm apart), and then steps out one pace to the right; at this point the single-whip posture is resumed, but the weight is biased toward the right leg. (Figs. 116, 117)
  • ④ The left foot steps forward in front of the right foot, the tip of the foot turned outward and set down diagonally, the two legs bent; at the same time the two hands go downward and cross in front (the palms turned slightly outward, the left hand above, the right hand below, the two arms slightly curved), and immediately separate to left and right, each drawing a circle to the front of the chest, the right palm facing upward, the left palm facing downward; the eyes look at the lower front. (Figs. 118, 119)
Fifty-Seventh Posture: Lazily Tucking in the Robe (懒扎衣, Lǎn Zhā Yī)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the right foot steps forward; the left foot then follows up behind the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground, pausing briefly and then withdrawing; at the same time the weight of the body shifts to the left leg, the tip of the right foot raised; the left hand supports the right wrist and the two push forward together (the right palm facing upward, the left palm facing downward), then wind level to the right and to the rear to the front of the right shoulder, both palms facing outward. (Figs. 120, 121, 122)
  • ② The two hands push forward together; the left foot follows up to about 10 cm behind the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look at the index finger of the right hand. (Fig. 123)

Fifty-Ninth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

Elbowing (肘, zhǒu) means to drive the elbow against the opponent.

Leaning (靠, kào) means to press and lean against the opponent with the shoulder.

The footwork of the great roll-back is a wide and swift stride; only when the two legs have skill can one be nimble and changeable.

4. The Use of Force and the Listening to Force in Push-Hands (推手的用劲和听劲, Tuī Shǒu de Yòng Jìn hé Tīng Jìn)

In beginning push-hands one must not use clumsy strength, but must seek out the secret within the four words warding-off, rolling-back, pressing and pushing; these four words contain infinite transformations, and the student must experience them deeply.

For example: warding-off has the distinctions of straight warding-off and lateral warding-off, above and below. In rolling back one must stick to the opponent's hand, then immediately change direction and trace a circle, so that the opponent's force cannot issue forth, or if it issues forth is at once dissolved.

Warding-off is divided into upward, downward and level warding-off. In thrusting, one hand must press and hold the opponent's wrist and the other hand press the opponent's elbow, so that the opponent has no room to move and is thrust out along the line of his own force. Again, within the thrust there is also a warding-off force, which should not be used lightly.

Pressing has various methods: straight pressing, slanting pressing, and pressing with the addition of the elbow. If one presses with the arm along a curve, one can change the point of force at any moment and with any configuration, and force may be issued from any place.

Pushing includes lightness and nimbleness or heaviness and solidity, left solid and right empty or right solid and left empty, the two hands opening or closing; in sum, one must change according to the configuration.

When two people drill push-hands together, besides attending to experiencing the methods of using force, one must accomplish bending and extending in accord with the other, neither losing contact nor resisting, not using clumsy strength, calming the mind and listening to force. In time, one can lead the opponent in to fall into emptiness and move a thousand catties with a pull of four ounces.

As for "listening to force" (听劲, tīng jìn), one must on no account mistake it for two parties opposing each other with strength. One commonly sees, in push-hands, two people locking strength against each other, one asking whether the other has force yet, the other answering that he has or has not — this is a great error. "Listening to force" is to sense the magnitude and direction of the opponent's applied force and so change at once; one must on no account lock against it. In beginning practice, train the two arms first; with long practice the whole body can sense it. If one can listen to force, then when the opponent issues force one can dissolve it and make him fall into emptiness. If one cannot listen to force, one need not measure oneself against others; the student must certainly attend to this.

Book page 708

2. The Martial Application of Taijiquan (太极拳技击, Tàijíquán Jì Jī)

2. The Martial Application of Taijiquan (太极拳技击, Tàijíquán Jì Jī)

The martial application of Taijiquan is nothing other than the eight methods: warding-off, rolling-back, pressing, pushing, plucking, rending, elbowing and leaning. These eight methods are all contained within the Taijiquan form; push-hands is the practising of these eight methods for use. At present, whether one practises the form or practises push-hands, both are the familiarising of these eight methods, and so it is said that the eight methods are the application of Taijiquan. But to practise the form alone is to have substance without application, and its defect lies in having no change. To practise push-hands alone is to have application without substance, and its defect lies in having no root. If one practises only for the cultivation of body and mind, then practising the form is already sufficient; but if one wishes to obtain its application, one must practise both.

In terms of practising substance, Taijiquan is the art of knowing oneself (知己功夫, zhī jǐ gōng fu); only after long and thoroughly proficient practice can one make the whole body insubstantial and numinous, round and lively without obstruction, heavy and still as Mount Tai, light and nimble as a feather, with spirit (神, shén) and vital energy (气, qì) blended and fused, whereby one may of oneself dispel illness and prolong life. In terms of practising application, it is the art of knowing others (知人功夫, zhī rén gōng fu); only after long practice with pure skill can the hands and feet be nimble and alive, leading the opponent in to fall into emptiness and moving a thousand catties with a pull of four ounces. Hence only by practising both substance and application does one come to know oneself and know others; if one cannot know oneself and know others, one cannot measure oneself against others. One commonly sees those who claim to study only "martial application": using force for the sake of using force, they must apply clumsy strength, and so enter a wrong road. The student is asked to guard against this.

To become proficient in the martial application of Taijiquan, one should take the practice of the form as the main thing and seek skill from the waist and legs. For martial application first demands quick reaction; to react quickly one must have each single hand and each single posture thoroughly proficient, with waist and legs nimble and strong, before one can respond to the opponent with lightness, nimbleness, roundness and liveliness. Further, one must be able to "listen to force", for only thus can one stick to the opponent, respond to the moment and adapt, hear one and know a hundred, and change without limit.

In Part One the methods of use of some of the postures have been outlined, but the student must not memorise them by rote and rigidly. One should make the form proficient and practise push-hands diligently. In beginning the static-step push-hands, the work lies mainly in the waist; when the waist is extremely nimble, one has more than enough for dissolving the opponent's force. Once proficient, one practises the moving-step push-hands, where the work lies mainly in the legs; when the skill is pure, one advances, retreats and changes direction swiftly. Thereafter one goes through the four corners, and after that the free hand (散手, sàn shǒu). The two parties may then disregard the rules and attack and dissolve at will, each against the other.

In sum, the martial application of Taijiquan — that is, free hand — has no fixed rule or method, but changes at any time and in any configuration as the opportunity arises; this is the meaning of the saying that free hand has no fixed forms. A single posture in the art may be used in several ways, and several postures may be used as one, but one must always weigh the time and gauge the configuration before acting. Exactly as the classic says, "When the other does not move, "I do not move; if the opponent moves, I move first." This is what is meant by "the intent (意, yì) precedes the enemy." That is to say: however fierce and swift the opponent's action, one can dissolve it and turn it to one's own use. One must not wait for the opponent's technique to land upon one's own body; nor may one always use a single technique, for without change one is controlled by others. It is hoped that the student will draw inferences from one instance to three, know the applications without being bound by the applications, and diligently practise push-hands; then one may attain the mystery of Taijiquan as a fighting art.

Appendix: Reference Materials I. Wang Zongyue: A Treatise on Taijiquan Taiji (太极, Tàijí) is born of Wuji (无极, Wújí); it is the mechanism of movement and stillness, the mother of yin and yang (阴阳, yīn yáng). When moved, they separate; when still, they unite. Neither excess nor deficiency — follow the bend and yield the extension. When the opponent is hard and I am soft, this is called "yielding" (走); when I am favourable and the opponent adverse, this is called "sticking" (黏). If he moves quickly, respond quickly; if he moves slowly, follow slowly. Though the transformations are countless, the principle is one throughout. From familiarity with the techniques one gradually awakens to "understanding energy" (懂劲, dǒng jìn); from understanding energy one ascends step by step to spiritual clarity (神明, shén míng). Yet without long effort one cannot suddenly penetrate it. With an insubstantial and numinous uplifting of the crown (虚灵顶劲, xū líng dǐng jìn), the qi (气) sinks to the elixir field (丹田, dāntián). Neither leaning nor inclining, now hidden, now appearing. Where the left is heavy, the left is made empty; where the right is heavy, the right is made obscure. Raise it and it becomes higher still; lower it and it becomes deeper still. Advance upon it and it grows longer; retreat from it and it grows more urgent. Not a feather may be added, not a fly may alight. Others do not know me; I alone know others. The hero who meets no match wherever he turns attains this through nothing else. There are many side doors to this art; though the postures differ, they come to no more than the strong bullying the weak and the slow yielding to the fast. Strength beating weakness, a slow hand yielding to a fast hand — all of these are inborn natural abilities, and have nothing to do with what is achieved by study. Consider the saying "four ounces deflect a thousand catties": it is plain that this is not a victory of force. Observe the form whereby the aged can hold off a crowd: what can speed do there? Stand like a balance, move like a wheel. Lean to one side and you follow; double-weight (双重, shuāng zhòng) and you stagnate. One often sees those whose pure effort of many years cannot transform — all are controlled by others and in the end cannot control others; this is simply that the fault of double-weighting has not been understood. To avoid this fault one must know yin and yang. Sticking is yielding, and yielding is sticking. Yin does not depart from yang, yang does not depart from yin; only when yin and yang aid each other is there understanding of energy. After understanding energy, the more one practises the finer one becomes; silently recognizing and pondering, one gradually arrives at "doing as the heart desires." The root is to "give up oneself and follow others" (舍己从人, shě jǐ cóng rén); most mistake it by giving up the near to seek the far. As it is said, "a hairsbreadth's difference, and the error is a thousand li" — the student must not fail to examine this with care.

Long Boxing (长拳, cháng quán) is like the great Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, flowing on without cease. The Thirteen Postures (十三势, shísān shì) are: warding-off (掤, bēng), roll-back (捋, lǚ), press (挤, jǐ), push (按, àn), pluck (采, cǎi), rend (挒, liè), elbow (肘, zhǒu), lean (靠, kào) — these are the eight trigrams; and advancing step, retreating step, leftward looking, rightward glancing and central equilibrium — these are the five phases. Taken together they make the Thirteen Postures. Warding-off, roll-back, press and push correspond to Kan, Li, Zhen and Dui — the four cardinal directions; pluck, rend, elbow and lean correspond to Qian, Gen, Xun and Kun — the four diagonal corners; advance, retreat, look, glance and settle correspond to metal, wood, water, fire and earth.

II. Wu Yuxiang: A Treatise on Taijiquan Before heaven and earth existed, within the infinite void, there was one undifferentiated qi — this is Wuji, and Wuji gives rise to Taiji. Taiji is the root of heaven and earth, the origin of all things. In Taijiquan, as soon as there is the slightest movement, the whole body must be light and nimble, and above all threaded through. The qi should be stirred and agitated; the spirit (神, shén) should be gathered inward. Let there be no place of defect, no place of bulge or hollow, no place of break or interruption. The root is in the feet, issued through the legs, commanded by the waist (腰, yāo), and expressed in the fingers. From foot to leg to waist, there must always be one complete qi. Only then, advancing and retreating, can one seize the moment and the configuration. If there is any place where one fails to seize the moment and configuration, the body becomes scattered. The fault for this must be sought in the waist and legs. This holds above and below, before and behind, left and right. All of this lies in the intent (意), not outside but within. Where there is above there is below; where there is front there is back; where there is left there is right — if the intent is to rise, then a downward intent is lodged within it. It is like lifting up an object while adding to it the intent of filing it down. Then its root is severed of itself, and one may push it and hasten it without obstruction. Empty and full (虚实, xū shí) must be clearly distinguished. Each place has its own empty and full; every place is altogether this one empty and full. The whole body is threaded joint by joint, with not the slightest hair's-breadth of interruption permitted. (Original note: these were the bequeathed teachings of the venerated Master Zhang Sanfeng of Wudang Mountain, wishing that heroes under heaven might prolong their years and increase their longevity, and not merely make of it the least of the martial arts.)

III. An Explanation of the Heart of Practice in the Thirteen Postures Use the heart to move the qi (以心行气, yǐ xīn xíng qì); one must make it sink and settle, for only then can it be gathered and drawn into the bones. Use the qi to move the body; one must make it smooth and compliant, for only then can it be convenient and follow the heart. If the spirit of vitality can be raised, there is no fear of sluggishness and heaviness — this is what is called the suspended crown (顶头悬, dǐng tóu xuán). The intent and the qi must be changed with nimbleness, for only then is there the delight of roundness and liveliness — this is what is called the transformation of empty and full. In issuing energy (发劲, fā jìn) one must sink and settle, be relaxed and still, and concentrate upon one direction. In standing the body one must be centred, upright, at ease and comfortable, supporting the eight directions; in moving the qi, be like a pearl of nine turnings, with no minute place unreached; in moving, be like steel a hundred times refined, with no hardness it cannot break. In form, like a falcon striking a rabbit; in spirit, like a cat catching a mouse. Still, like a mountain; moving, like a river. Storing energy (蓄劲, is like drawing a bow; issuing energy is like loosing an arrow. Seek the straight within the curved; store and then issue. Force issues from the spine (脊, jǐ); the step changes with the body. Gathering is issuing, and issuing is gathering; broken and then reconnected, going and returning must have folding, advancing and retreating must have conversion. Utterly soft, and thereafter utterly hard; able to breathe, and thereafter able to be nimble. The qi is nourished by straightness and so does no harm; energy is stored by curving and so has surplus. The heart is the command, the qi the banner, the waist the great standard. First seek expansion, then seek compactness, and only then does one arrive at fine closeness.

It is also said: first in the heart, afterward in the body; the belly is relaxed and clean, the qi is gathered into the marrow of the bones. The spirit at ease, the body still — this must be in the heart at every moment. Remember firmly: when one thing moves, there is nothing that does not move; when one thing is still, there is nothing that is not still. In pulling and moving to and fro, the qi clings to the back and is gathered into the spinal bones. Inwardly consolidate the spirit; outwardly show ease and rest. Step like a cat walking; move energy like drawing silk. In the whole body the intent lies in the spirit, not in the qi; to be in the qi is to stagnate. Where there is qi it drags force along; where there is no qi it is purely hard — qi is like the wheel, the waist is like the axle.

IV. Verse of the Thirteen Postures Do not lightly regard the thirteen general postures; The source of life and intent lies in the hollow of the waist. In changing and turning empty and full, take care; Let the qi pervade the body without the least stagnation. In stillness, touched, one moves, yet moving is still as before; Changing according to the opponent, one shows the marvellous. In every posture keep the heart, weigh and use intent; What is attained is won without noticing the effort spent. At every moment keep the heart upon the waist; Within the belly, relaxed and clean, the qi rises up. With the tailbone centred, the spirit runs through the crown; The whole body light and nimble, the crown suspended. Attend with care and seek it out in push-hands; Bending and extending, opening and closing, follow what is natural. To enter the gate and find the road, an oral transmission is needed; The exercise never ceases, and the method is self-cultivated. If you ask what standard governs substance and function: Intent and qi are the ruler, bone and flesh the minister. Consider what the use of intent finally comes to — Prolonging life and lengthening years, a spring that does not age. Sing it, sing it — a hundred and forty words; Every word is true and exact, the meaning leaves nothing out. If you do not seek it out in this direction, Your effort is wasted, and you will be left lamenting.

V. Verse of Push-Hands Warding-off, roll-back, press and push must be taken in earnest; Above and below following one another, the opponent finds it hard to enter.

Let him come at me with giant force; A pull of four ounces deflects a thousand catties. Draw him in to fall into emptiness, and issue as he closes; Stick, connect, continue, follow — neither losing contact nor butting.

VI. Li Yiyu: The Five-Word Formula Stillness of Heart If the heart is not still, it is not single-minded: as soon as one raises a hand, front and back, left and right, there is no fixed direction at all — hence the need for stillness of heart. At first one's movements cannot be governed by oneself; one must calm the heart and experience it in the body, moving as the other moves, following the bend and yielding the extension, neither losing contact nor butting, and not shortening or lengthening of oneself. If he has force, I also have force, and my force is first; if he has no force, I also have force, and my intent is still first. One must keep watch at every moment: wherever contact is made, the heart must be applied there, and one must seek the news within "neither losing contact nor butting." Working on from this, with days and months accumulated, one can then apply it in the body; this is entirely the use of intent, not the use of strength, and in time others are controlled by me, and I am not controlled by others.

Nimbleness of Body If the body is sluggish, one cannot advance and retreat freely — hence the need for nimbleness of body. In raising a hand there must be no appearance of dullness; no sooner does his force begin to intrude upon my skin than my intent has already entered into his bones. The two hands prop each other up, one qi threaded through. When the left is heavy, the left is made empty, and the right has already gone; when the right is heavy, the right is made empty, and the left has already gone. The qi is like a wheel, and the whole body must follow along with it. Where there is any place that does not follow, the body becomes scattered and loses its power; the fault is to be sought in the waist and legs. First use the heart to command the body, following others and not oneself; afterward bring the body to follow the heart, so that although from oneself it still follows others. From oneself, one stagnates; following others, one lives. If one can follow others, the hands have measure. Measure the size of his energy, and not a fraction is mistaken; weigh the length of his coming, and not a hair's-breadth is off. Advancing and retreating, every place fits exactly. The longer the practice, the finer the skill. Gathering of Qi If the qi's force is scattered and diffuse, there is no containment; the body is easily disordered — one must make the qi gather into the spinal bones. Breathing becomes penetrating and numinous, with no gap anywhere in the body. The in-breath is closing (合, hé) and storing (蓄, xù); the out-breath is opening (开, kāi) and issuing (发, fā). For the in-breath can naturally lift up, and can also lift a person up; the out-breath can naturally sink down, and can also send a person out. This is to move the qi by intent, not to move the qi by strength.

Whole Energy The energy of the whole body is trained into a single family. Distinguish clearly between empty and full, and the issuing of energy must have a root. Energy rises from the heels, is governed at the waist, takes form in the fingers, and issues from the spine. Further, one must raise up the whole of one's spirit: at the moment when his energy is about to come out but has not yet issued, my energy has already joined his energy, exactly neither after nor before — like skin catching fire, like a spring gushing forth. Advancing and retreating, there is not the slightest scattering or disorder. Seek the straight within the curved; store and then issue — only thus does it take effect as the hand moves. This is called borrowing force to strike the man, four ounces deflecting a thousand catties.

Gathering of Spirit When the preceding four are all complete, they return altogether to the gathering of spirit (神聚, shén jù). When the spirit is gathered, then the one qi is forged and smelted. Train the qi to return to the spirit, and the momentum of the qi shifts and manoeuvres. The spirit is poured in continuously; opening and closing have their proper order, and empty and full are clear. When the left is empty, the right is full; when the right is empty, the left is full. Empty is not being wholly without force — the momentum of the qi must be able to shift and manoeuvre. Full is not occupying everything to the death — the spirit must value continuous pouring in. The essential point lies entirely in the chest and the waist; the application is not on the outside. Force is borrowed from the other; qi issues from the spine. How can qi issue from the spine? The qi sinks downward, and from the two shoulders is gathered into the spinal bones and poured into the waist — this is the qi going from above to below, and is called closing (合, hé). From the waist it takes form in the spinal bones, spreads to the two arms, and is applied at the fingers — this is the qi going from below to above, and is called opening (开, kāi). Closing is gathering; opening is issuing. If one can understand opening and closing, one knows yin and yang. On reaching this stage, one day of practice brings one day of refinement in skill, until gradually one follows the heart's desire and nothing fails to accord with one's intent.

VII. Secret Formula of Release and Discharge The Four Words: Lifting, Drawing, Loosening, Releasing Lifting opens his energy and borrows his force — within it is the word ling (灵, numinous). Drawing him to the front of the body, his energy then begins to store — within it is the word lian (敛, gathering). Loosening my own energy, do not let it bend — within it is the word jing (静, stillness). At the release, the waist and feet must recognize the target — within it is the word zheng (整, wholeness).

VIII. Essential Words on Practising the Form and Practising the Hands The men of old said: if one can draw the other in to fall into emptiness, one can then four ounces deflect a thousand catties; if one cannot draw the other in to fall into emptiness, one cannot four ounces deflect a thousand catties. The saying is very summary; the beginner has no way to grasp it. I add several phrases to explain it, so that those who have the will for this art may have a point of entry, and so advance a little each day in achievement. If one wishes to draw [the other] in to fall into emptiness and four ounces deflect a thousand catties, one must first know oneself and know the other. If one wishes to know oneself and know the other, one must first give up oneself and follow the other. If one wishes to give up oneself and follow the other, one must first gain the opportunity and gain the position. If one wishes to gain the opportunity and gain the position, one must first make the whole body one family. If one wishes to make the whole body one family, one must first have no flaw anywhere in the whole body. If one wishes to have no flaw anywhere in the whole body, one must first have spirit and qi drumming and surging. If one wishes to have spirit and qi drumming and surging, one must first raise up the spirit. If one wishes to raise up the spirit, one must first keep the spirit from scattering outward. If one wishes to keep the spirit from scattering outward, one must first gather spirit and qi into the bones. If one wishes to gather spirit and qi into the bones, one must first have strength in the front section of the two legs. The two shoulders loosen and open, the qi sinks downward, energy rises from the heels, exchanges in the legs, is contained in the chest, moves in the two shoulders, and is governed in the waist; above it connects with the two arms, below it follows the two legs, and energy changes from within. Gathering is closing; issuing is opening. When still, all is still; stillness is closing, and within closing is lodged opening. When moving, all moves; movement is opening, and within opening is lodged closing. Touch it, and it revolves freely, with nothing that does not gain force — only then can one draw the other in to fall into emptiness and four ounces deflect a thousand catties. Practice of the form on ordinary days is the work of knowing oneself. At each movement one must first ask oneself whether the whole body accords with these several items. If it accords only slightly not, change it at once. This is why in practising the form one wants slowness, not speed. Push-hands is the work of knowing others; stillness and movement are indeed knowing others, yet it is still a question of asking oneself. If one has arranged oneself well, then when the other touches me, I do not move him the least bit, but enter along his tendency, join and fix his energy, and he falls out of himself. If one has a place where one does not gain force, that is double-weighting not yet transformed, and it must be sought in the opening and closing of yin and yang. This is what is called knowing oneself and knowing the other, and in a hundred battles a hundred victories.
